# Apache Spark Metric Views: One Definition for Every Dashboard, Application, and AI Agent

URL: https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/metric-views-spark-42
Republished at: https://openlakehouse.io/blog/apache-spark/metric-views-spark-42
Original publisher: systems/null
Date: 2026-11-23
Category: Apache Spark

import img0 from "./metric-views-spark-42-file.gif";
import img1 from "./metric-views-spark-42-query.gif";
import img2 from "./metric-views-spark-42-define.gif";
import img3 from "./metric-views-spark-42-register.gif";
import img4 from "./metric-views-spark-42-jdbc.gif";
import img5 from "./metric-views-spark-42-dashboard.gif";
import img6 from "./metric-views-spark-42-agent.gif";

*Originally published on [systems/null](https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/metric-views-spark-42).*

[Metric views](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-54119) landed in Spark 4.2 this past summer, and they address a common, hard-to-catch issue in many organizations: incongruent statistics. For instance, a dashboard's revenue figure may differ depending on 1) who owns it and is in charge of the query and 2) the data they are using to calculate it. Agents issuing ad hoc queries indefinitely compound this by creating inconsistent definitions and then circulating them, and a figure itself is hard to judge correctness from without domain knowledge.

An analyst-built dashboard and a vibe-coded dashboard can both look correct when viewed individually. For example, 43% and 57% look equally plausible as a growth percentage, and the hilarious part is that they can *both* be wrong. Then, on top of that, there's the even worse issue of these figures propagating into other computations and not being updated easily. In an ideal world, the analyst writes it once, updates it when they need to update the query itself, and then everyone's agents/applications/dashboards pull from that and get updated automatically.

Lucky for us, Apache Spark 4.2's release has come to save us from this special type of data engineering hell before it gets any more out of hand.

**I defined one metric view, `delivery_metrics`, and then asked Spark SQL, a JDBC client, a dashboard, and a Claude agent for the same conversion rate. All four used the definition stored in Spark's catalog and returned 0.0923 for the month, with the same regional breakdown. Without that definition, valid SQL produced 0.2384, and the raw-table agent began with the wrong year before spending six statements reconstructing the answer.**

A metric view in Spark is a view stored in YAML instead of a script or traditional query. It names a source table, dimensions that queries can group by, and measures, each of which is an aggregate formula with no grouping attached. A query asks for a measure with `MEASURE()` and brings its own `GROUP BY`, and Spark evaluates the formula at the defined level. The formula is written once, queried at any breakdown, and gives the same answer a hand-written query would provide. It sounds complicated, but once you look at the YAML file itself you'll go "Oh, is that it?"

## A metric view in one screen

The definition is one file accessible to Spark, in this case `metrics/delivery_metrics.yaml`:

```yaml
version: 0.1
source: default.sessions
dimensions:
  - name: region
    expr: region
  - name: session_date
    expr: session_date
measures:
  - name: total_sessions
    expr: COUNT(1)
  - name: converted_sessions
    expr: SUM(CAST(converted AS INT))
  - name: conversion_rate
    expr: SUM(CAST(converted AS INT)) / COUNT(1)
  - name: active_users
    expr: COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)
```

<img src={img0} alt="metrics/delivery_metrics.yaml open in nvim: version 0.1, the source, two dimensions and four measures" />

Registering it is one statement with the file's contents between the dollar-sign markers:

```sql
CREATE VIEW default.delivery_metrics WITH METRICS LANGUAGE YAML AS $$
  ...the file...
$$
```

A query names measures with `MEASURE()` and supplies its own grouping:

```sql
SELECT region,
       MEASURE(total_sessions) AS sessions,
       ROUND(MEASURE(conversion_rate), 4) AS conversion_rate,
       MEASURE(active_users) AS active_users
FROM delivery_metrics
GROUP BY region
ORDER BY sessions DESC
```

```
+--------+--------+---------------+------------+
|  region|sessions|conversion_rate|active_users|
+--------+--------+---------------+------------+
|   metro|   50000|         0.0787|        6370|
|   urban|   20000|          0.099|        2519|
|suburban|    8000|         0.1218|         974|
|   rural|     800|         0.3775|          99|
|  remote|     200|          0.515|          32|
+--------+--------+---------------+------------+
```

<img src={img1} alt="Example 04 running beside its queries: the month's conversion rate 0.0923, 9,994 active users and 79,000 sessions, then one row per region and per day" />

Without the `GROUP BY`, the same measures come back for the month: 79,000 sessions, a conversion rate of 0.0923, 9,994 active users. The formula appears in one place and each query evaluates it at its own grain.

That matters because a conversion rate is a ratio and an active-user count is a distinct count; neither can be assembled from smaller pieces. The unweighted average of the five regional rates above is 0.2384, against a monthly rate of 0.0923. The sum of thirty daily active-user counts is 69,420, against 9,994 distinct users in the month. Both wrong answers come from valid SQL that runs without error.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  classDef rows fill:#3a5f96,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#3a5f96,color:#ffffff
  classDef bad fill:#4b5563,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#4b5563,color:#ffffff
  classDef good fill:#d97706,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#d97706,color:#ffffff
  R["five regional rows<br/>metro 50,000 sessions, 0.0787<br/>urban 20,000, 0.0990<br/>suburban 8,000, 0.1218<br/>rural 800, 0.3775<br/>remote 200, 0.5150"]:::rows
  R -->|"AVG(conversion_rate)<br/>every region weighs the same"| A["0.2384<br/>200 remote sessions count<br/>as much as 50,000 metro ones"]:::bad
  R -->|"SUM(converted) / COUNT(1)<br/>over all 79,000 sessions"| B["0.0923<br/>the monthly rate"]:::good
```

## Defining one

A definition is five fields:

| Field | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `version` | The format version; `0.1` in Spark 4.2 |
| `source` | What the measures are computed over: a table, a view, or a SQL query |
| `filter` | Optional. A boolean expression applied to every query of the view |
| `dimensions` | Scalar expressions queries can group and filter by, each with a `name` and an `expr` |
| `measures` | Aggregate expressions with no grouping, each with a `name` and an `expr` |

A measure is any aggregate expression Spark SQL accepts, and a dimension is any scalar expression. `source` can be a query; `metrics/order_metrics.yaml` uses one to join sessions to orders, bake in a filter, derive two dimensions that exist as columns in neither table, and define measures over the join:

```yaml
version: 0.1
source: >
  SELECT s.session_id, s.user_id, s.region, s.session_date, s.converted,
  o.order_id, o.order_total
  FROM default.sessions s LEFT JOIN default.orders o ON s.session_id = o.session_id
filter: region <> 'remote'
dimensions:
  - name: region
    expr: region
  - name: session_date
    expr: session_date
  - name: day_type
    expr: CASE WHEN dayofweek(to_date(session_date)) IN (1, 7) THEN 'weekend' ELSE 'weekday' END
  - name: region_tier
    expr: CASE WHEN region IN ('metro', 'urban') THEN 'core' ELSE 'long_tail' END
measures:
  - name: sessions
    expr: COUNT(1)
  - name: conversion_rate
    expr: SUM(CAST(converted AS INT)) / COUNT(1)
  - name: paying_users
    expr: COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN order_id IS NOT NULL THEN user_id END)
  - name: orders
    expr: COUNT(order_id)
  - name: revenue
    expr: SUM(order_total)
  - name: aov
    expr: SUM(order_total) / NULLIF(COUNT(order_id), 0)
  - name: arppu
    expr: SUM(order_total)
      / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN order_id IS NOT NULL THEN user_id END), 0)
```

<img src={img2} alt="metrics/order_metrics.yaml open in nvim: a SQL source joining sessions to orders, the remote-region filter, the day_type and region_tier dimensions and seven measures" />

The left join keeps sessions that never ordered, so the conversion rate counts them. The filter excludes the remote region from every query of the view. `day_type` and `region_tier` are defined once, in the view. The measures fix the definitions: a paying user is a distinct user with an order, and ARPPU divides revenue by that count. Qualified names (`default.sessions`, not `sessions`) keep the definition meaning the same thing from any current database.

## Registering it in the catalog

Spark reads the catalog object, not the file. `make register` runs `apps/register.py`, which sends the `CREATE VIEW` statement for each file in `metrics/` (dropping any existing view first, since `OR REPLACE` doesn't replace a metric view in 4.2.0) and describes the result. Spark plans the aggregation at create time to infer each column's type. A measure with no aggregate, or a reference to a column the source lacks, fails at registration rather than at the first query:

```
default.delivery_metrics  <-  metrics/delivery_metrics.yaml
    region               string
    session_date         string
    total_sessions       bigint
    converted_sessions   bigint
    conversion_rate      double
    active_users         bigint
```

<img src={img3} alt="apps/register.py on its register function, run on both YAML files: each view is created WITH METRICS and its dimensions and measures are listed with their types" />

From then on the definition has the catalog-backed lifetime and discovery of a view. It appears in `SHOW VIEWS`, `DESCRIBE TABLE` lists dimensions and measures as typed columns, and `DESCRIBE TABLE EXTENDED` shows `Type: METRIC_VIEW` with the YAML itself under `View Text`. The dashboard and the agent in the demo both read the definition from there.

The demo's server keeps its catalog in a Hive metastore on a Docker volume, so a view registered from one session is visible to every session and survives a restart. On another deployment it is an entry in whatever catalog Spark already uses.

## Querying at any grain

`measure` is registered as an aggregate function, but it never runs. The analyzer finds an aggregate sitting on a metric view, looks each `MEASURE(name)` up in the definition, substitutes the formula, projects the source through the dimension expressions, and hands the optimizer an ordinary aggregation. The query's `GROUP BY` sets the grain because it is the only `GROUP BY` in the plan.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  classDef you fill:#9a7b00,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#9a7b00,color:#ffffff
  classDef def fill:#c0661a,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#c0661a,color:#ffffff
  classDef plan fill:#3a5f96,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#3a5f96,color:#ffffff
  classDef out fill:#d97706,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#d97706,color:#ffffff
  Q["your query<br/>SELECT region, MEASURE(conversion_rate)<br/>FROM delivery_metrics GROUP BY region"]:::you
  D["definition stored with delivery_metrics<br/>source: sessions<br/>conversion_rate: SUM(CAST(converted AS INT)) / COUNT(1)"]:::def
  P["what the analyzer hands the optimizer<br/>SELECT region, SUM(CAST(converted AS INT)) / COUNT(1)<br/>FROM sessions GROUP BY region"]:::plan
  O["one conversion rate per region<br/>metro 0.0787 · urban 0.0990 · suburban 0.1218 · rural 0.3775 · remote 0.5150"]:::out
  Q -->|"MEASURE(conversion_rate) is looked up"| P
  D -->|"and replaced by this expression"| P
  P -->|"evaluated at the query's grain"| O
```

`EXPLAIN` confirms it. The optimized plan contains no metric view, only an aggregate over the two columns the measure needs:

```
== Optimized Logical Plan ==
Aggregate [region], [region, round((cast(sum(cast(converted as int)) as double) / cast(count(1) as double)), 4) AS conversion_rate]
+- Project [converted, region]
   +- Relation spark_catalog.default.sessions[...] parquet
```

That is the plan a hand-written aggregate query produces, with the same column pruning and partial aggregation. The optimized plan has no metric-view operator; execution receives the same aggregate plan as the hand-written query.

Filters on dimensions and on source columns, `GROUP BY ALL`, `MEASURE()` inside expressions, aliases in `HAVING` and `ORDER BY`, and `F.expr("measure(active_users)")` from the DataFrame API all work.

One rule follows from the rewrite: a measure is evaluated at the grain of the query that calls `MEASURE()`, and its result is an ordinary column after that. Rolling a `MEASURE()` result up in an outer query aggregates that column, not the measure. Ask for each number at the grain it will be shown.

## Using it from everywhere

The view is in the catalog, so anything that can send SQL to the server can use it, and none of them needs to know how a measure is computed. I used the same `default.delivery_metrics` definition in four contexts; this was not four implementations of conversion rate, but four clients asking Spark for the same catalog measure:

| Client | What it asked for | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Spark SQL | Monthly and regional `MEASURE(conversion_rate)` | 0.0923 overall; metro 0.0787, urban 0.0990, suburban 0.1218, rural 0.3775, remote 0.5150 |
| Command-line JDBC client | Regional `MEASURE(conversion_rate)` | The same five regional rates |
| Streamlit dashboard | The measures and `region` dimension discovered from the catalog | The same five regional rates, rendered as a table and chart |
| Claude agent | June conversion rate overall and by region | 0.0923 overall and the same five regional rates, in two statements |

The agreement is the point. The SQL client, dashboard and agent do not carry separate copies of the formula `SUM(CAST(converted AS INT)) / COUNT(1)`; they carry a request for `conversion_rate`, and Spark resolves that request from the one definition above.

| Client | What it is | What it needs |
|---|---|---|
| `make jdbc` | A command-line client using Spark Connect's JDBC driver | The driver jar; any BI tool with a JDBC connection is in the same position |
| `make dashboard` | A Streamlit page that discovers metric views in the catalog and renders them | The dimension and measure names from `DESCRIBE` |
| `make agent` | A Claude agent with one `run_sql` tool | The views' YAML in its context, and a rule to ask at the right grain |

**JDBC, with no Python at all.** `apps/jdbc.sh` fetches `spark-connect-client-jdbc` from Maven Central and runs a command-line JDBC client (Beeline) from the Spark image:

```bash
make jdbc SQL="SELECT region, MEASURE(total_sessions) AS sessions,
  ROUND(MEASURE(conversion_rate), 4) AS conversion_rate, MEASURE(active_users) AS active_users
  FROM delivery_metrics GROUP BY region ORDER BY sessions DESC"
```

```
+-----------+-----------+------------------+---------------+
|  region   | sessions  | conversion_rate  | active_users  |
+-----------+-----------+------------------+---------------+
| metro     | 50000     | 0.0787           | 6370          |
| urban     | 20000     | 0.099            | 2519          |
| suburban  | 8000      | 0.1218           | 974           |
| rural     | 800       | 0.3775           | 99            |
| remote    | 200       | 0.515            | 32            |
+-----------+-----------+------------------+---------------+
```

<img src={img4} alt="make jdbc running a MEASURE query through a command-line JDBC client over jdbc:sc://, printing the by-region table" />

**A dashboard with no formula in it.** `apps/dashboard.py` asks the catalog which views are metric views, reads each one's YAML, offers the dimensions and measures as controls, and runs the `MEASURE()` query for whatever is picked. A measure added to the file and registered with `make register` appears in the dropdown with no change to the dashboard.

```python
for view in spark.sql("SHOW VIEWS").collect():
    name = f"{view.namespace}.{view.viewName}"
    info = {r.col_name: r.data_type for r in spark.sql(f"DESCRIBE TABLE EXTENDED {name}").collect()}
    if info.get("Type") == "METRIC_VIEW":
        definition = yaml.safe_load(info["View Text"])
```

With `default.delivery_metrics` selected, `region` as the group-by and three measures ticked, the page runs this and draws the result as a table and a bar chart, with the definition it read from the catalog in a collapsed section underneath:

```sql
SELECT region,
       MEASURE(total_sessions)     AS total_sessions,
       MEASURE(converted_sessions) AS converted_sessions,
       MEASURE(conversion_rate)    AS conversion_rate
FROM default.delivery_metrics
GROUP BY region ORDER BY total_sessions DESC
```

```
+--------+--------------+------------------+---------------+
|  region|total_sessions|converted_sessions|conversion_rate|
+--------+--------------+------------------+---------------+
|   metro|         50000|              3937|         0.0787|
|   urban|         20000|              1979|          0.099|
|suburban|          8000|               974|         0.1218|
|   rural|           800|               302|         0.3775|
|  remote|           200|               103|          0.515|
+--------+--------------+------------------+---------------+
```

<img src={img5} alt="The Streamlit dashboard on default.delivery_metrics: one measure is removed, the table and query update, and the definition read from the catalog opens underneath" />

**An agent using the same view.** `apps/agent.py` gives Claude one tool, `run_sql`, the metric views' definitions read from the catalog, and one rule: ask for a measure at the grain the answer needs. When I asked for June's conversion rate overall and by region, it used `default.delivery_metrics` twice: once at the regional grain and once for the month.

```sql
SELECT region,
       MEASURE(conversion_rate) AS conversion_rate,
       MEASURE(total_sessions) AS sessions
FROM default.delivery_metrics
GROUP BY region
ORDER BY region;

SELECT MEASURE(conversion_rate) AS conversion_rate,
       MEASURE(total_sessions) AS sessions
FROM default.delivery_metrics;
```

The answer was 0.0923 overall across 79,000 sessions, followed by the same regional rates returned by Spark SQL, JDBC and the dashboard. With only the raw tables, the same model's first statement filtered for June **2024**, returned no rows because the data was from 2026, and then needed five more statements to inspect the date range, calculate the rates and verify the `converted` flag against the orders table. It eventually got the right answer, but only after reconstructing context and business logic that the metric view supplied immediately.

**A harder agent question.** The second definition, `default.order_metrics`, tests semantics that cannot be inferred from column names alone. I asked:

```text
$ make agent Q="What's the average order value and revenue per paying user
                for core regions on weekends?"

[sql]
SELECT MEASURE(aov) AS aov, MEASURE(arppu) AS arppu, MEASURE(revenue) AS revenue,
       MEASURE(orders) AS orders, MEASURE(paying_users) AS paying_users
FROM default.order_metrics WHERE region_tier = 'core' AND day_type = 'weekend'

[answer]
For weekend sessions in core regions (metro and urban):
- Average order value: about $31.52. That's $49,020.84 in revenue across 1,555 orders.
- Revenue per paying user: about $34.35. That's the same revenue across 1,427 paying users.
```

<img src={img6} alt="make agent asking for average order value and revenue per paying user in core regions on weekends: the agent runs one MEASURE query over order_metrics and answers 31.52 and 34.35" />

One statement at the right grain, checkable without re-deriving it. The agent was not told what "core" means or what a paying user is; both definitions came from the catalog. With only the tables, it needed eight statements, including five attempts to find and read the metric view definition so it could discover that `core` meant metro and urban.

## The agent with and without the metric view

The script has a second mode, `--context tables`, that shows the model only the raw tables. Same model, same tool, same questions:

| Question | With the metric view | With only the tables |
|---|---|---|
| Conversion rate, overall and by region | 2 statements, both `MEASURE()` | 6, including a wrong-year filter, a date-range check, and a join to verify the flag |
| Users active in June | 2 | 2, plus the sum of the daily counts, computed to show why not to use it |
| AOV and ARPPU for core regions on weekends | 1 | 8, five of them finding and reading the metric view's definition in the catalog to learn what "core" means |

The model eventually got every number right both ways, but that final correctness hides the experiment. With the metric views, it issued short queries against named measures whose definitions were already fixed. With only the tables, it guessed the wrong year, explored the schema, verified flags and searched the catalog for the meaning of a business term. The metric view changed the shape of the work: one definition reused by every client, SQL that is checkable without re-deriving its business logic, and an agent that can ask for a metric instead of inventing one. Full transcripts are in [`apps/RUNS.md`](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-demos/blob/main/demos/01_metrics_views/apps/RUNS.md).

## Get started

The demo needs Docker, [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), Make, and an Anthropic API key for the agent:

```bash
make setup           # client venv, plus streamlit and the anthropic SDK
make data            # generate the dataset
make up              # Spark Connect on apache/spark:4.2.0, Hive metastore on a volume
make register        # metrics/*.yaml into the catalog
make jdbc SQL="..."  # beeline over jdbc:sc://
make dashboard       # http://localhost:8501
make agent Q="..."   # add CONTEXT=tables to hide the metric views from it
```

- [spark-demos/01_metrics_views](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-demos/tree/main/demos/01_metrics_views): the definitions, the register script, the JDBC wrapper, the dashboard, the agent and its transcripts, and the tests that pin every number quoted from the demo
- [SPARK-54119](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-54119), the epic, with the [SPIP](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1xVTLijvDTJ90lZ_ujwzf9HvBJgWg0mY6cYM44Fcghl0/edit) by Linhong Liu, Can Efeoglu, Justin Talbot, Gengliang Wang, Liang-Chi Hsieh and Daniel Tenedorio
- [Databricks metric views](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/metric-views/), where the format is heading: declared joins, window measures, composed measures

The useful part is still the simple one: I defined conversion rate once, then Spark SQL, JDBC, a dashboard and an agent all asked for it at the grain where they needed to show it. That is a much better boundary for an agent-native data system than hoping every client independently writes the same correct SQL.

---

# The Top 10 Data Engines in 2026, and What Each One Is Actually For

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/blog/apache-spark/top-10-data-engines-2026
Date: 2026-11-22
Category: Apache Spark

**Short answer:** the top data engines in 2026 are **Apache Spark** (general purpose batch, streaming and pipelines at any scale), **Apache Flink** (event-at-a-time streaming), **DuckDB** (single-node analytics), **Trino** (federated SQL over a lakehouse), **Apache DataFusion** (an embeddable query engine for building other engines), **Polars** (single-node DataFrames), **ClickHouse** (real-time analytical serving), **StarRocks** (low-latency lakehouse queries), **Ray** (distributed Python and multimodal AI data) and **Velox** (a native execution library that speeds up other engines). Spark ranks first because it is the only open engine that covers batch, low-latency streaming, declarative pipelines and remote multi-language clients over the same open tables.

---

Every year someone publishes a "top data engineering tools" list, and every year it's a logo wall: an orchestrator next to a BI tool next to a vector database next to a catalog, ranked by vibes. I wanted to write a narrower one, about engines specifically (the thing that actually reads your files, plans a query and runs it), because that's where the interesting change happened over the last couple of years, and because it's the decision people keep getting wrong in the same way. I've tried to make the case for my first pick on things you can check rather than on loyalty.

The change is this: open table formats (Apache Iceberg and Delta Lake, plus the REST catalogs in front of them) made storage engine-neutral, so the same table can be written by Spark, queried by Trino, poked at by DuckDB on a laptop and served by StarRocks without anyone copying it. I went through exactly that in [How to Build an Open Lakehouse on Your Laptop](https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/open-lakehouse-on-your-laptop) and again in [Spark Connect from Rust: Pull Spark outputs into DuckDB and Polars](https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/spark-connect-rust-duckdb-polars), where Spark, DuckDB and Polars ended up passing the same Arrow data around like it was nothing. Once the data stops belonging to an engine, the old question ("which platform do we standardize on?") stops making sense.

**My thesis: because open table formats made storage engine-neutral, a 2026 engine should be chosen by the shape of the workload rather than by where the data lives, and Spark ranks first because it is the only open engine that covers every shape (batch, streaming, pipelines and remote clients) well enough to be the default, with every other engine on this list best understood by the one shape it does better than Spark.**

## How I ranked them

The ranking weighs four things: how many distinct workload shapes an engine handles well, whether it reads and writes open tables (Iceberg or Delta) natively, how mature and widely deployed it is, and how actively it's developed this year. Versions and dates below were checked on 22 November 2026.

| Rank | Engine | Shape it's best at | Scale | Open table formats | Current release (Nov 2026) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Apache Spark | Batch, streaming, pipelines, ML prep | Laptop to thousands of nodes | Iceberg, Delta (read and write) | 4.3.0 |
| 2 | Apache Flink | Event-at-a-time streaming | Cluster | Iceberg, Paimon | 2.2.1 |
| 3 | DuckDB | Interactive single-node analytics | One machine | Iceberg, Delta, DuckLake | 2.0.0 LTS |
| 4 | Trino | Federated interactive SQL | Cluster | Iceberg, Delta, Hive | 48x line |
| 5 | Apache DataFusion | Embedded query engine (a library) | Library | Via integrations | 55.x |
| 6 | Polars | Single-node DataFrames | One machine (plus Polars Cloud) | Iceberg, Delta | 2.0 line |
| 7 | ClickHouse | Real-time analytical serving | Cluster | Iceberg read and write | 26.x |
| 8 | StarRocks | Low-latency lakehouse SQL | Cluster | Iceberg (native writes since 4.0) | 4.x |
| 9 | Ray | Distributed Python, multimodal AI data | Cluster, GPU-heavy | Iceberg, Delta via Ray Data | |
| 10 | Velox | Native vectorized execution (a library) | Library | Through host engine | |

---

## 1. Apache Spark: the default engine for everything that isn't a special case

Spark is first because, as of [Spark 4.3](https://www.databricks.com/blog/introducing-apache-spark-43-now-available-databricks-runtime-19) (released at the end of October 2026, and the first release on Spark's new quarterly train), it's the only open engine where batch ETL, low-latency streaming, declarative pipelines and SQL all run over the same open tables with one execution model, and that breadth is precisely what you want in a default. The headline of 4.3 is stateful [Real-Time Mode](https://apache.github.io/spark/streaming/real-time-mode.html): Structured Streaming can now run aggregations, deduplication and `transformWithState` with sub-second latency (Databricks reported P99 end-to-end latencies of 136 to 141 ms across their three benchmarks), which removes the single most common reason teams ran Flink beside Spark. I walked through that in [Introducing Real-time Mode's Stateful Queries on Spark](https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/real-time-mode-spark-43), and the rest of the release (ASOF JOIN in SQL, nanosecond timestamps, Variant improvements) is in [The Ultimate Guide to Apache Spark 4.3](https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/ultimate-guide-spark-43).

The other two things that changed Spark's position are less flashy. [Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/declarative-pipelines-programming-guide.html) let you declare tables and flows and have Spark work out the order, retries and incremental processing (with AUTO CDC turning a change feed into current state, which I covered in [AUTO CDC with Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/auto-cdc-declarative-pipelines)), and Spark Connect split the client from the server, so a job can be driven from Python, Scala, Go, Rust or even OCaml without carrying a JVM around in your process ([An Idiot's Guide to Spark Connect Clients](https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/idiots-guide-spark-connect-clients) has the full tour).

- **Best for:** the bulk of a lakehouse's ETL; anything that has to scale past one machine; teams that want batch and streaming on one engine; feature and training-data preparation.
- **Not ideal for:** sub-second interactive dashboards on small data (cluster startup and query planning overhead dominate), or a quick query on a laptop, where DuckDB or Polars will beat it on wall clock.

```python
# A stateful count per user in Real-Time Mode (Spark 4.3); swap the trigger
# for processingTime=... and the same code runs as ordinary micro-batches
events = (spark.readStream.format("kafka")
          .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "broker:9092")
          .option("subscribe", "events").load())
(events.selectExpr("CAST(key AS STRING) AS user_id")
   .groupBy("user_id").count()
   .selectExpr("user_id AS key", "CAST(count AS STRING) AS value")
   .writeStream.format("kafka")
   .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "broker:9092")
   .option("topic", "user_counts")
   .option("checkpointLocation", "/chk/user_counts")
   .outputMode("update")                 # Real-Time Mode requires update
   .trigger(realTime="30 seconds")       # checkpoint interval; records don't wait for it
   .start())
```

## 2. Apache Flink: still the specialist for event-at-a-time streaming

Flink remains the engine built from the ground up for streams, with record-at-a-time processing, mature event-time semantics and very fine control over state and checkpoints, which is why it's still the choice for complex event processing and long-lived stateful applications. [Flink 2.2](https://flink.apache.org/2025/12/04/apache-flink-2.2.0-advancing-real-time-data--ai-and-empowering-stream-processing-for-the-ai-era/) (December 2025, with the 2.2.1 bug fix release in May 2026) leaned into AI with `VECTOR_SEARCH` in Flink SQL and Materialized Tables, and AWS's managed Flink picked up 2.2 in March. The honest pressure on Flink in 2026 is that Spark's Real-Time Mode now covers the common stateful cases, so the question for a new project is whether you need Flink's lower-level control or just low latency.

- **Best for:** fraud detection, CEP, event-driven applications, very large keyed state.
- **Not ideal for:** batch-heavy teams who'd be running a second engine only for streaming.

## 3. DuckDB: the laptop that ate the small cluster

DuckDB is the in-process analytical database that made "just run it locally" a serious answer for datasets that used to get a cluster by reflex, and it ranks third because a surprising share of real analytical work fits on one machine. [DuckDB 2.0.0 LTS](https://duckdb.org/2026/10/21/announcing-duckdb-200) arrived on 21 October 2026 as a feature release with breaking changes (and, sensibly, its own team is telling people to wait for the first patch before production), alongside the Quack protocol and continued work on Iceberg, Delta and its own DuckLake format.

- **Best for:** interactive analysis, local development against lakehouse tables, embedded analytics in apps, CI tests for pipelines.
- **Not ideal for:** data that doesn't fit on one machine's disk, or concurrent writers.

## 4. Trino: SQL across everything you already have

Trino is the federated SQL engine: one query can join an Iceberg table, a Postgres table and a Kafka topic, which is why it's the default interactive layer over many lakehouses. Its 2026 releases added [Python UDFs](https://trino.io/docs/current/release/release-481), Iceberg v3 geometry and geography types, and the [PIVOT clause](https://trino.io/docs/current/release/release-483.html).

- **Best for:** ad hoc and BI queries across many sources without moving data.
- **Not ideal for:** long-running, failure-prone ETL (it's improved here with fault-tolerant execution, but Spark is still the more natural fit).

## 5. Apache DataFusion: the engine people build engines on

DataFusion is a Rust query engine shipped as a library, and it's on this list because a growing number of the systems you use are DataFusion underneath, which makes it infrastructure rather than a product. The [Comet](https://datafusion.apache.org/blog/2026/08/07/datafusion-comet-1.0.0) accelerator for Spark, which swaps Spark's JVM operators for native DataFusion ones, reached 1.0 in August 2026 and started following semantic versioning, and the core project is on its 55.x line.

- **Best for:** teams building a database, a query service or a domain-specific engine.
- **Not ideal for:** anyone who wants an engine to run, rather than to build with.

## 6. Polars: DataFrames that finally replaced pandas for serious work

Polars is the Rust DataFrame library with a lazy query optimizer, and its 2.0 line makes the [streaming engine the default](https://pola.rs/posts/announcing-polars-2/), so out-of-core work on one machine is the normal path rather than an opt-in (with the caveat that the streaming engine doesn't preserve row order by default for joins and group-bys, which will surprise somebody). [Polars Cloud](https://pola.rs/posts/polars-cloud-launch) adds distributed execution, though that's still young next to Spark.

- **Best for:** Python data work on one machine, feature engineering, replacing pandas.
- **Not ideal for:** multi-node production pipelines today.

## 7. ClickHouse: real-time analytics you can put behind a product

ClickHouse is the columnar database built for fast aggregations on fresh data, which is why it ends up powering observability tools and customer-facing dashboards. Its move toward the lakehouse is the 2026 story: it [added full insert, delete, update and schema changes on Iceberg tables](https://clickhouse.com/blog/clickhouse-is-data-lake-ready), so it can serve open tables rather than only its own storage.

- **Best for:** user-facing analytics, logs and metrics, high-concurrency queries on recent data.
- **Not ideal for:** heavy multi-stage transformations and large joins.

## 8. StarRocks: the low-latency query layer for the lakehouse

StarRocks is an MPP SQL engine that competes with Trino and ClickHouse for sub-second queries directly on Iceberg, with native Iceberg writes since 4.0, a cost-based optimizer and materialized views that it rewrites queries against automatically.

- **Best for:** dashboards and serving workloads that must query lakehouse tables directly at low latency.
- **Not ideal for:** general ETL.

## 9. Ray: the engine for Python and GPUs, where AI data lives

Ray is a distributed runtime for Python, and Ray Data is its data processing layer, built for the workloads tabular engines handle badly: images, audio, video and documents flowing through GPU models for embedding, inference and training. It's here because AI data pipelines are now a real share of data engineering, and the usual pattern is Spark preparing tabular data and Ray handling the GPU-heavy, multimodal step.

- **Best for:** batch inference, embedding pipelines, multimodal preprocessing.
- **Not ideal for:** SQL-shaped analytics and classic ETL.

## 10. Velox: the execution layer hiding inside other engines

Velox, from Meta, is a C++ library of vectorized operators that other engines plug in to replace their own execution, and it closes the list because it's the clearest sign of where engines are heading: Apache Gluten uses it to run Spark plans natively, and Presto's native workers run on it. Like DataFusion, you're more likely to use Velox without knowing it than to choose it directly.

- **Best for:** engine builders and platform teams accelerating Spark or Presto.
- **Not ideal for:** anyone looking for something to run by itself.

---

## How to choose a data engine in 2026

Most teams end up with two or three engines over the same open tables, and that's fine (it's the point of open tables), but there should be one default and a clear reason for each addition. In order:

1. **Does the data fit on one machine?** If yes, start with DuckDB or Polars and add nothing until something breaks.
2. **Is it ETL, pipelines, or anything bigger than one machine?** Use Spark; with Real-Time Mode in 4.3, that includes most streaming.
3. **Do you need event-at-a-time processing with very fine state control?** Add Flink.
4. **Do analysts need interactive SQL across many sources?** Add Trino.
5. **Are you serving queries to users or dashboards at sub-second latency?** Add ClickHouse or StarRocks.
6. **Is the data images, audio or text going through GPU models?** Add Ray.
7. **Are you building an engine yourself?** Start from DataFusion or Velox.

The only real mistake left is letting an engine own your data. Keep the tables in Iceberg or Delta behind an open catalog and every choice above becomes reversible, which is a better position than any single engine on this list can give you on its own.

## FAQ

**What is the most popular data engine in 2026?**
Apache Spark is still the most widely deployed engine for large-scale data processing, and with Spark 4.3 it covers batch, low-latency streaming and declarative pipelines in one engine.

**Is DuckDB replacing Spark?**
No. DuckDB replaces Spark for work that fits on one machine, which is more work than people assumed; Spark is still the tool when data or concurrency outgrows a single node, and the two read the same Iceberg and Delta tables, so most teams use both.

**Spark or Flink for streaming in 2026?**
For most new projects, Spark: Real-Time Mode in Spark 4.3 handles stateful aggregations, deduplication and custom state at sub-second latency. Choose Flink when you need record-at-a-time semantics or very fine control over state and checkpoints.

**What's the difference between a data engine and a data engineering tool?**
An engine reads data, plans and executes queries (Spark, DuckDB, Trino). Tools around it orchestrate (Airflow), catalog (Unity Catalog, Polaris), store tables (Iceberg, Delta) or transform via SQL models (dbt), and those rely on an engine to do the actual work.

**Which data engines support Apache Iceberg?**
All ten on this list can work with Iceberg directly or through a host engine; Spark, Flink, Trino, StarRocks and ClickHouse support both reading and writing.

## Further reading

- [The Ultimate Guide to Apache Spark 4.3](https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/ultimate-guide-spark-43): everything new in Spark 4.3, with runnable demos.
- [Introducing Real-time Mode's Stateful Queries on Spark](https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/real-time-mode-spark-43): what stateful Real-Time Mode does, measured.
- [Spark Connect from Rust: Pull Spark outputs into DuckDB and Polars](https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/spark-connect-rust-duckdb-polars): Spark, DuckDB and Polars sharing the same Arrow data.
- [How to Build an Open Lakehouse on Your Laptop](https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/open-lakehouse-on-your-laptop): running several of these engines over one open lakehouse at home.
- [Apache Spark 4.3 announcement](https://www.databricks.com/blog/introducing-apache-spark-43-now-available-databricks-runtime-19): the release overview and Real-Time Mode benchmarks.
- [DuckDB 2.0.0 announcement](https://duckdb.org/2026/10/21/announcing-duckdb-200): the LTS release and its breaking changes.

# Introducing Real-time Mode's Stateful Queries on Spark

URL: https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/real-time-mode-spark-43
Republished at: https://openlakehouse.io/blog/apache-spark/real-time-mode-spark-43
Original publisher: systems/null
Date: 2026-11-17
Category: Apache Spark

import img0 from "./real-time-mode-spark-43-basics.gif";
import img1 from "./real-time-mode-spark-43-trigger.gif";
import img2 from "./real-time-mode-spark-43-stateful.gif";
import img3 from "./real-time-mode-spark-43-processor.gif";
import img4 from "./real-time-mode-spark-43-grade.gif";
import img5 from "./real-time-mode-spark-43-live.gif";

*Originally published on [systems/null](https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/real-time-mode-spark-43).*

## Spark 4.3 is out, and Real-time Mode does state now (!!)

Spark 4.3.0 landed on PyPI and Maven Central at the end of October, and for anyone who works on streaming the headline is pretty easy to pick out of the release: Real-time Mode, which arrived in 4.1 as millisecond Structured Streaming for stateless queries only, can now run stateful queries too (deduplication, aggregations, and the JVM `transformWithState` API). This is what makes it applicable to workloads such as fraud scores, sessions, alerts and recommendations, all of which need to retain state between records.

A Real-time query uses the same DataFrame or Dataset transformations, state store and checkpointing model as a micro-batch query, but it keeps its tasks running and processes records as they arrive instead of scheduling a fresh set of tasks for every small batch. Spark 4.3 extends that model across a shuffle, which is what lets a record reach the task that owns its key and update state without waiting for the batch to finish.

**Real-time Mode changes what sets the latency of a Structured Streaming query: a record no longer waits for Spark to schedule its batch, so its latency is determined by the work it touches on its way through the pipeline.** That is why a per-shopper recommender that scores a few thousand books on every click can answer in milliseconds, but it is also why the remaining waits, including network buffering, state access and checkpoint boundaries, are worth understanding before you put it in front of anything.

So this post starts from Structured Streaming basics in the default micro-batch mode, then moves the same kinds of queries to Real-time Mode, then makes them stateful, and ends with a recommender written with `transformWithState` that keeps a taste vector per shopper. Each step is a runnable file in [spark-demos](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-demos/tree/main/demos/14_real_time_mode), and every latency here comes out of one script (`bin/bench.sh`) run against Spark 4.3.0 on one Linux machine, recorded in the demo's `NOTES.md`.

## Example: a bookshop that re-ranks while you browse

The shop sells 5,817 books from [Project Gutenberg's catalog](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/offline_catalogs.html), sorted into twelve aisles (Poetry, Romance, Science-Fiction & Fantasy, Cooking & Drinking and so on, from Gutenberg's own "Category" bookshelves). A generator plays 200 shoppers, each with one or two favourite aisles that Spark never gets to see; most of a shopper's clicks land in a favourite aisle and the rest land anywhere, every click is a view, a cart add or a purchase, and a small share of events get sent twice with the same `event_id`, the way a retrying mobile client would. Clicks go to a Kafka topic, and each step reads them from there.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  classDef old fill:#4b5563,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#4b5563,color:#ffffff
  classDef new fill:#d97706,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#d97706,color:#ffffff
  classDef jvm fill:#3a5f96,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#3a5f96,color:#ffffff
  gen[shoppers.py<br/>200 shoppers] --> clicks[(clicks)]
  cat[catalog.parquet<br/>5,817 books + embeddings]
  clicks --> s1[Step 1: console<br/>micro-batch]
  clicks --> s2[Step 2: enrich<br/>stream-static join] --> enriched[(enriched)]
  clicks --> s3[Step 3: dedup +<br/>windowed count] --> trending[(trending)]
  clicks --> s4[Step 4: recommender<br/>transformWithState] --> recs[(recs)]
  cat -.broadcast.-> s2
  cat -.broadcast.-> s3
  cat -.broadcast.-> s4
  class gen,clicks,enriched,trending,recs,cat old
  class s1,s2,s3 new
  class s4 jvm
```

Before any streaming happens there's a batch step, `00_build_catalog.py`, that reads the catalog CSV, keeps English texts that sit in exactly one of the twelve aisles (up to 500 per aisle, picked by a hash so reruns get the same books), and embeds each book's title, author and subject headings with [`BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5`](https://huggingface.co/BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5) (384 dimensions) inside Spark, using `mapInPandas` and [fastembed](https://github.com/qdrant/fastembed) so each task loads the model once and embeds its rows in batches. The aisle label is deliberately left out of the embedded text, so when the recommender later puts a shopper's picks in their favourite aisles it's because the subjects and titles are similar, not because it read the answer key.

```python
def embed(batches: Iterator[pd.DataFrame]) -> Iterator[pd.DataFrame]:
    from fastembed import TextEmbedding
    model = TextEmbedding(MODEL, cache_dir=str(DATA / "models"), threads=1)   # one core per Spark task
    for pdf in batches:
        vectors = list(model.embed(pdf["text"].tolist(), batch_size=64))
        yield pdf.drop(columns=["text"]).assign(vector=[v.astype("float32").tolist() for v in vectors])

shop.mapInPandas(embed, "book_id long, title string, author string, aisle string, vector array<float>")
```

The embedding is the expensive, model-shaped part of the personalisation, and it happens once, offline, in batch; what the streaming side does per click is arithmetic against those vectors. That split isn't only a design preference, it's forced by Real-time Mode, which I'll come back to.

## Step 1: Structured Streaming basics

Structured Streaming treats a stream as a table that keeps growing: `readStream` gives you a DataFrame over it, you write ordinary DataFrame code against that DataFrame, and `writeStream` keeps running that code on each new slice of input. In the default execution mode each slice is a micro-batch, a small batch job that Spark plans, schedules as a fresh set of tasks, runs over the offsets that arrived since the last one, and commits to the checkpoint before planning the next.

```python
raw = (s.readStream.format("kafka")
       .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP)
       .option("subscribe", "clicks")
       .option("startingOffsets", "latest")
       .load())

clicks = (raw.select(F.from_json(F.col("value").cast("string"), CLICK_SCHEMA).alias("c"))
          .select("c.*")
          .where(F.col("action").isin("cart", "purchase"))
          .select("user_id", "book_id", "action", F.timestamp_millis("ts").alias("clicked_at")))

q = (clicks.writeStream.format("console")
     .option("checkpointLocation", str(CHECKPOINTS / "01-basics"))
     .outputMode("append")
     .trigger(processingTime="5 seconds")
     .start())
```

The source hands records over with their Kafka partition and offset, which lets Spark track what it has and has not processed, while the transformation remains ordinary DataFrame code; neither `from_json` nor `where` knows that its input is streaming. The trigger decides when the next micro-batch starts (every 5 seconds here; `processingTime="0 seconds"` means back to back, as fast as they go), and the checkpoint records the query's progress and, for a stateful query, its state so it can resume after a restart. The output mode (`append`, `update` or `complete`) determines which rows of the result table each batch writes; it does not make much difference for this filter, but it will once the query begins updating state.

```text
-------------------------------------------
Batch: 1
-------------------------------------------
+-------+-------+------+-----------------------+
|user_id|book_id|action|clicked_at             |
+-------+-------+------+-----------------------+
|u0178  |4745   |cart  |2026-11-04 21:22:40.141|
|u0099  |32495  |cart  |2026-11-04 21:22:40.041|
|u0136  |47805  |cart  |2026-11-04 21:22:40.166|
|u0196  |13184  |cart  |2026-11-04 21:22:39.616|
```

<img src={img0} alt="real-time-mode-spark-43-basics" />

The cost of the micro-batch model is in how it works: every batch pays for planning, task scheduling and a commit, and every record waits for the batch it lands in. That fixed work puts a practical floor under latency, which [the Spark 4.3 Real-time Mode docs](https://spark.apache.org/docs/4.3.0/streaming/real-time-mode.html) put at roughly 100 ms.

## Step 2: The same query in Real-time Mode

Real-time Mode keeps the API and changes the execution: instead of launching short tasks for every slice, it launches one long-running task per Kafka partition, and those tasks stay up for the length of a (long) batch and process records as they arrive. Records flow source to transformation to sink without waiting for a batch boundary, so the batch duration stops being a latency setting and becomes, mostly, a checkpoint interval; the default is 5 minutes, and records still come out in milliseconds.

Step 2 enriches every click with the book's title and aisle through a stream-static join, and writes the result to another Kafka topic. Turning it into a Real-time query is a trigger change, plus the `update` output mode Real-time Mode requires:

```python
books = s.read.parquet(CATALOG).select("book_id", "title", "author", "aisle")

enriched = (clicks.join(F.broadcast(books), "book_id")
            .select(F.col("user_id").alias("key"),
                    F.to_json(F.struct("event_id", "user_id", "action", "ts", "book_id",
                                       "title", "aisle")).alias("value")))

w = (enriched.writeStream.format("kafka")
     .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP)
     .option("topic", "enriched")
     .option("checkpointLocation", str(CHECKPOINTS / f"02-enrich-{a.mode}"))
     .outputMode("update"))
if a.mode == "rtm":
    w = w.trigger(realTime="30 seconds")       # a checkpoint every 30 s; records don't wait for it
else:
    w = w.trigger(processingTime="0 seconds")  # micro-batches back to back, as fast as they go
```

The `broadcast` hint isn't optional here: a stream-static join in Real-time Mode must not introduce a shuffle, so the static side has to be broadcast to every task. In Scala and Java the trigger is `Trigger.RealTime("30 seconds")`; in Python the duration is required, and anything under 5 seconds is rejected at start.

I measured end-to-end latency the strict way: the output topics are created with `message.timestamp.type=LogAppendTime`, so every output record carries the time the broker appended it, and `bin/latency.py` subtracts the click's own timestamp (set by the generator when it produced the click) from that. The number covers the input hop, Spark, Spark's Kafka producer and the output hop; both clocks are the same machine's. The generator ran at 200 clicks a second for 45 seconds per run, against a 4-partition topic.

| Step 2, stateless enrich | p50 | p90 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|
| micro-batch, back-to-back trigger | 115 ms | 161 ms | 204 ms |
| Real-time Mode | 0 ms | 1 ms | 1 ms |

The micro-batch numbers are the floor the docs talk about: even with no trigger interval at all, a record waits for the batch it lands in to be planned, scheduled, run and committed. The Real-time numbers are a single machine on localhost at a modest rate, and both timestamps have millisecond resolution, so a median of 0 ms means only that at least half the records arrived within the same measured millisecond; it does not establish zero or sub-millisecond latency. The point is the shape: a record's latency is now dominated by its own path through the query rather than the scheduling and completion of its batch.

<img src={img1} alt="real-time-mode-spark-43-trigger" />

The execution model comes with a fairly strict set of requirements:

| Real-time Mode requires | What happens otherwise |
|---|---|
| `outputMode("update")` | `STREAMING_REAL_TIME_MODE.OUTPUT_MODE_NOT_SUPPORTED` at start |
| a batch duration of at least 5 s | `INVALID_STREAMING_REAL_TIME_MODE_TRIGGER_INTERVAL` |
| a Kafka source | `STREAMING_REAL_TIME_MODE.INPUT_STREAM_NOT_SUPPORTED` (the `rate` source isn't supported either) |
| a Kafka, `foreach`, console or memory sink | `STREAMING_REAL_TIME_MODE.SINK_NOT_SUPPORTED`; `foreachBatch` is out because it works on whole batches |
| every operator on the allowlist | `STREAMING_REAL_TIME_MODE.OPERATOR_OR_SINK_NOT_IN_ALLOWLIST`, which names the operator |
| enough cores for every long-running task at once | the query doesn't make progress |

The cores line is the one that bites on a laptop. A Real-time task holds its core for the whole batch, so a 4-partition topic needs 4 free cores before the query can move at all, and a stateful query needs more (next section). The docs also recommend one Real-time query per cluster, for the same reason; anything else on the cluster competes for slots the Real-time query is sitting on.

## Step 3: Stateful queries, and the shuffle that doesn't wait

Stateless operators work record by record inside one task, so long-running tasks are all they need. A stateful operator is different: a `dropDuplicates` on `event_id` or a `groupBy` on an aisle needs every record for a key to reach the same task, regardless of which Kafka partition it arrived on, which means a shuffle. In the micro-batch engine a shuffle is a hard boundary (the producer stage writes shuffle files, and only once they're complete does the consumer stage read them back grouped by key), and a long-running Real-time task never completes, so an ordinary shuffle would simply deadlock.

4.3 gets around that with two pieces that work together. A **pipelined shuffle** changes the scheduling: the source stage and the stateful stage are marked as one pipelined group and scheduled at the same time, both as long-running tasks. A **streaming shuffle** changes the transport: since both stages are running at once, the producer sends output incrementally over the network to the consumer tasks rather than materialising the whole shuffle as files first. Records may still spend a short time in network buffers, as the benchmark below makes rather obvious, but they do not wait for the producer stage or batch to finish before being regrouped by key and merged into state. The state itself still lives in the state store and is checkpointed each batch, preserving the same exactly-once processing semantics as micro-batch; delivery to an external sink remains a separate guarantee. None of this needs configuring because it is what a Real-time trigger does to a supported shuffle on the streaming path.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  classDef old fill:#4b5563,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#4b5563,color:#ffffff
  classDef new fill:#d97706,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#d97706,color:#ffffff
  subgraph mb[Micro-batch: one batch at a time]
    direction LR
    a1[scan offsets n..m] --> f1[(shuffle files)] --> b1[stateful stage<br/>reads when files complete] --> c1[commit, plan next batch]
  end
  subgraph rt[Real-time: one long batch, both stages running]
    direction LR
    a2[scan task per partition<br/>runs for the whole batch] -- records over the network --> b2[stateful task per key range<br/>merges into state, emits]
  end
  class a1,f1,b1,c1 old
  class a2,b2 new
```

Step 3 drops retried events by `event_id`, then counts clicks and purchases per aisle per minute. It's the code you'd write for micro-batch, with the Real-time trigger:

```python
trending = (clicks
            .dropDuplicates(["event_id"])                       # stateful: every event_id seen so far
            .join(F.broadcast(books), "book_id")
            .withWatermark("event_time", "30 seconds")
            .groupBy(F.window("event_time", "1 minute"), "aisle")   # stateful: a running count per window and aisle
            .agg(F.count("*").alias("clicks"),
                 F.sum(F.when(F.col("action") == "purchase", 1).otherwise(0)).alias("purchases"),
                 F.max("ts").alias("last_ts")))
```

There is an important production caveat hiding in the first line: `dropDuplicates(["event_id"])` retains every event ID it has seen, and the watermark applied later to `event_time` belongs to the windowed aggregation rather than the deduplication. `dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark`, the bounded version of this operation, is not supported in Real-time Mode in 4.3, so this demo's deduplication state grows for as long as the query runs.

Because the output mode is `update`, each window's row is emitted every time it changes, and in Real-time Mode it changes on every record; the watermark doesn't hold results back here, it only governs when a closed window's state can be evicted. The latency is measured from the newest click counted into each emitted row (`last_ts`):

| Step 3, dedup + windowed aggregation | rows out | p50 | p90 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| micro-batch, back-to-back trigger | 1,943 | 237 ms | 408 ms | 645 ms |
| Real-time Mode | 7,979 | 50 ms | 77 ms | 99 ms |
| Real-time Mode, shuffle flush wait 1 ms | 7,979 | 2 ms | 3 ms | 41 ms |

<img src={img2} alt="real-time-mode-spark-43-stateful" />

The row counts are the update semantics made visible: micro-batch emits one row per window and aisle per batch, with everything that arrived during the batch folded in, while Real-time Mode emits an updated count per click, which is roughly the input rate. If you're feeding a dashboard that's a lot of rows; if you're feeding something that acts on each change, it's the point.

The first time I made the query stateful, its median jumped from below the measurement's 1 ms resolution to 43 ms; in the benchmark run above it landed at 50 ms. That looked like the stateful operator being slow until I went through the 4.3 source and found the same number in the new streaming shuffle. It batches records into network buffers (32 KB by default), and a part-filled buffer is held for up to `spark.shuffle.streaming.networkBufferMaxWaitTimeMs` (50 ms by default) before it is flushed to the next task. At 200 clicks a second spread over four partitions, the buffers rarely fill, so most records wait for the timer. Setting it to 1 ms takes the median to 2 ms and the p99 from 99 ms to 41 ms.

The config's own docstring describes the trade directly: "Lower values reduce latency at the cost of smaller, less efficient messages." It is marked internal in 4.3, so this is not a documented tuning recommendation and the setting may change; the result instead shows why a lightly loaded stateful query can sit near 50 ms even when the state operation itself is cheap, and why latency and network efficiency cannot both be inferred from the name Real-time Mode.

The core budget follows the number of stages that must remain alive together, not merely the input rate. A query with one stateful operator needs a core for each Kafka partition plus one for each post-shuffle partition. Step 3 has two differently keyed stateful operators, deduplication by `event_id` followed by aggregation by window and aisle, so its pipelined group contains the source stage and two shuffle stages; with four partitions at each stage it needs twelve task slots. Leaving `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` at its default of 200 would make that requirement wildly larger. Inspect the physical plan, count every concurrent stage and set the partition count deliberately.

## Step 4: A recommender in `transformWithState`

Dedup and aggregation cover a lot, but personalisation needs arbitrary per-key logic, which in Spark means [`transformWithState`](https://spark.apache.org/docs/4.3.0/streaming/structured-streaming-transform-with-state.html): you write a `StatefulProcessor` class, Spark calls it with each key's rows, and you get typed state variables (value, list and map state), timers, and TTL on the state. In 4.3 it runs under a Real-time trigger, with one big caveat stated plainly in the docs: only the Scala and Java API. PySpark's `transformWithState` and `transformWithStateInPandas` are rejected, so step 4 is Scala, built with sbt and run through `spark-submit` on the 4.3.0 binary.

The processor keeps four things per shopper, all with a 30-minute TTL so shoppers who leave stop costing memory:

| State | Type | What it holds |
|---|---|---|
| `taste` | `ValueState[Array[Float]]` | a decayed, action-weighted sum of the clicked books' embeddings |
| `clicks` | `ValueState[Long]` | how many distinct clicks fed it |
| `seen` | `MapState[Long, Long]` | books already clicked, so they're never recommended back |
| `events` | `MapState[String, Long]` | event ids already applied, so a retried event is ignored |

On every click the processor decays the taste vector, adds the clicked book's embedding weighted by the action (a view counts 1, a cart add 3, a purchase 5), scores every book in the catalog against it by cosine similarity, and emits the top five it hasn't seen. The catalog is collected on the driver once and broadcast, so every task has all 5,817 vectors in memory; scoring all of them is a couple of million multiply-adds per click, which fits comfortably inside the 3 ms end-to-end median measured below.

```scala
override def handleInputRows(user: String, rows: Iterator[Click], timers: TimerValues): Iterator[Recs] = {
  val cat = catalog.value
  val vec = if (taste.exists()) taste.get() else new Array[Float](cat.dim)
  var n = if (clicks.exists()) clicks.get() else 0L
  var last: Click = null
  rows.foreach { c =>
    if (!events.containsKey(c.event_id)) {          // a retried event is ignored
      events.updateValue(c.event_id, c.ts)
      cat.row(c.book_id).foreach { r =>
        val w = weight(c.action)
        var i = 0
        while (i < cat.dim) { vec(i) = vec(i) * decay + w * cat.vecs(r * cat.dim + i); i += 1 }
        seen.updateValue(c.book_id, c.ts)
        n += 1
        last = c
      }
    }
  }
  if (last == null) return Iterator.empty
  taste.update(vec)
  clicks.update(n)

  // One idle timer per shopper, pushed back on every click.
  getHandle.listTimers().foreach(t => getHandle.deleteTimer(t))
  getHandle.registerTimer(timers.getCurrentProcessingTimeInMs() + idleMs)

  Iterator.single(Recs(user, "picks", last.event_id, last.ts, n, topK(cat, vec)))
}
```

<img src={img3} alt="real-time-mode-spark-43-processor" />

The loop over `rows` matters more than it looks. In micro-batch, `handleInputRows` gets all of a key's rows for the batch in one call; in Real-time Mode it's called once per row, with a one-row iterator. A processor that only looks at the first row, or that emits once per call assuming it has seen the whole batch, will behave differently in the two modes, so the docs' advice (write it to be correct either way) is the thing to follow. The job itself is the usual Dataset pipeline, ending in the Real-time trigger:

```scala
val recs = clicks                       // Dataset[Click], parsed from the clicks topic
  .groupByKey(_.user_id)
  .transformWithState(
    new Recommender(catalog, Duration.ofMinutes(30), idleMs),
    TimeMode.ProcessingTime(),
    OutputMode.Update())

recs.select($"user_id".as("key"), to_json(struct($"*")).as("value"))
  .writeStream.format("kafka")
  .option("topic", "recs")
  .option("checkpointLocation", s"$demo/data/checkpoints/04-recs-$mode")
  .outputMode("update")
  .trigger(Trigger.RealTime("30 seconds"))
  .start()
```

`TimeMode.ProcessingTime()` is there because TTL needs it; event-time mode works in Real-time too, with a watermark that's fixed for the whole batch and only moves between batches. And the first time I ran the micro-batch version for comparison, it refused to start:

```text
[UNSUPPORTED_FEATURE.STORE_BACKEND_NOT_SUPPORTED_FOR_TWS] The feature is not supported: Store backend
org.apache.spark.sql.execution.streaming.state.HDFSBackedStateStoreProvider is not supported by
TransformWithState operator. Please use RocksDBStateStoreProvider.
```

`transformWithState` needs the RocksDB state store. A Real-time query sets RocksDB, changelog checkpointing and checkpoint format v2 for you as soft defaults (only if you haven't set them yourself), and a micro-batch query doesn't, so a processor that works under `Trigger.RealTime` fails the moment you switch the trigger back. Every step in the demo now sets those three configs explicitly, which also means both modes in the tables run on the same state store. Watch out for the reverse trip too: Real-time Mode rejects a checkpoint written with format v1, so an existing micro-batch query that's been running on v1 needs a fresh checkpoint location before it can move to a Real-time trigger.

### Grading the recommendations

The generator writes each shopper's hidden favourite aisles to a file Spark never reads, so the recommendations can be graded: what share of the recommended books sit in one of the shopper's favourite aisles, grouped by how many clicks the shopper had made when the picks came out, against what picking books at random would score for the same shoppers. This run had the shoppers browse at 100 clicks a second for 60 seconds.

| Clicks so far | Picks | In a favourite aisle | Random picks would be |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1,000 | 64% | 12% |
| 2 to 4 | 3,000 | 73% | 12% |
| 5 to 9 | 5,000 | 79% | 12% |
| 10 to 19 | 9,905 | 82% | 12% |
| 20+ | 11,095 | 84% | 12% |

<img src={img4} alt="real-time-mode-spark-43-grade" />

One click is already most of the way there, which says a single book's nearest neighbours in embedding space mostly share its aisle (its subject headings do a lot of the work); the gain after that is the taste vector averaging out the 20% of clicks that land anywhere. Watching one shopper live (`bin/watch.py`) shows the less flattering side of a decayed sum: a shopper whose favourites were Philosophy and Travel Writing added one detective novel to their cart, and because a cart add weighs three views, their next rounds of picks were almost all detective stories, even after two more Philosophy views. That's a weighting decision, not an engine one, but it's the kind of thing you only see when the picks update on every click.

<img src={img5} alt="real-time-mode-spark-43-live" />

| Step 4, recommender | p50 | p90 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|
| micro-batch, back-to-back trigger | 190 ms | 275 ms | 396 ms |
| Real-time Mode | 29 ms | 49 ms | 158 ms |
| Real-time Mode, shuffle flush wait 1 ms | 3 ms | 3 ms | 216 ms |

The recommender has the same shape as step 3, which makes sense; `groupByKey` is a shuffle, so the streaming shuffle's flush timer sets most of the Real-time median, and the full-catalog scoring barely registers next to it (3 ms end to end once the timer is at 1 ms). The p99 didn't improve with the shorter wait, and I haven't isolated why; the docs note that a Real-time query stops processing while it commits and starts the next batch, which is the obvious suspect for a tail in a 45-second run with 30-second batches. Micro-batch also emitted fewer rows (7,274 against 7,931 in Real-time), because a shopper's clicks that land in the same batch come in through one `handleInputRows` call and get one set of picks.

### Timers on a quiet shopper

The idle timer is the one place the per-record story doesn't hold, and it's documented. Each click pushes the shopper's timer 20 seconds out; when it fires, the processor emits a "nudge" (the picks you'd email to someone who wandered off). In Real-time Mode, Spark checks for expired timers after each input row reaches a state partition and once more when the batch ends; there's no background thread polling idle partitions. When I stopped the shoppers, all 200 nudges did fire, but with a median of 4.3 seconds and a maximum of 12.5 seconds after they were due, because with no input arriving the only thing left to trigger the check was the end of the 30-second batch. A second run (the one in the film) came out at a median of 18.9 seconds and a maximum of 28.8, which is the same mechanism with the batch boundary landing later relative to when the shoppers stopped; anywhere inside the batch duration is fair game.

In a busy shop, other shoppers' clicks landing on the same partition trigger the check almost immediately; on a quiet partition, a timer's precision is bounded by the batch duration. Event-time watermarks have the same bound, since they advance only between batches. If a timer needs to be punctual on idle keys, the batch duration is the knob, with the checkpointing overhead that comes with a shorter one.

## What about running the model in the stream?

Precomputing the catalog embeddings leaves an obvious question: why not call the model per record, using a Python UDF or a `pandas_udf` to embed a search query as it arrives? Under a Real-time trigger, neither version I tested in Spark 4.3 starts; both planned to `ArrowEvalPythonExec` and failed with the same error:

```text
[STREAMING_REAL_TIME_MODE.OPERATOR_OR_SINK_NOT_IN_ALLOWLIST] Streaming real-time mode has the following
limitation: The operator(s): org.apache.spark.sql.execution.python.ArrowEvalPythonExec is not in the
operator allowlist for Real-Time Mode.
```

Scalar UDFs are on the supported list in the docs, but that means JVM UDFs; anything that sends rows to a Python worker is a separate physical operator, and none of the Python ones are allowlisted in 4.3 (there's a `spark.sql.streaming.realTimeMode.allowlistCheck` config that turns the check off, at your own risk, which I didn't try).

That's why the demo embeds offline and scores in the JVM. It's not a bad split for personalisation in general (the catalog changes slowly, the shopper changes constantly, and dot products are cheap), but it does mean that in 4.3 the model-shaped work in a Real-time pipeline is either precomputed, written in Scala or Java, or called from a `foreach` sink or a JVM UDF talking to a model server.

## What I did not test

Everything ran on one machine (16 cores, Spark in local mode, a single Kafka broker in Docker), so there is no network between executors, and the stateless result below the measurement's 1 ms resolution will not survive a real cluster unchanged. The load was modest (200 clicks a second for the latency runs) and each run was 45 seconds after a warm-up, so I haven't looked at sustained throughput, at what happens to the streaming shuffle when buffers actually fill, or at long-running state growth. The unbounded event-ID deduplication in step 3 makes that last omission especially important rather than hypothetical.

I didn't kill and restart anything, so the recovery behaviour (exactly-once processing, at-least-once delivery through the Kafka sink, which can re-write records emitted before a failure) is not something I tested. Stopping a stateful Real-time query logs `ERROR ErrorNotifier: A fatal error has occurred` with `Connection to streaming shuffle writer N closed before termination`; in every run that was the job being cancelled by `stop()`, not a failure, but it's alarming the first time.

## In a Nutshell

- **Real-time Mode is a trigger.** `Trigger.RealTime("30 seconds")` in Scala, `.trigger(realTime="30 seconds")` in Python, with `outputMode("update")`, a Kafka source and a Kafka, `foreach`, console or memory sink.
- **The batch duration is a checkpoint interval**, not a latency setting; records come out per record, and the duration bounds recovery work, timers on idle partitions and watermark progress.
- **Count your cores**: every stage in a pipelined group runs at once, so count the source partitions and the partitions in each shuffle stage; set `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` deliberately.
- **Stateful queries are new in 4.3**: `dropDuplicates`, `groupBy(...).agg(...)` including windows, and JVM `transformWithState`, through a pipelined, streaming shuffle; stream-stream joins, `flatMapGroupsWithState`, session windows and `dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark` aren't supported yet. Plain `dropDuplicates` is unbounded, so its state grows with every new key.
- **The streaming shuffle holds part-filled buffers for up to 50 ms** (`spark.shuffle.streaming.networkBufferMaxWaitTimeMs`, internal), which sets the median of a lightly loaded stateful query.
- **`transformWithState` in Real-time Mode is Scala or Java only**, gets one row per `handleInputRows` call, and needs RocksDB, which Real-time Mode sets for you and micro-batch doesn't.
- **Timers and watermarks are bounded by input or the batch end**, so a quiet key's timer can be up to a batch duration late.

## Further reading

- [Real-time Mode](https://spark.apache.org/docs/4.3.0/streaming/real-time-mode.html), the Spark 4.3 docs page: requirements, the supported-operator list, state store defaults, and every example used here.
- [`transformWithState` programming guide](https://spark.apache.org/docs/4.3.0/streaming/structured-streaming-transform-with-state.html), for the processor API, state variables, timers, TTL and initial state.
- [Structured Streaming programming guide](https://spark.apache.org/docs/4.3.0/streaming/index.html), for sources, sinks, output modes and checkpointing in the micro-batch engine.
- [spark-demos/14_real_time_mode](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-demos/tree/main/demos/14_real_time_mode), the code for every step, the benchmark script and `NOTES.md` with every measured number.
