import img13 from "./spark-4-3-guide-json-table.gif";
import img14 from "./spark-4-3-guide-variant.gif";
import img15 from "./spark-4-3-guide-nanos.gif";
import img16 from "./spark-4-3-guide-sql-extras.gif";
import img17 from "./spark-4-3-guide-archives.gif";

*Originally published on [systems/null](https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/ultimate-guide-spark-43).*

<img src={img0} alt={"Pixel-art illustration: a Starfleet engineer in a red uniform kneeling to repair wiring in a starship engine room full of Spark-branded reactors, server racks, dashboards and small helper robots, under the title \"The Ultimate Guide to Apache Spark 4.3\""} />

## A release about time (mostly)

Spark 4.3.0 came out on October 30, including the more in depth [Databricks release blog](https://www.databricks.com/blog/introducing-apache-spark-43-now-available-databricks-runtime-19), which means my feeds are about to fill with listicles that paste the release notes into a numbered list and call it a day. I wanted to do something a little more in depth by reviewing each of the major features in this release as closely as possible, so that people can get a better idea of the expected behaviours and what it's like to actually run the changes. Funnily, I expect a blog like this to have a shorter shelf life than usual as these releases are currently en track for a quarterly cadence, meaning Spark is about to get much more fully featured in the next year as it moves towards 5.0.

Reading the [release notes](https://spark.apache.org/releases/spark-release-4-3-0.html) end to end, I kept noticing that the big items all circle the same thing from different angles. Real-time Mode is about how quickly one record gets through a stateful query; SCD Type 2 is about how long a row's history survives; ASOF JOIN is about which version of a fact was true at a given moment; and nanosecond timestamps are about how finely Spark can tell two moments apart in the first place. The remaining features (Project Feather, the Spark Connect observability work, `DataFrame.zip`, Python UDF transpilation) are about a different clock, which is yours: how long you wait between writing a query and seeing it run.

**Most of Spark 4.3 is about time, both the data's and yours: the scheduler learned to pipeline shuffles, so stateful streaming queries now run at millisecond latency; Auto CDC learned to keep history; SQL learned point-in-time joins and nanosecond precision; and the rest of the release shortens the loop between writing Spark code and finding out whether it works.**

Every example here is a runnable script in [spark-demos/demos/16_spark_43_guide](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-demos/tree/main/demos/16_spark_43_guide), and every clip below is that script running against Spark 4.3.0 (`pip install pyspark==4.3.0`) on my machine. The Real-time Mode clips come from the [Real-time Mode demo](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-demos/tree/main/demos/14_real_time_mode), which is a teaser for one of my upcoming Spark Streaming blog posts ;) 

Below is a rundown of the new features and how to enable or take advantage of them.

| Feature                                             | Area                  | On by default?                   | How to turn it on                                                                       |
| --------------------------------------------------- | --------------------- | -------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Stateful Real-time Mode                             | Structured Streaming  | Yes (with the Real-time trigger) | `.trigger(realTime="...")`, update mode                                                 |
| SCD Type 2 in Auto CDC                              | Declarative Pipelines | Yes                              | `STORED AS SCD TYPE 2` / `stored_as_scd_type=2`; target must support DSv2 row-level ops |
| Shuffle-free single-task execution                  | Project Feather       | No                               | `spark.sql.optimizer.singleTaskExecution.enabled=true`                                  |
| Arrow-native Dataset cache                          | Project Feather       | No                               | `spark.sql.cache.serializer=...ArrowCachedBatchSerializer` (static)                     |
| Operation IDs, REST endpoints, `with` sessions      | Spark Connect         | Yes                              | nothing                                                                                 |
| Persistent local Connect server                     | Spark Connect         | No                               | `SPARK_LOCAL_CONNECT_REUSE=1`                                                           |
| `DataFrame.zip`                                     | PySpark, Connect      | Yes                              | nothing                                                                                 |
| Python UDF transpilation                            | PySpark               | No (experimental)                | `spark.sql.experimental.optimizer.transpilePyUDFs=true` plus ANSI mode                  |
| `ASOF JOIN`                                         | SQL                   | No (preview)                     | `spark.sql.join.asofJoin.enabled=true`                                                  |
| `JSON_TABLE`, VARIANT edit functions                | SQL                   | Yes                              | nothing                                                                                 |
| Nanosecond timestamps                               | SQL                   | No (preview)                     | `spark.sql.timestampNanosTypes.enabled=true`                                            |
| `UNNEST`, `counter_diff`, `jaro_winkler_similarity` | SQL                   | Yes                              | nothing                                                                                 |
| Reading inside tar, zip and 7z archives             | File sources          | No                               | `spark.sql.files.archive.reader.enabled=true`                                           |

## Stateful Real-time Mode

Real-time Mode landed in 4.1 as a new trigger for Structured Streaming: instead of slicing a stream into micro-batches and waiting for each one to be planned, scheduled and committed, the query runs long-lived tasks that process records as they arrive and checkpoint on a much longer interval. The catch in 4.1 and 4.2 was that it only ran stateless queries (filters, projections, stream-static joins), because anything stateful needs a shuffle, and a classic shuffle is a blocking barrier where every map task has to finish writing before a single reduce task can read.

A new `PipelinedShuffleDependency` ([SPARK-58185](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-58185)) routes data through a new `StreamingShuffleManager` ([SPARK-57141](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-57141)), which pushes records to downstream tasks over Netty while the upstream tasks are still running. The `DAGScheduler` now schedules a pipelined group of stages together, fails them together, and refuses to start a group without enough task slots ([SPARK-58263](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-58263), [SPARK-58398](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-58398)). This admission check prevents deadlock on a busy cluster: a consumer stage started without its producer would sit idle while holding cores. With that machinery in place, Real-time Mode supports streaming aggregation ([SPARK-58635](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-58635)), `dropDuplicates` ([SPARK-58508](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-58508)) and Scala/Java `transformWithState` ([SPARK-57228](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-57228)), and is no longer marked `@Experimental`.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef old fill:#6b4a9b,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#6b4a9b,color:#ffffff
    classDef new fill:#c0661a,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#c0661a,color:#ffffff
    subgraph MB["Micro-batch: SortShuffleManager"]
        M1["map tasks<br/>write all output"]:::old --> W["shuffle files<br/>(barrier)"]:::old --> R1["reduce tasks<br/>start after"]:::old
    end
    subgraph RT["Real-time: StreamingShuffleManager"]
        M2["map tasks<br/>(long-running)"]:::new -->|"records pushed<br/>as they arrive"| R2["stateful tasks<br/>(running at the same time)"]:::new
    end
```

The query itself doesn't change shape. In this deduplication and windowed-count step from the bookshop demo, only the trigger and output mode are specific to Real-time Mode:

```python
trending = (clicks
    .withWatermark("ts", "10 seconds")
    .dropDuplicates(["event_id"])                       # resent clicks counted once
    .groupBy(F.window("ts", "10 seconds"), "aisle")
    .count())

(trending.writeStream.format("kafka")
    .outputMode("update")
    .trigger(realTime="30 seconds")                     # the whole change
    .start())
```

<img src={img1} alt="Real-time Mode running dedup and a windowed count, measured in Real-time Mode and then with the streaming shuffle's flush wait at 1 ms" />

Measured end to end on my machine (from the click's own timestamp to the broker's append time on the output topic, 200 clicks a second for 45 seconds), the same query looks like this in each mode:

| Step | Mode | p50 ms | p99 ms |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dedup + windowed count | micro-batch | 237 | 645 |
| Dedup + windowed count | Real-time | 50 | 99 |
| Dedup + windowed count | Real-time, flush wait 1 ms | 2 | 41 |
| `transformWithState` recommender | micro-batch | 190 | 396 |
| `transformWithState` recommender | Real-time | 29 | 158 |

The 50 ms median comes from a timer. The streaming shuffle flushes when its buffer fills or `spark.shuffle.streaming.networkBufferMaxWaitTimeMs` expires; the default is 50 ms, and a lightly loaded query does not fill the buffer first. Reducing the wait to 1 ms brought the median down to 2 ms at the cost of more small network writes, a tradeoff to tune per workload rather than a useful global default. (The shorter run in the clip measured a 67 ms median and 96 ms p99 at the default, then 2 ms and 3 ms at 1 ms; the table contains the longer benchmark, and this amount of variation is normal for a single-machine test.) Databricks reports p99 latencies of 136 ms for `dropDuplicates`, 139 ms for a window aggregation and 141 ms for `transformWithState` on its benchmark workloads ([SPARK-58884](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-58884)). Those results are not guarantees, and neither are mine, which come from one desktop with Kafka running in Docker.

For a stateful example, the recommender keeps a taste vector per shopper, built from book embeddings, in `transformWithState` and rescores the catalog on every click. The recommendations therefore change a few milliseconds after each click:

<img src={img2} alt="One shopper browsing: each click goes through Kafka into a transformWithState processor and comes back as fresh picks a few milliseconds later" />

Real-time Mode still has several limits. `transformWithState` supports only Scala and Java, requires the RocksDB state store, and fires a processing-time timer on an idle key only when another row reaches its partition or the Real-time batch ends. `ASOF JOIN` is not supported. Pipelined stages also require cores concurrently, so the cluster must be sized for the whole pipeline rather than its widest stage.

## SCD Type 2 in Auto CDC

Auto CDC arrived in 4.2 as the Declarative Pipelines way to turn a change feed into current state: give it keys, a sequencing column and a delete rule, and it keeps a target table in sync with MERGE, handling out-of-order and replayed events for you. In 4.2 that meant SCD Type 1, where the target only ever holds the latest version of each row. 4.3 adds SCD Type 2 ([SPARK-58321](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-58321)), in Python (`stored_as_scd_type=2`, `track_history_column_list`), in SQL (`STORED AS SCD TYPE 2`, `TRACK HISTORY ON`) and through Spark Connect, so the target keeps every version, each bounded by `__START_AT` and `__END_AT`.

I reused the ghost kitchen from that post, this time tracking its menu. Each dish change arrives on a Kafka topic as a JSON event, as it would from a CDC tool. The pipeline has a Python source that reads the topic,

```python
@dp.table
def menu_changes():
    return (spark.readStream.format("kafka")
        .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "localhost:29292")
        .option("subscribe", "menu-changes")
        .option("startingOffsets", "earliest")
        .load()
        .select(from_json(col("value").cast("string"), CHANGE).alias("e"))
        .select("e.*"))
```

and this one SQL statement:

```sql
-- Keep every version of every dish, not just the latest one.
CREATE STREAMING TABLE menu
FLOW AUTO CDC
FROM STREAM(menu_changes)
KEYS (dish_id)
SEQUENCE BY seq
APPLY AS DELETE WHEN op = 'DELETE'
COLUMNS * EXCEPT (op)
STORED AS SCD TYPE 2
TRACK HISTORY ON (price, station);
```

<img src={img3} alt="The Kafka source for the menu change feed, then the Auto CDC flow in SQL with STORED AS SCD TYPE 2 and TRACK HISTORY ON (price, station)" />

`TRACK HISTORY ON` controls which changes open a new version. Changes to unlisted columns update the current version in place, which prevents corrections such as typo fixes from creating history entries. Publishing change events in batches and running the pipeline after each batch shows both cases:

<img src={img4} alt="Batch 1: two dishes go on the menu, each with one open-ended version" />

<img src={img5} alt="Batch 2: the smash burger goes up to 15.00 and the tacos move to the plancha, so their old versions close at 2 and new ones open; khao soi arrives" />

<img src={img6} alt={"Batch 3: fixing the \"Birra\" typo updates the tacos' current row in place, and taking khao soi off the menu closes its window instead of erasing it"} />

After the third run, the table contains the full history of each dish:

| dish_id | dish | price | station | `__START_AT` | `__END_AT` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Birra tacos | 14.00 | grill | 1 | 2 |
| 1 | Birria tacos | 14.00 | plancha | 2 | NULL |
| 2 | Smash burger | 13.50 | grill | 1 | 2 |
| 2 | Smash burger | 15.00 | grill | 2 | NULL |
| 3 | Khao soi | 16.00 | wok | 1 | 2 |

The typo fix at sequence 3 did not open a third row for the tacos because `dish` is not tracked; it updated the current version instead. Removing khao soi closed its window at sequence 2 rather than deleting it, preserving the previous menu state. `__START_AT` and `__END_AT` contain the sequencing value, which is an integer here but could instead be a commit timestamp.

As with Type 1, the target must support DSv2 row-level operations because Auto CDC applies each micro-batch with `MERGE`. Spark's built-in file formats, including Parquet, fail at startup with `AUTOCDC_TARGET_DOES_NOT_SUPPORT_MERGE`; Apache Iceberg is the usual choice. Iceberg has not published a Spark 4.3 runtime yet (Maven Central currently stops at `iceberg-spark-runtime-4.1`), so I used an Iceberg runtime built from a branch with Spark 4.3 support. The Iceberg runtime, Kafka connector jars and `spark.sql.extensions` are static configurations and must be passed to `spark-pipelines run`, which accepts `spark-submit` arguments. Putting them in `spark-pipeline.yml` makes the CLI apply them to a live session and fail with `CANNOT_MODIFY_CONFIG`.

## Project Feather: faster on small data

Spark has always been a slightly absurd tool for a 500-row file because its planning assumes the data is large: a `groupBy` gets a partial aggregate, a hash shuffle and a final aggregate, while an `orderBy` adds a range shuffle. Each exchange creates a stage boundary and another scheduling round trip. That overhead disappears into the work on a cluster; on a laptop, in a test suite, or in an agent running hundreds of small queries, it becomes the work. Project Feather ([SPARK-56978](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-56978)) addresses that overhead, and 4.3 includes its first two pieces, both opt-in.

Shuffle-free single-task execution ([SPARK-57851](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-57851), `spark.sql.optimizer.singleTaskExecution.enabled`) notices when a query fragment reads something that fits in one partition (by default a single non-empty small file, or a local relation of up to 1,000 rows) and plans the scans, aggregations, distincts, windows, sorts and limits above it as one task with no exchanges at all. The same aggregation, with the flag off and then on:

```python
def run(single_task, runs=20):
    spark.conf.set("spark.sql.optimizer.singleTaskExecution.enabled",
                   single_task)
    t = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(runs):
        # a fresh DataFrame each time, like a notebook cell or a test
        df = (spark.read.parquet(small)
              .groupBy("store").count().orderBy("store"))
        df.collect()
    return df, (time.perf_counter() - t) / runs * 1000
```

<img src={img7} alt="The same small aggregation with single-task execution off (two Exchanges in the plan) and on (none), with the time per query for each" />

| singleTaskExecution | Operators in the executed plan | Time per query |
|---|---|---|
| false | Sort, Exchange (range), HashAggregate, Exchange (hash), HashAggregate, FileScan | 82.9 ms |
| true | Sort, HashAggregate, FileScan | 51.2 ms |

Both exchanges (and the shuffle query stages AQE wraps around them) are gone, and the query takes about 60% of the time, warm, on a session that's already paid for JVM startup. The loop builds a new DataFrame every time on purpose, because that's what a notebook cell, a test or an agent does. My first version collected the same DataFrame twenty times, and from the second collect on AQE reuses the shuffle output it already has, skipping the very stages Feather removes, so the two settings came out within a few milliseconds of each other. I wrote up the full benchmark (more queries, cold starts, and a test suite that went from 12.6 s to 5.2 s) in Benchmark Project Feather on a Fresh DataFrame.

The second piece is Arrow-native Dataset caching ([SPARK-57268](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-57268)): set `spark.sql.cache.serializer=org.apache.spark.sql.execution.columnar.ArrowCachedBatchSerializer` when the application starts (it's static) and `df.cache()` stores Arrow batches instead of Spark's own columnar format, which pairs nicely with everything Arrow already does between the JVM and Python. Compression is available through `spark.sql.execution.arrow.compression.codec`, but it defaults to `none`, so out of the box the Arrow cache is bigger than the default one. Broader in-process local repartitioning was deferred to the next release ([SPARK-57399](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-57399)).

## Spark Connect: operation IDs and REST endpoints

In my idiot's guide to Connect I complained that debugging a Connect app means correlating a client-side error with a server you can't see, and 4.3 fixes the two halves of that. First, the Python and Scala clients now generate an operation ID before every `ExecutePlan` request ([SPARK-58547](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-58547)) and hand it back on success (`df.executionInfo.operation_id`) and, more usefully, on failure (`e.operation_id` on the exception), because a request that fails before its first response never learned a server-generated ID. The server publishes the same ID as a Spark local property, so listeners and executor tasks can see it too.

```python
remote = SparkSession.builder.remote("sc://localhost:15043")
with remote.getOrCreate() as spark:      # new in 4.3: sessions are context managers
    ok = spark.sql("SELECT count(*) AS n FROM range(1000000)")
    ok.collect()
    print("succeeded, operation", ok.executionInfo.operation_id)

    try:
        spark.sql("SELECT revenue FROM range(10)").collect()
    except Exception as e:   # the client knows the ID even on failure
        print("failed,    operation", e.operation_id)
```

<img src={img8} alt="A Connect session in a with block printing the operation ID of a successful query and of a failed one" />

Second, the server's sessions and operations are now in the monitoring REST API ([SPARK-57941](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-57941)), next to the SQL and streaming endpoints, where before they only lived in the Connect tab of the UI:

```bash
curl -s $API/connect/sessions | jq
curl -s $API/connect/operations | jq '.[] | select(.operationId == env.OP)'
```

Take the ID the client printed for the failure, and the server's record of that same operation has its state, timings, the SQL execution it ran and the full error:

<img src={img9} alt="curl against the new /connect/sessions and /connect/operations endpoints, then the failed operation looked up by the ID the client printed" />

Because the Connect listener writes these events to the event log, the same endpoints work in the History Server after the application exits. Other Connect changes include the session context manager above ([SPARK-58159](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-58159)), a `SQLContext` wrapper for existing code ([SPARK-57021](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-57021)), an experimental `SPARK_LOCAL_CONNECT_REUSE=1` setting that keeps a local Connect server alive between runs ([SPARK-57787](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-57787)), and broader support in the Connect JDBC driver for complex types, `DatabaseMetaData` keys and SQLSTATE class `08` connection errors. The `INVALID_HANDLE.SESSION_*` errors changed SQLSTATE from `HY000` to `08003`, so retry logic that matches SQLSTATE may need updating. Connect Gateway and the Rust-backed Python client are concurrent projects, not Spark 4.3 features.

## PySpark: DataFrame.zip and UDF transpilation

`DataFrame.zip` ([SPARK-55886](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-55886), with Connect support in [SPARK-57247](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-57247)) places two column projections of the same DataFrame side by side, row for row, without a join key. It replaces joins built on `monotonically_increasing_id()`, whose rows are not guaranteed to align. Both sides must originate from the same plan, with matching filters, sorts, joins and aggregations beneath the projections.

<img src={img10} alt="Two projections of one DataFrame zipped back together row by row" />

The experimental Python UDF transpiler ([SPARK-55206](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-55206)) is the one I've been waiting for since the UDF showdown, where the conclusion was that the fastest Python UDF is the one that never runs Python. With `spark.sql.experimental.optimizer.transpilePyUDFs=true` and ANSI mode on, PySpark reads simple UDF bodies when you define them and lowers them to Catalyst expressions, so `len(dish)` becomes Spark's own `length` and the `BatchEvalPython` step (and the Python worker, and the serialization) drops out of the plan:

```python
spark = (SparkSession.builder
         .config("spark.sql.ansi.enabled", "true")  # transpiling needs ANSI
         .getOrCreate())

@udf("int", useArrow=False)
def name_length(dish: str) -> int:
    return len(dish)
```

<img src={img11} alt="The plan for the same UDF with transpilation off (BatchEvalPython, a Python worker) and on (no Python step, Spark's length)" />

The restrictions are not all documented together, so I read `pyspark/sql/udf.py` to collect them. Transpilation applies only to non-Arrow batched UDFs (hence `useArrow=False`), classic PySpark, ANSI mode, and function bodies that PySpark can recover from source, excluding an inline lambda passed directly to `udf()`. With ANSI mode disabled, PySpark warns and falls back because the generated expressions use ANSI semantics. The transpiler also preserves Python behavior where Spark differs: a transpiled `len` raises on NULL as CPython would, represented in the full plan by a `raise_error` branch. Parameter type hints keep the generated plan small. Other PySpark changes bound UDF input batches by bytes, implement more pandas API on Spark functions natively, remove Python 3.10 support, and raise the minimum NumPy version to 1.23.2.

## Spark SQL: ASOF JOIN, JSON_TABLE, VARIANT edits and nanoseconds

`ASOF JOIN` ([SPARK-58092](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-58092)) is the point-in-time join: for each row on the left, the single closest row on the right that satisfies a `MATCH_CONDITION` comparison, optionally within an equality `ON` or `USING` key. In my Rust client post I had to pull a Spark result into DuckDB to do exactly this, so it's nice to have it native, with a dedicated sort-merge operator. The canonical ML case is matching each prediction to the feature version that had actually been published when the prediction was made:

```sql
SELECT p.made_at, p.score, f.version AS features_used, f.published_at
FROM predictions p
ASOF JOIN feature_versions f
MATCH_CONDITION (p.made_at >= f.published_at)  -- latest one out by then
```

<img src={img12} alt="ASOF JOIN matching a 10:03 prediction to the features published at 10:00, not the ones from 10:05" />

The 10:03 prediction gets `v1` from 10:00 and never `v2` from 10:05, which didn't exist yet (using it would be leakage), and the 10:07 prediction gets `v2` alone, where a plain `>=` join would return both versions and leave you to pick the latest yourself, which is exactly where the leakage bugs usually creep in. It's a preview: `spark.sql.join.asofJoin.enabled` is off by default (and internal, so it won't show up in `SET -v`), only `INNER` and `LEFT OUTER` are supported, and in streaming only stream-static works, with the stream on the left.

`JSON_TABLE` ([SPARK-58366](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-58366)) is the SQL-standard table function for expanding a JSON array into typed rows. It also supports `FOR ORDINALITY` and `EXISTS` columns:

<img src={img13} alt="JSON_TABLE expanding one order's items array into typed rows with an ordinal and an EXISTS column" />

And VARIANT values can finally be edited in place with `variant_set`, `variant_insert`, `variant_delete`, `variant_array_append` and `variant_strip_nulls` (plus `try_` versions), instead of being parsed into a struct and serialized back:

<img src={img14} alt="variant_set, variant_delete, variant_array_append and variant_strip_nulls applied to one profile" />

Nanosecond timestamps ([SPARK-56876](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-56876)) add `TIMESTAMP_NTZ(p)` and `TIMESTAMP_LTZ(p)` for precisions 7 to 9, with `unix_nanos`, `timestamp_nanos`, `current_timestamp(p)`, datetime functions, interval arithmetic, and Parquet, ORC, JSON, CSV, Avro, JDBC, Arrow and Connect support. Spark's `TIMESTAMP` has been microseconds since forever, which means two market events a nanosecond apart (or two rows from a Parquet file written by something that does use nanoseconds) silently became the same instant:

<img src={img15} alt="Two trades one nanosecond apart: identical at microsecond precision, distinct at TIMESTAMP_NTZ(9)" />

Nanosecond timestamps remain a preview behind `spark.sql.timestampNanosTypes.enabled`, and the Databricks release post warns that they may change incompatibly. Typed literals such as `TIMESTAMP_NTZ(9) '...'` do not parse yet, so values must be cast from strings. I would not use the type for production work yet: while building this demo, I found a query that returns an incorrect count when a nanosecond column appears beside other `DISTINCT` aggregates in the same `SELECT`; I am reducing the reproduction before filing it. The `TIME` type also gained nanosecond precision and broader connector support, but remains disabled behind an internal flag.

Other SQL additions include ANSI `UNNEST` in `FROM`, with `WITH ORDINALITY`; `counter_diff`, a window function that converts a running counter such as requests served or bytes sent into per-interval deltas and returns NULL after a reset; and `jaro_winkler_similarity` for fuzzy name matching:

<img src={img16} alt="UNNEST with ORDINALITY, counter_diff turning a running counter into deltas with a reset as NULL, and jaro_winkler_similarity" />

Also new and not filmed: `@`-syntax time travel on table names (`t@v3`, or `t@20261105093000000` in the fixed 17-digit `yyyyMMddHHmmssSSS` form), `COMMENT ON COLUMN`, dynamic table options on `UPDATE`, `MERGE` and `DELETE`, `AS JSON` output for `SHOW TABLES` and `SHOW PARTITIONS`, `collect_union`, `to_base32`/`from_base32`, and a `BIN BY` relation operator behind a flag.

## Reading files inside archives

The archive reader may be the feature I use most. With `spark.sql.files.archive.reader.enabled=true`, file sources read entries inside tar, zip and 7z archives as separate files, including during schema inference; `archivePathFilter` selects the entries to read. This removes the usual step of unpacking a vendor's nightly archive into a temporary directory:

<img src={img17} alt="CSV files read straight out of a tar, with archivePathFilter skipping the README inside" />

## Other changes in Spark 4.3

A lot of 4.3 is engine work you get for free. `ReplaceHashWithSortAgg` and combining adjacent partial and final aggregates are now on by default, whole-stage codegen covers `UNION`, AQE can convert a sort-merge join to a shuffled hash join in the physical plan, nested column pruning reaches into `transform` over arrays of structs, and the vectorized Parquet reader got faster decoding paths and a `BYTE_STREAM_SPLIT` reader. There's an opt-in to spread NULL outer join keys across partitions (a classic skew source), fractional `spark.task.cpus`, `spark.rdd.compress` on by default, and the Spark UI's Content Security Policy on by default. On Kubernetes the official images move to Ubuntu 26.04 with Python 3.14, and containers drop `allowPrivilegeEscalation` by default.

A few changes can change results or break things on upgrade, all in the [migration guide](https://spark.apache.org/docs/4.3.0/sql-migration-guide.html): exact `percentile`/`median` may differ in the last ULP; `Dataset.observe` metrics now count only the last successful task attempt; `HAVING` is applied before window functions when the `SELECT` also has a generator (fixing wrong results); non-deterministic filters are no longer pushed to DSv2 sources; Thrift Server sessions can no longer set JVM system properties; and the AQE rule `DynamicJoinSelection` was renamed `DemoteBroadcastHashJoin`, so an exclusion by the old name now silently does nothing.

## In Summary

- **Stateful Real-time Mode**: pipelined shuffles let dedup, aggregation and `transformWithState` (Scala/Java) run at millisecond latency with only a trigger change, and the default median is a 50 ms flush timer you can tune.
- **SCD Type 2 in Auto CDC** keeps every version with `__START_AT`/`__END_AT`; `TRACK HISTORY ON` decides what opens a new version, and the target needs a row-level-capable catalog like Iceberg (whose 4.3 runtime isn't published yet).
- **Project Feather** is opt-in: single-task execution removes the exchanges from small queries (about 1.6x faster here, warm), and the Arrow cache serializer is a static config.
- **Spark Connect** gives you an operation ID on success and failure, and the same operation in the server's REST API.
- **`DataFrame.zip`** replaces the `monotonically_increasing_id` join hack; **UDF transpilation** removes Python from simple UDFs if you're on classic PySpark with ANSI on.
- **ASOF JOIN, nanosecond timestamps and archive reading** are all behind flags; **JSON_TABLE, VARIANT edits, UNNEST and `counter_diff`** just work.

Most of it comes back to time: a record's few milliseconds through a stateful query, a dish's price history that never gets overwritten, the feature version that was true at 10:03, the nanosecond between two trades, and the milliseconds a small query no longer spends on shuffles. On a quarterly cadence, expect all of it to keep moving faster than it used to.

## Further reading

- [Introducing Apache Spark 4.3](https://www.databricks.com/blog/introducing-apache-spark-43-now-available-databricks-runtime-19), the Databricks launch post, with the Real-time Mode benchmarks.
- [Spark 4.3.0 release notes](https://spark.apache.org/releases/spark-release-4-3-0.html), every change with its JIRA.
- [SQL migration guide, 4.2 to 4.3](https://spark.apache.org/docs/4.3.0/sql-migration-guide.html), for the behaviour changes above.
- [spark-demos/demos/16_spark_43_guide](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-demos/tree/main/demos/16_spark_43_guide), every script in this post, plus the film scripts.
- AUTO CDC: Turning an event log into current state, the SCD Type 1 post this builds on.

---

# Spark Connect from Rust: Pull Spark outputs into DuckDB and Polars

URL: https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/spark-connect-rust-duckdb-polars
Republished at: https://openlakehouse.io/blog/apache-spark/spark-connect-rust-duckdb-polars
Original publisher: systems/null
Date: 2026-11-03
Category: Apache Spark

import img0 from "./spark-connect-rust-duckdb-polars-deps.gif";
import img1 from "./spark-connect-rust-duckdb-polars-data.gif";
import img2 from "./spark-connect-rust-duckdb-polars-arrow.gif";
import img3 from "./spark-connect-rust-duckdb-polars-duckdb.gif";
import img4 from "./spark-connect-rust-duckdb-polars-polars.gif";
import img5 from "./spark-connect-rust-duckdb-polars-back.gif";

*Originally published on [systems/null](https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/spark-connect-rust-duckdb-polars).*

## Setting the Rust-Native Scene

In the OCaml post we walked through the process of building a Connect client from scratch, but in truth the Rust client is probably the only one you really need if you're working right now in the data engineering field. It gives you in-process interoperability with engines like Polars (written in Rust) and DuckDB (C++, with official Rust bindings), meaning you no longer have to choose between Spark and &lt;INSERT COOL, TRENDY, HIP NEW ENGINE HERE>. In my connect idiot's guide I only hinted at the Rust client as part of a way to gauge supported operations. In this follow-up, I want to deep dive into the Rust Client. It'll be helpful to know what Spark connect is ahead of time, but you'll probably figure it out pretty easily if you're a smart cookie. TLDR on the previous posts: Connect is Spark's attempt to decouple the JVM from the user's environment by implementing a client-server architecture where a very lightweight client sends unresolved logical plans to a remote cluster. 

Spark Connect sends query results to the client as Arrow record batches (thank god). The client builds a plan, the server runs it, and results are returned as Arrow. If you want to know why this is important, I'd suggest reading my previous blog on Arrow batches replacing pickle serialization between the JVM and Python process in Spark. Every Connect client gets those same Arrow batches, so this isn't unique to Rust: in Python, PySpark's `toArrow()` (4.0 and later) hands you a pyarrow table that DuckDB and Polars can read directly. What Rust adds is doing it in one compiled program with no Python in the process, where DuckDB and Polars read the batches as Rust libraries. This separation allows Spark to do the work that needs a cluster (the scan, the join across a billion rows, the group-by), and when the result comes down as Arrow,  DuckDB or Polars can be used in the same process without writing intermediary data files. 

The demo and code in this blog can be found in [spark-demos/demos/09_spark_connect_rust](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-demos/tree/main/demos/09_spark_connect_rust) with its full run log.

**With the official Rust client, one Spark result comes out as Arrow IPC bytes that DuckDB and Polars both read cheaply, DuckDB registers it without a further copy, and the answer goes back to Spark.**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    SRV["Spark 4.2.0<br/>Connect server"] -->|"Arrow batches over gRPC"| CLI["apache-spark-connect<br/>(arrow-rs 58)"]
    CLI -->|"to_arrow() IPC bytes"| DUCK["DuckDB 2.0<br/>(arrow-rs 60)"]
    CLI -->|"to_arrow() IPC bytes"| POL["Polars<br/>(polars-arrow)"]
    POL -->|"Arrow IPC bytes"| DUCK
    DUCK -->|"create_dataframe()<br/>saveAsTable"| SRV
```
## What the Rust client actually is

[apache/spark-connect-rust](https://github.com/apache/spark-connect-rust) is the Apache Spark project's own Rust client, listed on the [Spark Connect page](https://spark.apache.org/spark-connect/) next to the Go and Swift ones, with its documentation at [apache.github.io/spark-connect-rust](https://apache.github.io/spark-connect-rust/). The crate is `apache-spark-connect`, used in code as `spark_connect`, and the version number is the Spark version it speaks: `4.2.0` means Spark 4.2.0 and later, which is a nice convention more clients should steal.

The [architecture page](https://apache.github.io/spark-connect-rust/architecture/) describes one Rust core (plan building, gRPC via tonic, Arrow decoding) with two faces on it: a synchronous Rust API shaped like PySpark, and a `pyspark-client-rust` wheel on PyPI that installs as `pyspark` and is meant as a drop-in for the reference Python client. This blog uses the Rust API. If you've used other Rust gRPC clients, "synchronous" is the part to notice: no `async`, no runtime to set up, and no `.await` anywhere in your code. The hello world from the docs is the entire API in miniature:

```rust
use spark_connect::{SparkSession, functions as f, lit};

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let spark = SparkSession::builder()
        .remote("sc://localhost:15002")
        .get_or_create()?;

    let df = spark
        .range(1_000_000)?
        .select([(f::col("id") * lit(2)).alias("x")])
        .filter((f::col("x") % lit(3)).eq(lit(0)));

    println!("count = {}", df.count()?);
    Ok(())
}
```

The [compatibility page](https://apache.github.io/spark-connect-rust/compatibility/) says the goal is full API parity with the reference PySpark Connect client, that the protobuf plans it builds are checked byte-for-byte against the reference Python client in CI, and that the official PySpark Connect test suite is run against it. In practice, if you know PySpark you can mostly guess the Rust method name (`spark.sql()`, `df.filter()`, `df.group_by()`, `df.write().save_as_table()`), and when you guess wrong the compiler tells you, which is more than Python does.

## Setting up the environment

**The server.** Any Spark 4.2 or later Connect server will do. The demo's `compose.yaml` starts the official image's Connect server (it listens on all interfaces by default) and gives it a health check, so `docker compose up --wait` returns when the port actually answers rather than when the container starts:

```yaml
services:
  spark-connect:
    image: apache/spark:4.2.0-scala2.13-java21-python3-ubuntu
    entrypoint:
      - /opt/spark/sbin/start-connect-server.sh
      - --wait
      - --conf
      - spark.driver.memory=4g
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:${CONNECT_PORT:-15002}:15002"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "bash", "-c", "</dev/tcp/127.0.0.1/15002"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 40
```

```sh
docker compose up -d --wait
```

The published port is the one thing you may need to change. My machine already had a Spark Connect server on 15002 from another demo the first time I ran this (this keeps happening to me; it's the first item in the idiot's guide's debugging section), so that run used `CONNECT_PORT=15902`. It's also why the first thing the program prints is the server's version.

**The crate.** Three things have to be installed before `cargo build` works, and each fails at build time if you skip it. You need `protoc`, because the client compiles the Spark Connect `.proto` files when it builds; a C++ compiler plus CMake, because DuckDB is built from source; and Rust 1.98, because polars 0.55 uses standard library APIs stabilised after 1.92 (`std::hint::cold_path` among them) and won't compile on anything older. The demo pins 1.98 in `rust-toolchain.toml`, so `rustup` fetches the right compiler on its own, and the other two are one package each:

```sh
sudo apt-get install protobuf-compiler build-essential cmake   # Debian/Ubuntu
brew install protobuf cmake                                    # macOS
```

Then this `Cargo.toml`, which is the part worth copying exactly. The `polars` feature list is the demo's own needs (lazy frames, IPC, rolling windows) plus four I found the slow way on 0.54 so you don't have to: `parquet`, `strings` and `temporal`, without which `lazy` doesn't compile, and `timezones`, without which a timestamp column from Spark won't print:

```toml
[dependencies]
# The official client. Its `polars` feature (to_polars()) is left off: it pins polars 0.54.
spark-connect = { package = "apache-spark-connect", version = "4.2" }

# arrow-rs (the Rust Arrow library), at DuckDB 2.0's major. The client uses 58 internally.
arrow = { version = "60", features = ["prettyprint"] }

# duckdb-rs for DuckDB 2.0, statically linked. `vtab-arrow` lets DuckDB query arrow-rs batches.
duckdb = { version = "1.20000.1", features = ["bundled", "vtab-arrow", "appender-arrow"] }

# The newest polars crate. It reads Arrow IPC with its own Arrow implementation.
polars = { version = "0.55.2", features = [
    "lazy", "ipc", "ipc_streaming", "dtype-full", "fmt", "timezones",
    "rolling_window", "pct_change", "round_series", "parquet", "strings", "temporal",
] }
```

<img src={img0} alt="spark-connect-rust-duckdb-polars-deps" />

Two version facts are worth knowing before you touch that file. DuckDB 2.0 came out on 2026-10-21, and its Rust crate (`duckdb` 1.20000.1; the crate encodes DuckDB 2.0.0 in the minor version) is built on arrow-rs 60, while the client is still on 58. Different arrow-rs majors are different Rust types, so a `RecordBatch` from the client won't type-check where DuckDB wants one; the hand-off is the Arrow IPC bytes from `to_arrow()`, which any arrow-rs major can read. Polars doesn't use arrow-rs at all; it ships its own Arrow implementation (`polars-arrow`) and reads the same IPC bytes. The client's `to_polars()` does exactly that internally, but against polars 0.54, so the demo leaves that feature off and calls Polars' IPC reader itself, which works with whatever polars you have. As for Polars 2.0, it's a Python release (2.0.0 on 2026-10-06, 2.1 since). There's no 2.x `polars` crate yet, and the 2.x source only builds with Polars' own patched `hashbrown` and a nightly toolchain, so the newest crate, 0.55.2, is what a Rust program gets. (The client's own [installation page](https://apache.github.io/spark-connect-rust/installation/) says Rust 1.70 or later, which is true of the client alone; Polars is what raises the floor.) The first build took 4m23s in a clean container, since DuckDB compiles from source, and a rebuild after a code change takes seconds.

## Step 1: Some data to play with

Nothing is downloaded. Spark builds a 20-million-row orders table from `range()` and hash functions, so the whole demo runs anywhere a Spark 4.2 server is reachable and nobody has to find a dataset:

```rust
let spark = SparkSession::builder().remote("sc://localhost:15002").get_or_create()?;
println!("Spark {}", spark.version()?);

spark.sql(
    "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS orders USING parquet AS
     SELECT id AS order_id,
            element_at(array('sfo','lax','sea','nyc','chi','aus','den','pdx','phx','mia','bos','atl'),
                       CAST(pmod(xxhash64(id, 7), 12) AS INT) + 1)            AS city,
            timestamp_seconds(1756684800 + pmod(xxhash64(id, 1), 2592000))     AS ts,
            CAST(round(5 + pmod(xxhash64(id, 2), 9500) / 100.0, 2) AS DOUBLE)  AS amount,
            CAST(1 + pmod(xxhash64(id, 3), 6) AS INT)                         AS items,
            element_at(array('delivered','delivered','delivered','cancelled','refunded'),
                       CAST(pmod(xxhash64(id, 4), 5) AS INT) + 1)             AS status
     FROM range(20000000)",
)?
.collect()?;
```

The `.collect()` on the end is not a typo. Everything in this client is lazy, the same as PySpark: `spark.sql()` builds a plan, and nothing runs on the server until an action asks for a result, which for a `CREATE TABLE` means you have to ask for its (empty) result on purpose.

```
Spark 4.2.0 at sc://localhost:15002
  orders: 20000000 rows
```

<img src={img1} alt="spark-connect-rust-duckdb-polars-data" />

## Step 2: Getting a result out as Arrow (four ways, and one of them is wrong)

The client has four ways worth knowing to turn a DataFrame into something you hold in Rust (there are others, such as `to_local_iterator()` for streaming rows and `to_datafusion()` behind a feature flag), and picking the right one is most of the performance story in this blog:

| Method | You get | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| `collect()` | `Vec<Row>`, each value boxed as a `Value` enum | You want to look at a few rows |
| `collect_record_batches()` | `Vec<arrow::RecordBatch>`, the server's batches as decoded | The result is going to DataFusion or your own arrow-rs 58 code |
| `to_arrow()` | `Vec<u8>`, one Arrow IPC file | The result is going to a file, a socket, or another Arrow library |
| `to_polars()` | `polars::DataFrame` (polars 0.54) | The result is going to Polars and you're on 0.54; otherwise read `to_arrow()` with Polars' `IpcReader` |

One city's orders, as batches and as one IPC file (the form DuckDB and Polars get below):

```rust
let sfo = spark.sql("SELECT order_id, city, ts, amount, items, status FROM orders WHERE city = 'sfo'")?;
let batches = sfo.collect_record_batches()?;
let ipc = sfo.to_arrow()?;
```

```
176 RecordBatches, 1667285 rows
arrow-rs schema: order_id: Int64, city: Utf8, ts: Timestamp(µs, "Etc/UTC"),
                 amount: Float64, items: Int32, status: Utf8
as Arrow IPC: 77.3 MiB
```

<img src={img2} alt="spark-connect-rust-duckdb-polars-arrow" />

The batch count is the server's choice, not yours. Connect caps each batch at `spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch` rows (default 10,000) and at a byte size, `spark.connect.grpc.arrow.maxBatchSize` (default 128 MiB in Spark 4.x, of which it uses 70%), and the client hands you the batches exactly as they arrived. Here the row cap is the one that bites (176 batches rather than the 167 the cap alone would give, since a batch never spans two partitions), and `arrow::compute::concat_batches` joins the pieces into one when a consumer wants that.

The same 1.67 million rows, each way, on one machine with the server in a container on the same host. Each path re-runs the query on the server, and each number includes that scan (an earlier count and sum on the same table had already put the files in the OS page cache and warmed up the JVM):

| Path | ms |
|---|---|
| `collect_record_batches()` | 683 |
| `to_arrow()` | 477 |
| `collect()` | 1475 |

**Rows cost about twice what batches cost for the same data.** Most of the difference is client-side work. (These are single runs: `to_arrow()` calls `collect_record_batches()` internally and still came in faster, so the noise is a couple of hundred milliseconds; the doubling for rows is well outside it.) In the client's source, `collect()` decodes the same Arrow batches and then builds a `Row` for every row and a `Value` for every cell, which is a perfectly reasonable thing to do for twenty rows you intend to print and a silly thing to do for 1.67 million you intend to hand to DuckDB. If the result is going to another engine, it should never pass through `collect()`.

## Step 3: DuckDB 2.0 gets the batch

First the result crosses from the client's arrow-rs to DuckDB's: the `to_arrow()` bytes from step 2, read with arrow 60's IPC reader and joined into one batch. For the 1.67 million rows that takes 70 ms:

```rust
use arrow::ipc::reader::FileReader;   // arrow 60, DuckDB's major

fn ipc_to_batch(ipc: &[u8]) -> Result<RecordBatch, Box<dyn Error>> {
    let reader = FileReader::try_new(Cursor::new(ipc), None)?;
    let schema = reader.schema();
    let batches: Vec<RecordBatch> = reader.collect::<Result<_, _>>()?;
    Ok(concat_batches(&schema, &batches)?)
}
```

duckdb-rs has an Arrow table function behind the `vtab-arrow` feature. In DuckDB 2.0's crate you register a `RecordBatch` by wrapping it in an `ArrowBatchRegistration`, which you pass to `arrow(?)` as a query parameter. The batch isn't copied; it stays registered until the registration is dropped. A view can't take a prepared parameter, so to get a view the registration goes into a DuckDB variable first:

```rust
use duckdb::vtab::arrow::{ArrowBatchRegistration, ArrowVTab};

fn arrow_view(db: &Connection, name: &str, rb: RecordBatch) -> duckdb::Result<ArrowBatchRegistration> {
    let reg = ArrowBatchRegistration::new(rb);
    db.execute(&format!("SET VARIABLE {name}_batch = ?"), [&reg])?;
    db.execute_batch(&format!(
        "CREATE VIEW {name} AS SELECT * FROM arrow(getvariable('{name}_batch'))"
    ))?;
    Ok(reg)
}

let db = Connection::open_in_memory()?;
db.register_table_function::<ArrowVTab>("arrow")?;
let _orders = arrow_view(&db, "orders", ipc_to_batch(&ipc)?)?;
let _surge = arrow_view(&db, "surge", surge_schedule(&ts_type)?)?;   // built in Rust; its timestamps use Spark's ts type
```

Keep the registrations in variables for as long as you query the views. Dropping one unregisters the batch, and the view then fails with `is not registered` rather than reading freed memory, which is the right failure but a confusing one if you discarded the return value with a `?;`. (DuckDB 1.5's crate took two integers and a pair of `::UBIGINT` casts instead, and kept every batch alive for the life of the process; the new API is an improvement on both counts.)

Now the reason I brought DuckDB in at all. The `surge` table is a per-six-hour price multiplier that exists only in the client process, and each order needs the latest multiplier at or before its timestamp. (It's built in Rust, with its `starts_at` column given the same Arrow timestamp type and zone as Spark's `ts`, so DuckDB sees two `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` columns rather than one with a zone and one without.) That is an ASOF join (match each row to the nearest earlier key instead of an equal one), which DuckDB has as a first-class SQL operator. Spark has an as-of join inside it (pandas-on-Spark's `merge_asof`, and an `AsOfJoin` relation in the Connect protocol), but 4.2 has no SQL syntax for it (4.3 adds `ASOF JOIN`, off by default) and the Rust client doesn't expose it, so from Rust today this part is DuckDB's job:

```sql
WITH surged AS (
    SELECT o.ts, o.amount, s.multiplier, o.amount * s.multiplier AS surged
    FROM orders o
    ASOF JOIN surge s ON o.city = s.city AND o.ts >= s.starts_at
)
SELECT CAST(CAST(ts AS TIMESTAMP) AS DATE) AS day,
       count(*) AS orders, round(sum(amount), 2) AS revenue,
       round(sum(surged), 2) AS surged_revenue, round(avg(multiplier), 4) AS avg_multiplier
FROM surged GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
```

```
+------------+--------+------------+----------------+----------------+
| day        | orders | revenue    | surged_revenue | avg_multiplier |
+------------+--------+------------+----------------+----------------+
| 2025-09-01 | 55829  | 2933784.48 | 3482949.81     | 1.1868         |
| 2025-09-02 | 55924  | 2927311.35 | 3476037.04     | 1.1881         |
| 2025-09-03 | 55491  | 2913342.93 | 3459069.6      | 1.1877         |
...
  PASS  DuckDB count == Spark count: 1667285
  PASS  DuckDB sum(amount) == Spark sum(amount): 87512653.61 vs 87512653.61
  PASS  ASOF JOIN kept every order: 1667285
```

<img src={img3} alt="spark-connect-rust-duckdb-polars-duckdb" />

The double cast on `ts` is the one seam in this step. Spark's `timestamp` arrives tagged with the session time zone (`Timestamp(µs, "Etc/UTC")`), DuckDB maps that to `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE`, and a direct cast to `DATE` fails with `Conversion Error: Unimplemented type for cast (TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE -> DATE)`. Zone-aware casts are what DuckDB's ICU extension provides, and the `bundled` build doesn't include it (duckdb-rs has an `icu` feature that does). Casting through plain `TIMESTAMP` sidesteps it for a UTC session; for any other zone, add the feature or do the date arithmetic in Spark before collecting.

**One practical rule for this step, and it's the one that surprised me.** Registering the batch is free, and a count and sum through the view take 65 ms. But the identical ASOF rollup took 1901 ms through the view and 139 ms on a native table that cost 146 ms to create from the same view:

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders_native AS SELECT * FROM orders;   -- 146 ms for 1.67M rows
```

So if you're going to run more than one query over the rows, or any join, copy them into a table first; the copy pays for itself on the first join. I had assumed the zero-copy view was the fast path because zero-copy sounds like the fast path, and it isn't. I haven't profiled why. Part of it is in the duckdb-rs source: every scan through the table function converts the Arrow vectors into DuckDB's own format again, so each query pays the copy that the native table paid once. My guess for the rest is that the view is a single sequential source with no statistics. The gap was the same on DuckDB 1.5.6 (2226 ms against 177), so 2.0 didn't change this rule.

## Step 4: Polars gets Spark's aggregate

Spark is the right place for the 20-million-row group-by. Polars is the nicer place for what comes after, which here is a per-city rolling window and a day-over-day change, both of which are one expression in Polars and a window specification you'd have to think about in Spark SQL. `to_arrow()` runs the query and gives you the result as an in-memory Arrow IPC file, and Polars' `IpcReader` turns that into a `polars::DataFrame`. That's all `to_polars()` does inside the client; doing it yourself means it works with polars 0.55. It costs a copy into IPC bytes and a decode into Polars' own buffers, because Polars has its own Arrow implementation.

```rust
let daily = spark.sql(
    "SELECT city, CAST(ts AS DATE) AS day, count(*) AS orders, round(sum(amount), 2) AS revenue
     FROM orders GROUP BY 1, 2",
)?;
let pl_daily = IpcReader::new(Cursor::new(daily.to_arrow()?)).finish()?;   // Spark runs the group-by; 360 rows cross as IPC

let rolling = pl_daily.lazy()
    .sort(["city", "day"], SortMultipleOptions::default())
    .with_columns([
        col("revenue")
            .rolling_mean(RollingOptionsFixedWindow { window_size: 7, min_periods: 1, ..Default::default() })
            .over([col("city")])?
            .alias("revenue_7d"),
        col("revenue").pct_change(lit(1)).over([col("city")])?.alias("revenue_pct"),
    ])
    .collect()?;
```

```
polars schema: {"city": String, "day": Date, "orders": Int64, "revenue": Float64}
┌──────┬────────────┬────────┬───────────┬────────────┬─────────────┐
│ city ┆ day        ┆ orders ┆ revenue   ┆ revenue_7d ┆ revenue_pct │
│ str  ┆ date       ┆ i64    ┆ f64       ┆ f64        ┆ f64         │
╞══════╪════════════╪════════╪═══════════╪════════════╪═════════════╡
│ atl  ┆ 2025-09-01 ┆ 55524  ┆ 2.9116e6  ┆ 2.9116e6   ┆ null        │
│ atl  ┆ 2025-09-02 ┆ 55327  ┆ 2.9054e6  ┆ 2.9085e6   ┆ -0.002129   │
│ atl  ┆ 2025-09-03 ┆ 55638  ┆ 2.9335e6  ┆ 2.9168e6   ┆ 0.009665    │
...
  PASS  Polars sum(orders) == Spark count(orders): 20000000
```

<img src={img4} alt="spark-connect-rust-duckdb-polars-polars" />

Getting the aggregate into Polars took 695 ms here (nearly all of it Spark running the group-by) and the rolling computation after it 5 ms, which is the ratio you'd hope for when Spark is doing the heavy part. (Since polars 0.54, `over()` returns a `Result`, hence the `?` inside the expression list; nothing I read warned me about that.) The IPC copy is cheap: once `to_arrow()` has produced the 77.3 MiB IPC file for the whole 1.67-million-row slice, reading it into Polars takes 72 ms.

A Polars frame can keep going into DuckDB too, by the same route the Spark result took. Polars writes the Arrow IPC stream format with `IpcStreamWriter`, arrow-rs reads it with `StreamReader`, and the result is a `RecordBatch` for the same table function; for the 360 rolling rows that is 17.5 KiB and 1 ms:

```rust
let mut buf = Vec::new();
IpcStreamWriter::new(&mut buf).finish(&mut rolling.clone())?;
let back: Vec<RecordBatch> = StreamReader::try_new(Cursor::new(buf), None)?.collect::<Result<_, _>>()?;
let _rolling = arrow_view(&db, "rolling", concat_batches(&back[0].schema(), &back)?)?;
```

After that `rolling` is a DuckDB view like `orders` was, and `QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY revenue_7d DESC) = 1` (a clause that filters on a window function's result, which Spark SQL also picked up in 4.2) picks each city's best week out of it.

## Step 5: Sending the answer back to Spark

Spark Connect already takes Arrow inbound: `createDataFrame` is sent as a `LocalRelation`, the protocol's message for client-side data, whose payload is Arrow IPC bytes (step 6 of the OCaml post was writing exactly that by hand). The Rust client's public entry point for it is `create_dataframe(rows, schema)`, which takes `Row` values. So a `RecordBatch` that came out of DuckDB gets unpacked into rows first (a loop over columns and a `match` on the Arrow type; the demo's `record_batch_to_rows` is about forty lines) and then written like any other DataFrame:

```rust
let (rows, schema) = record_batch_to_rows(&surge_daily)?;
spark.create_dataframe(rows, schema)?
    .write().mode("overwrite").save_as_table("sfo_surge_daily")?;
```

```
struct<day:date,orders:bigint,revenue:double,surged_revenue:double,avg_multiplier:double>
  PASS  Spark table rows == DuckDB rows: 30
  PASS  Spark sum(surged_revenue) == DuckDB sum: 103926081.03 vs 103926081.02
```

<img src={img5} alt="spark-connect-rust-duckdb-polars-back" />

That is 157 ms for 30 rows, timed as one step from Arrow to the saved table. (The cent between the sums is floating point, not lost data: Spark and DuckDB add the same thirty doubles in a different order, so the check allows five cents rather than demanding an exact match.) The row conversion grows with row count the same way `collect()` does in the other direction, so for big data going back, write it somewhere both sides can read and `spark.read()` it instead. A `create_dataframe` that took batches directly would be a very welcome addition to the client, since the IPC writer it needs is already in there.

## Spark Type Mapping to DuckDB and Polars
  
The full table with the values is in the demo README; this is the part to keep nearby:

| Spark type | arrow-rs | DuckDB | Polars |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tinyint` to `bigint` | `Int8` to `Int64` | `TINYINT` to `BIGINT` | `i8` to `i64` |
| `float`, `double` | `Float32`, `Float64` | `FLOAT`, `DOUBLE` | `f32`, `f64` |
| `decimal(p,s)` | `Decimal128(p, s)` | `DECIMAL(p,s)`, digits intact | `decimal[p,s]`, digits intact |
| `string` (a `char(n)` literal also arrives as `string`) | `Utf8` | `VARCHAR` | `str` |
| `binary` | `Binary` | `BLOB` | `binary` |
| `boolean` | `Boolean` | `BOOLEAN` | `bool` |
| `date` | `Date32` | `DATE` | `date` |
| `timestamp` | `Timestamp(µs, "<session zone>")` | `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` | `datetime[μs, <zone>]` |
| `timestamp_ntz` | `Timestamp(µs)` | `TIMESTAMP` | `datetime[μs]` |
| `array<T>` | `List` | `T[]` | `list[T]` |
| `map<K,V>` | `Map` | `MAP(K, V)` | `list[struct[2]]` (Polars has no map type) |
| `struct<...>` | `Struct` | `STRUCT(...)` | `struct[n]` |
| `interval day to second` | `Duration(µs)` | `INTERVAL` | `duration[μs]` |
| `interval year to month`, calendar `interval` | `Interval` | `INTERVAL` | polars 0.55 panics building the frame (calendar intervals can be imported as a struct with `POLARS_IMPORT_INTERVAL_AS_STRUCT=1`, marked unstable); cast to a number in Spark first |
| `time` | fails on the server with `UNSUPPORTED_TIME_TYPE`: Spark's Arrow serialiser doesn't handle TIME, so it never leaves | | |
| `variant` | `Struct(value Binary, metadata Binary)` | `STRUCT(value BLOB, metadata BLOB)` | `struct[2]`; opaque bytes in both |
| `void` (a bare `NULL` literal) | `Null` | duckdb-rs can't bind it (`Unsupported data type: Null`) | `null` |

For example, `timestamp` carries the server's session zone into DuckDB's and Polars' type systems (which is correct, and is why the `DATE` cast in step 3 needed care); `timestamp_ntz` doesn't. And Polars has no year-month interval type, so turn any such column into a number in Spark before it heads that way. Everything else, decimals included, keeps its precision and lands as a native column type in both engines (in pandas a decimal column becomes a column of Python `Decimal` objects, exact but slow, which is a thing I'd rather not think about).

## Limitations

All of it ran on one machine with the server in a container on the same host, so the Spark-to-client times contain no real network; across a network the transfer would dominate and the gap between `collect()` and batches would matter less in proportion. Every timing is a single run in a warm process, not a benchmark harness, and the DuckDB view-versus-table gap is an order of magnitude, not a precise ratio. The server ran with default Arrow batch settings. The type sweep didn't include GEOMETRY or GEOGRAPHY, which are new in Spark 4.2. Neither `to_datafusion()` nor the client's WebAssembly UDF path (Rust functions compiled to wasm and run on the executors) was exercised; the latter is its own blog and probably a fun one. The Polars findings are for the 0.55.2 crate, not Polars 2.0, which Rust can't use yet.

## Summarizing the Stack

- **Server:** any Spark 4.2+ Connect server; `docker compose up -d --wait` with the official image and a health check on the port.
- **Build:** `protoc`, a C++ toolchain and CMake installed; the Cargo.toml above, copied exactly; `rust-toolchain.toml` pinned to 1.98.
- **Connect:** `SparkSession::builder().remote("sc://host:15002").get_or_create()?`, then print `spark.version()` before anything else.
- **Get results out as Arrow:** `to_arrow()` for DuckDB 2.0 and Polars (the IPC bytes cross any arrow-rs major), `collect_record_batches()` for your own arrow-rs 58 code, `collect()` only for rows you intend to read.
- **DuckDB:** register `ArrowVTab`, wrap the batch in an `ArrowBatchRegistration` and keep it alive, put a view over it, and copy it into a table if you'll query it more than once or join it at all.
- **Polars:** `IpcReader` over the `to_arrow()` bytes and go; turn on the `timezones` feature before the first timestamp.
- **Back to Spark:** `create_dataframe(rows, schema)` for small results; shared storage for large ones.
- **Types:** decide between `timestamp` and `timestamp_ntz` before data crosses a boundary, and keep intervals out of Polars.

The idiot's guide said to check that the client you pick supports what you need before you build on it. For the Rust client that check comes out well, and what it's best at is the thing the protocol was designed around in the first place: the result is already Arrow, so the only question left is where you want to send it.

## Further reading

- [apache/spark-connect-rust](https://github.com/apache/spark-connect-rust) and its [docs](https://apache.github.io/spark-connect-rust/): [installation](https://apache.github.io/spark-connect-rust/installation/), [quickstart](https://apache.github.io/spark-connect-rust/quickstart/), [DataFrames](https://apache.github.io/spark-connect-rust/dataframes/), [architecture](https://apache.github.io/spark-connect-rust/architecture/), [compatibility](https://apache.github.io/spark-connect-rust/compatibility/), and [Rust UDFs via WebAssembly](https://apache.github.io/spark-connect-rust/udfs/), the part this blog skipped
- [`apache-spark-connect` on docs.rs](https://docs.rs/apache-spark-connect), for `collect_record_batches`, `to_arrow`, `to_polars` and `to_datafusion`
- [DuckDB 2.0.0's release notes](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/releases/tag/v2.0.0) and [duckdb-rs 1.20000.1's](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-rs/releases/tag/v1.20000.1)
- [Spark Connect overview](https://spark.apache.org/spark-connect/), which lists the Go, Rust and Swift clients, and the [Connect server docs](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/spark-connect-overview.html) for starting one without Docker
- [duckdb-rs](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-rs) and its `vtab-arrow` feature; [DuckDB's ASOF join](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/guides/sql_features/asof_join), which Spark 4.2 has no SQL for
- [Polars](https://pola.rs/) and [`polars-arrow`](https://crates.io/crates/polars-arrow), its own Arrow implementation and the reason for the IPC hop
- [The demo](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-demos/tree/main/demos/09_spark_connect_rust), with the full run log and the complete type table in its README

# Apache Iceberg v4 Column Updates Are About to Change Feature Engineering

URL: https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/iceberg-column-updates
Republished at: https://openlakehouse.io/blog/iceberg/iceberg-column-updates
Original publisher: systems/null
Date: 2026-10-27
Category: Iceberg

import img0 from "./iceberg-column-updates-setup-flow.svg";
import img1 from "./iceberg-column-updates-table-and-updates.svg";

*Originally published on [systems/null](https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/iceberg-column-updates).*

## Efficient Column Updates in a Nutshell

Apache Iceberg has two common ways to change a row in a table, and both of them work at file or row granularity. Under ***copy-on-write***, the engine finds the data file that holds the row, rewrites the entire file with the new value, and swaps the old file out of the table's metadata. Under ***merge-on-read***, it leaves the old file alone, records the old row as deleted, and writes the new row into a new data file; readers apply the deletes while scanning. In the v2 version of my experiment, that delete was a *position delete file* (a list of file paths and row numbers). In the v3 version, it was a *deletion vector*, or DV (a compressed bitmap of positions for one data file). Either way, Iceberg is still changing rows, not individual columns.

Row-level updates are good enough for many workloads. They get expensive on very wide tables: feature stores, embedding tables, and model-scoring tables with hundreds or thousands of columns. A nightly job might recompute one feature, refresh one model's scores, or backfill one new column for every existing row. That is one column changing across the table, but today it can still mean rewriting every byte in the touched data files.

[Efficient column updates in Iceberg](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/issues/15146) is the v4 work aimed at that case. It builds on an earlier column-family proposal, where related columns would have been declared up front and written separately from the start. Column updates keep that idea in view, but the focus is narrower: make the cost of a write closer to the columns that changed instead of the current all-or-nothing shape.

At the heart of the design is a new ***column file***: a file that holds one or more whole columns for every row of an existing data file. That lets the data payload for a column update be the updated column, not the whole row. Iceberg finds column files the same way it finds everything else, through its ***manifests***: metadata files that list every data file in the table along with row counts, partition values and column statistics. A column file is recorded on the manifest entry for the data file it belongs to. The reader then uses that metadata to turn the base file plus its column files back into rows.

## Current Column Updates in Iceberg Are Expensive

Take a table shaped like a feature store: an `id` column plus two hundred `double` columns of random numbers, with 200,000 rows. I wrote it with Spark 4.0.1 and Iceberg 1.12.0 as a single 300.9 MB Parquet file, so every update has one base file to deal with and the snapshot history stays easy to read. Then I made two copies: one with `write.update.mode` set to copy-on-write, and one set to merge-on-read. I also ran the same experiment on v2 tables. The only difference was that v2 wrote a position delete file where v3 wrote a deletion vector, so I'm only showing v3 here.

Against each copy, I ran two `UPDATE` statements. The first is the backfill case: change one column, `c_1`, for every row. The second is the partial case: change one column, `c_2`, for one row in ten. After each statement, the newest snapshot summary and the `.files` metadata table show what the commit added and how large it was.

<img src={img0} alt="Setup and flow: one base table copied into a copy-on-write table and a merge-on-read table; against each copy a backfill update, a read of the snapshot and files tables, a partial update, and another read" />

<img src={img1} alt="The demo table as a grid of 200 columns by 200,000 rows, with the backfill touching one whole column and the partial update one column in every tenth row; beside it, what copy-on-write, merge-on-read and a v4 column file each write for both cases" />

```sql
-- the backfill case: every row, one column of two hundred
UPDATE local.db.wide_v3_merge_on_read SET c_1 = c_1 + 1;

-- the partial case: one row in ten, one column
UPDATE local.db.wide_v3_merge_on_read SET c_2 = c_2 + 1 WHERE id % 10 = 0;

-- what I read after each one
SELECT summary FROM local.db.wide_v3_merge_on_read.snapshots ORDER BY committed_at DESC LIMIT 1;
SELECT content, record_count, file_size_in_bytes FROM local.db.wide_v3_merge_on_read.files;
```

| Update mode                     | Statement                 | What the commit added                                                                                       | MB written          |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------- |
| copy-on-write                   | all rows, `c_1`           | one new data file, all 200 columns (the old file deleted)                                                   | 301.1         |
| merge-on-read                   | all rows, `c_1`           | one new data file, all 200 columns, plus one deletion vector                                                | 301.1 + under 0.01 (DV)   |
| copy-on-write                   | one row in ten, `c_2`     | one new data file, all 200 columns (the old file deleted)                                                   | 301.1         |
| merge-on-read                   | one row in ten, `c_2`     | one new data file of 20,000 rows, all 200 columns, plus one deletion vector                                 | 30.1 + 0.03 (DV) |
| **column file (v4, estimated)** | **all rows, `c_1`**       | **one column file holding `c_1` for every row, plus a rewritten manifest entry**                            | **about 1.6** |
| **column file (v4, estimated)** | **one row in ten, `c_2`** | **one column file holding `c_2` for every row (nine tenths carried over), plus a rewritten manifest entry** | **about 1.6** |

The bold rows are estimates. No released Iceberg can run a v4 column update.

For the backfill, both modes wrote a new 301.1 MB file, slightly larger than the 300.9 MB base file because the updated values compress a little differently. That is all 200 columns rewritten to change one. Copy-on-write does this by definition. Merge-on-read does it because Iceberg treats an `UPDATE` as a delete of the old row plus an insert of the new one. When every row changes, the insert half is a complete new data file. The deletion vector marks every row of the old file as gone, and until compaction the table holds both files.

The partial update is where the two modes differ. Merge-on-read wrote a 30.1 MB file holding every column of the 20,000 touched rows, about a tenth of the table. Copy-on-write rewrote the full 301.1 MB file again. Merge-on-read scales with the number of rows touched, but it still writes every column for each touched row.

A v4 column update changes the scale of the write. The column `c_1` on its own, with the same values in the same order, is 1.6 MB as a Parquet file: about half a percent of the base file.

In the current modes, write size is driven by rows touched times columns carried. Changing one column or 200 columns has the same shape.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  classDef cow fill:#3a5f96,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#3a5f96,color:#ffffff
  classDef mor fill:#6b4a9b,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#6b4a9b,color:#ffffff
  classDef v4 fill:#c0661a,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#c0661a,color:#ffffff
  U["UPDATE t SET c_1 = c_1 + 1"]
  subgraph COW["copy-on-write, 1.12.0: 301.1 MB written"]
    C1["new data file, all 200 columns (301.1 MB)<br/>old file deleted"]:::cow
  end
  subgraph MOR["merge-on-read, 1.12.0: 301.1 MB written"]
    M1["new data file, all 200 columns (301.1 MB)"]:::mor
    M2["deletion vector, every row of the old file (under 0.01 MB)"]:::mor
  end
  subgraph V4["v4 column update, proposed: about 1.6 MB written"]
    V1["column file for c_1, one column, all rows (about 1.6 MB)"]:::v4
    V2["manifest entry rewritten (under 0.1 MB)"]:::v4
  end
  U --> COW
  U --> MOR
  U --> V4
```

## Byte by Byte

For the data payload, a v4 column update writes one new file holding the updated column for every row. The dominant write is that one column. On this table every column is random doubles, so each column is roughly 1/200th of the file:

|                                                      |              |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------ |
| base file (200 columns, 200,000 rows)                | 300.9 MB     |
| one column, by proportion (300.9 MB ÷ 200)           | about 1.5 MB |
| `c_1` written on its own as a Parquet file, measured | 1.6 MB       |

The partial update lands at the same estimate. A column file must hold every row of the column, so changing one row in ten still writes the column in full. The untouched nine tenths are copied from the base file. The size depends on the column, not on how many rows changed.

Two small costs are left out of that estimate: the rewritten manifest entry, which is a fraction of a megabyte here, and a null at each deleted position if the base file has deletes. At typical deletion ratios, neither changes the rough size of the write.

The expected write drops from 301.1 MB to about 1.6 MB: nearly 200x on this table because the table has 200 similarly sized columns. For any table, the factor is the base file size divided by the updated column's size. `column_sizes` in the `.files` metadata table gives that size per column. A real writer will add overhead on top of the column file; this demo does not measure that yet.

## Anatomy of a Column File

The public v4 draft defines a column file as "a file that stores the values of one or more fields for each row of another file." That last part matters. A column file is not a list of changed cells. It has the same row count as the data file and holds the complete current value of one or more fields for every row. The data file's manifest entry lists which fields live in which column file:

```json
{
  "location": "s3://bucket/data/base_file_1.parquet",
  "record_count": 1000,
  "column_files": [
    {
      "location": "s3://bucket/data/column_update_7.parquet",
      "field_ids": [7],
      "file_format": "parquet",
      "file_size_in_bytes": 12345
    }
  ]
}
```

The sketch omits most tracked-file fields. The important part is the `column_files` list. Each entry names the column file's location, the live top-level field IDs it stores, the file format (`avro`, `orc` or `parquet`) and the file size in bytes. It may also carry encryption key metadata.

A reader that understands column files resolves each projected field from the column file that lists it and every other field from the data file. The remaining requirements:

| Requirement | Consequence |
|---|---|
| It is stored in a normal data-file format | The bytes are ordinary Parquet, ORC or Avro; stitching them into the base file still requires Iceberg v4 column-file support. |
| Whole top-level fields only | A struct is updated as a unit; one leaf cannot be updated alone. |
| One column file per field | Updating a field again replaces its column file instead of stacking another. |
| Every row, in the base file's order | The read is a column swap by position; the write has to line up exactly. |
| Unchanged rows are carried over | A partial update still writes the whole column. |
| Deleted rows are written as null | A heavily deleted file carries a few percent of filler. |
| The deletion vector decides what is deleted | A null is a filler, never a tombstone. |

The fifth requirement sets the size of a partial update. A column file for one row in ten is not 20,000 values keyed by position. It is 200,000 values: 20,000 new values and the rest copied from wherever the field lived before, or null where the row is deleted.

That is the 1.6 MB file from the demo, not a 0.03 MB delta.

**A column file is the whole column, not a delta. It mirrors its base file row for row and is swapped in by position at read time. Wide backfills get cheaper; row-level refreshes are not the sweet spot.**

> **"Column families" is a different thing**
> The earlier proposal was about *column families*: declaring which columns belong together so they are written as separate files from the start. The design doc keeps that as future work and the current column-file text does not define families. "Column file" in this post is the v4 spec term.

## Stitching It Back Together on Read

A read of a data file with column files has four steps:

1. Use the manifest entry to split the requested fields between the base file and column files.
2. Open the base file and only the column files needed for the projection.
3. Read those files in position order and combine each position's pieces into one row or batch.
4. Apply the deletion vector to the combined result.

Because the files are row-aligned, step 3 is what the design doc calls "reference substitution": the column file's array replaces the base file's array for the updated field. The intended read shape is a column-level substitution, not a join or keyed merge.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  classDef base fill:#3a5f96,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#3a5f96,color:#ffffff
  classDef col fill:#c0661a,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#c0661a,color:#ffffff
  classDef reg fill:#6b4a9b,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#6b4a9b,color:#ffffff
  E["manifest entry<br/>data file + column_files<br/>[7] in cf_7, [4,5] in cf_45"] --> P["projection splitter<br/>id,name from base<br/>7 from cf_7, 5 from cf_45"]:::reg
  P --> B["base file reader<br/>columns id, name"]:::base
  P --> C7["column file reader<br/>column 7"]:::col
  P --> C45["column file reader<br/>column 5 (4 not projected)"]:::col
  B --> S["stitcher<br/>one row / one batch per position"]:::reg
  C7 --> S
  C45 --> S
  S --> DV["apply deletion vector<br/>drop deleted positions and their null fillers"]
  DV --> R["rows as if from one file"]
```

In the Java implementation work, step 3 is a *stitcher*. There is one stitcher per engine row type, such as Spark `InternalRow`, Flink `RowData`, and the generic `Record`. Steps 1, 2 and 4 are shared across engines.

- A column file is opened only when a query projects one of its fields. A query on `c_200` reads the base file alone.
