- Column files do not need to share the base file's row groups, the chunks of rows a Parquet file is written and read in. When row groups do not line up, the reader slices batches to the overlapping window.
- Deletion vectors are applied after stitching, so a column file can hold nulls at deleted rows and is never consulted about deletion.

## Explaining every row

The every-row requirement is what makes partial updates less dramatic.

The alternative was a *sparse* column file: only the changed rows, each tagged with its position. A one-in-ten update would then weigh a tenth of the column. The design rejects that tradeoff because it moves cost to readers outside the JVM:

> The two representations have asymmetric read-side cost across language ecosystems. Spark's `ColumnVector` is an abstract class with virtual dispatch, so a custom stitching subclass can redirect per-row reads (`getInt(rowId)` → choose base vs column file) with no memory copy. Concrete Arrow array types in arrow-rs, PyArrow, and arrow-go do not support this yet.

In Spark, a sparse file can stay lazy on read. A `ColumnVector` subclass can answer `getDouble(i)` from the column file when position `i` was updated and from the base file otherwise, without materializing a replacement array.

An Arrow array in Rust, Python or Go is a contiguous buffer with no per-row redirect. Those readers would have to materialize a new array per batch by scattering the updated values over the base column. That read cost gives back much of what the sparse file saved on write.

With every row present, the stitch can be expressed as an array-level substitution instead of a sparse overlay.

v4 tables need a layout that works across those engines, so the draft standardizes the every-row representation instead of letting writers choose between dense and sparse column files. Once a layout is allowed, every reader has to handle it.

| | Every row (the spec) | Updated rows only (the alternative) |
|---|---|---|
| Partial update writes | the whole column | only the changed rows |
| Read in Spark | swap one array | cheap either way |
| Read in Rust, Python, Go | substitute an array | copy the column |

## How a column update effects manifest

A column update changes the manifest as well as the data. Conceptually, the new snapshot stops pointing at the old version of the tracked file and points at a successor entry for the same base file with a new `column_files` list. Earlier snapshots still see the old metadata for time travel. A field may appear in only one column file for a tracked file, so updating one field of an existing column file means rewriting that column file with its other fields carried over.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  classDef old fill:#555555,fill-opacity:0.6,stroke:#555555,color:#ffffff
  classDef new fill:#3a5f96,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#3a5f96,color:#ffffff
  classDef col fill:#c0661a,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#c0661a,color:#ffffff
  P["prior entry<br/>base_file_1.parquet<br/>seq 7<br/>column_files [ {4,5} -> cf_a ]<br/>DV: {12, 400}"]:::old
  P -->|"column update of fields 5 and 9<br/>in the snapshot with seq 11"| R["previous version<br/>kept for older snapshots"]:::old
  P --> M["current tracked entry<br/>base_file_1.parquet<br/>seq 11<br/>column_files [ {4} -> cf_b, {5,9} -> cf_c ]<br/>DV: every delete that applied so far<br/>stats for 4, 5, 9 from the column files"]:::new
  M --> CB["cf_b: field 4<br/>carried over from cf_a"]:::col
  M --> CC["cf_c: fields 5, 9 + _last_updated_sequence_number<br/>5 updated, 9 new"]:::col
```

The current tracked entry also gets a new *sequence number*: the file's age in commit order, which decides which delete files apply to it. With the new number, older deletes should not be replayed against the new column values.

That sequence-number change would otherwise make older deletes tricky. The v4 work handles this by folding deletes that already applied to the file, including equality deletes, into the entry's own deletion vector. The DV becomes the complete delete record for the current version of the tracked file, and the reader does not need to replay old delete files against the updated columns.

Stats for the updated fields are recomputed from the column file, so file pruning based on those fields can still work.

Row lineage is part of this too. Since v3, every row carries `_last_updated_sequence_number`, the sequence number of the commit that last changed it. One of the new column files has to hold that field: null for every row the update changed, so those rows inherit the new sequence number on read, and the previous value for every row it did not change. Row IDs do not change.

If the updated field is used for partitioning or sorting, metadata has to become conservative for that file because the rows may no longer match the old placement information. Plan for weaker pruning and ordering metadata on that file until compaction rewrites it.

| Step | Cost |
|---|---|
| Read the column's current values and the file's deletes | a read before the write, even for a partial update |
| Write one column file per base file | the column file |
| Rewrite the manifest entry, stats and partition info | small, but every touched file gets it |
| Compact later (`rewrite_data_files` folds column files back in) | stitching is a cost between compactions, not forever |

## But why not directly in Parquet?

The design doc evaluated a Parquet-level alternative and discarded it. Parquet's footer has a `ColumnChunk.file_path` field, so in theory a Parquet file could say that its `score` chunk lives in one file while its other chunks live in `users.parquet`. A column update could then be a narrow Parquet file whose footer describes the whole row. Iceberg would record it as an ordinary data file, with no spec change.

The catch is in the comment on that field in today's `parquet.thrift`: "there are no known reference implementations that will read externally stored column data if this field is populated within a standard parquet file. Making use of the field for this purpose is not considered part of the Parquet specification." The field exists, but readers do not honor it. "No Parquet change" would have become a parquet-format change after all, followed by changes in every Parquet reader Iceberg depends on.

| | In the manifest (chosen) | In the Parquet footer (discarded) |
|---|---|---|
| Who must change | Iceberg's spec and readers | parquet-format and every Parquet reader |
| Can the planner skip files? | yes, from the manifest | only after opening footers |
| Can cleanup jobs see every file? | yes | no, the link is inside a footer |
| Formats | Parquet, ORC, Avro | Parquet only |

The [File Format API](https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/iceberg-file-format-api) makes the same kind of choice: keep the bytes in plain data-file formats and put the table-level structure in Iceberg metadata, where every engine already has to look.

A column file is tracked by Iceberg, not by Parquet. v4-aware `expire_snapshots`, `remove_orphan_files` and `rewrite_data_files` implementations can account for column files from the manifest. A Parquet tool that opens a column file directly sees an ordinary narrow Parquet file with no link to its base file.

## State of the Implementation

Everything above is based on the public v4 draft, the proposal issue and open implementation work as of 2026-10-27. The public spec includes v4 column-file text, but v4 itself is still under active development and has not been formally adopted. The row-count requirement has changed once already; implementation details can still move.

| Piece | State | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Proposal | open, milestone "Iceberg V4 Spec" | [issue 15146](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/issues/15146) |
| Design doc | current | [doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Bd7JVzgajA8-DozzeEE24mID_GLuz6iwj0g4TlcVJcs) |
| Spec text | present in the public v4 draft, still part of active v4 work | Iceberg spec and linked PRs |
| Readers and writers | implementation work in progress | linked under Further reading |
| Format version 4 | not formally adopted; nothing here is in Iceberg 1.12.0 | |

The demo ran once on one machine, measured file sizes only, and used random doubles that make every column about the same width. The reference column is a Spark Parquet file, not an Iceberg column file, so a real column file may be slightly larger. The filler-overhead figures come from the design doc and were not reproduced here. I did not build the reader PR. The research, demo script and draft used AI assistance; the reading of the spec and the opinions are mine, and so are any mistakes.

## What you should know and how to proceed

- **You have a wide table with a regular column refresh.** Budget for the full rewrite until v4 ships in your engine, or keep the fast-moving columns in a narrower table on the same key and join at read time. That is column families by hand. Migrating to v4 later becomes a consolidation, not a full redesign.
- **Your refresh touches a few rows, not all of them.** Stay on merge-on-read unless the math says otherwise. A column file writes every row of the column, so compare the fraction of rows you touch against the column's share of bytes (`column_sizes` in the `.files` table) before expecting v4 to help.
- **You run compaction and orphan cleanup on a schedule.** Every query on an updated column reads the base file and the column file until `rewrite_data_files` folds them back together. Compaction is part of the column-update workflow, not an optional cleanup later.
- **You partition or sort on a column you might update.** Treat this as a conservative-metadata case. Pruning and ordering information can get weaker for the affected file until compaction rewrites it.
- **You write an engine.** The stitcher is the interface to watch. Every-row column files make the stitch an array-level substitution; Arrow arrays are the reason the layout is every-row.

## Further Reading

- [Efficient column updates in Iceberg](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/issues/15146), the proposal, and its [design doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Bd7JVzgajA8-DozzeEE24mID_GLuz6iwj0g4TlcVJcs)
- The code trail: the [spec text](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16425) and [reader work](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18324)
- `ColumnChunk.file_path` in [parquet.thrift](https://github.com/apache/parquet-format/blob/master/src/main/thrift/parquet.thrift); the [Parquet board minutes](https://whimsy-vm9.apache.org/board/minutes/Parquet.html)
- Lance [table format](https://lancedb.github.io/lance/format/) and [data overlay files](https://github.com/lancedb/lance/blob/main/docs/src/format/table/data_overlay_file.md); Paimon [data evolution](https://paimon.apache.org/docs/1.3/append-table/data-evolution/); Hudi [RFC-80](https://github.com/apache/hudi/blob/master/rfc/rfc-80/rfc-80.md)

---

# Building a Spark Connect Client in OCaml

URL: https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/build-a-spark-connect-client
Republished at: https://openlakehouse.io/blog/apache-spark/build-a-spark-connect-client
Original publisher: systems/null
Date: 2026-10-17
Category: Apache Spark

*Originally published on [systems/null](https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/build-a-spark-connect-client).*

## But Lisa, surely you must have a good reason for using OCaml?

No, not really. Well, yes. Sort of. 

In a previous blog post I wrote a cheeky little guide to Spark Connect Clients, which I enjoyed writing thoroughly and was pretty well received. But it ended on a warning: not all Connect Clients are built equally, and it highly depends on the language you're using and the love and care of the maintainers. Current gold standards include the Rust Client, for instance, which gives you full interoperability with Rust native engines like Polars or DuckDB. More on that in a follow up post, but it's pretty cool. 

The follow-up question is what it takes to build one then and how to test it. And to be honest, I've always defaulted to OCaml as sort of a joke language- partially from it's niche quality and mostly from my secret love for the finance industry and beasts like Jane Street.

OCaml is a useful language for the demonstration because it lacks all of the built in capabilities that would otherwise make life easy: there is no Arrow library, no concept of the gRPC protocol at all, and a protobuf compiler is its own project with its own parser rather than a plugin for Google's `protoc`. Every piece of the Connect client has to be manually built; making you realize how good the Go or Rust clients have it in comparison because of their respectively rich ecosystems. Naturally, I vibe coded most of this with my good friend Claude Code, and if you want to skip the entire droll on the implementation journey you can skip ahead to [the repo here](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-connect-ocaml). 

**Every Spark Connect client essentially has the same four basic requirements: compile the published protos, make a streaming gRPC call, build relation trees, and decode Arrow batches. The Connect server itself does so much of the work for you in this architecture that the only parts costing real effort are the two the protocol leaves to the client implementation: its protobuf toolchain and its Arrow codec.**

## The Roles and Responsibilities of a Connect Client

The client sits between the DataFrame calls and the server, and it never processes data itself. It turns method calls into a protobuf tree, sends the tree, and turns the Arrow that comes back into values:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  classDef you fill:#9a7b00,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#9a7b00,color:#ffffff
  classDef srv fill:#c0661a,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#c0661a,color:#ffffff
  A["DataFrame calls<br/>filter, join, group_by ..."]:::you --> B["Relation / Expression<br/>protobuf tree<br/>(step 4)"]:::you
  B -->|"ExecutePlan, gRPC over HTTP/2<br/>(steps 2 and 3)"| C["Connect server<br/>analyzer · Catalyst · executors"]:::srv
  C -->|"stream of responses,<br/>each with an Arrow IPC batch"| D["Arrow decoder<br/>(step 5)"]:::you
  D --> E["rows"]:::you
  F["local rows"]:::you -->|"Arrow writer (step 6)<br/>as a LocalRelation"| B
```

The analyzer, Catalyst and the executors are the server's. The rest is the client's.

## Step 1: Getting the protos to compile

The protocol *is* its protobuf definitions, published in the Spark repository under [`sql/connect/common/src/main/protobuf/spark/connect/`](https://github.com/apache/spark/tree/master/sql/connect/common/src/main/protobuf/spark/connect). A client starts by copying them out of the tag it targets (I used v4.2.0) and compiling them with whatever protobuf toolchain its language has. They import `google/protobuf/any.proto` and `timestamp.proto`, and Spark's error details also need `google/rpc/status.proto` and `error_details.proto`. None of these are in the Spark repo. If the language's toolchain does not ship them, each is a few lines to write by hand, and wire-compatible as long as the field numbers match.

This step is "mechanical" in Go, Rust, Swift and Java, where `protoc` and a maintained plugin do it. In OCaml the compiler is [`ocaml-protoc`](https://github.com/mransan/ocaml-protoc), a from-scratch parser and generator, and Spark's protos hit several things it disagrees with. Each fix is one line in a post-generation fix-up script:

| Problem                                                                            | Where                                                     | Fix                                      |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| Single-quoted strings (`syntax = 'proto3';`), legal but rare                       | every Spark proto                                         | rewrite to double quotes when vendoring  |
| `reserved "userId", "sessionId";` (field *name* reservations)                      | `relations.proto`                                         | drop the lines; they have no wire effect |
| A one-line default emitted before the function it calls exists                     | the mutually recursive ML relation messages               | move the line below its dependency       |
| Key and payload emitted in the wrong order for a oneof case whose message is empty | `Catalog.CurrentDatabase`, `CurrentCatalog`, `ClearCache` | swap the two generated lines             |

The oneof bug surfaced the way every protobuf mistake surfaces. Three catalog calls, and only those three, came back from the server as `UNKNOWN: Application error processing RPC`, with `Invalid protobuf byte sequence` in the server log. That message means the server could not parse the request at all, and the diagnostic is to dump the bytes:

```text
Catalog{current_database}  generated:  00 0a    length 0, then the key for field 1
Catalog{current_database}  correct:    0a 00    key for field 1, then length 0
AnalyzePlan{spark_version} generated:  52 00    same shape, inlined elsewhere, comes out right
```

`ocaml-protoc` encodes back to front (payload first, then its key, so a nested message's length is known before the key is written), and the standalone encoder for an empty message had the two lines in the wrong order. Nothing else in the API was affected: the bug lives in the encoder generated for a message that is nothing but a oneof, and `Catalog` is the only such message on the request path with empty cases. A client in Go never meets this, because `protoc` has been exercised by every Google service for a decade; a client in OCaml meets it immediately. **The protobuf compiler is the first dependency the protocol pushes onto the host language, and the Spark protos are a stress test for it.**

## Step 2: Speak gRPC

gRPC is small once HTTP/2 is available, and OCaml does have HTTP/2 ([`h2`](https://github.com/anmonteiro/ocaml-h2), with TLS through `ocaml-tls` and the system trust store). A call is a `POST` to `/spark.connect.SparkConnectService/<Method>` with two headers that matter, `content-type: application/grpc` and `te: trailers`, plus `authorization: Bearer <token>` when a token is set. The body in each direction is a sequence of messages, each framed as a compression flag byte, a big-endian length, and the protobuf bytes:

```ocaml
let frame payload =
  let n = String.length payload in
  let b = Bytes.create (5 + n) in
  Bytes.set b 0 '\000';                      (* not compressed *)
  Bytes.set_int32_be b 1 (Int32.of_int n);   (* length *)
  Bytes.blit_string payload 0 b 5 n;
  Bytes.unsafe_to_string b
```

The status comes back in HTTP/2 *trailers*, not in the response status line (which is always 200), as `grpc-status` and a percent-encoded `grpc-message`. Spark adds `grpc-status-details-bin`, base64 of a `google.rpc.Status`, which is where the useful error information lives. The reader side is the mirror of `frame`: buffer the body, peel off messages as their lengths complete, and finish when the trailers arrive.

```ocaml
let status_of_headers (h : H2.Headers.t) =
  match H2.Headers.get h "grpc-status" with
  | None -> None
  | Some code ->
      let code = try int_of_string code with _ -> 2 in
      let message = Option.value ~default:"" (Option.map percent_decode (H2.Headers.get h "grpc-message")) in
      let details = Option.map base64_decode (H2.Headers.get h "grpc-status-details-bin") in
      Some { code; message; details }
```

Spark Connect only uses two call shapes: unary (`AnalyzePlan`, `Config`, `Interrupt`, `ReleaseSession`, `FetchErrorDetails`, and friends) and server-streaming (`ExecutePlan`, `ReattachExecute`). A unary call is a streaming call where the client reads one message. There are no client-streaming or bidirectional methods except `AddArtifacts`, which is only needed to upload files to the server. That is the whole transport. It worked on the first query, and almost none of the effort in this project went into it.

## Step 3: A session, and the first RPC

Every request carries the same identity block: a `session_id` the client mints (a UUID), a `user_context` with a `user_id`, and a `client_type` string that is effectively a user agent. After the first reply the client also records the `server_side_session_id` the server sent and echoes it back as `client_observed_server_side_session_id` on every later request, which is how the server notices if it has restarted underneath the client.

The hello world of Connect is `AnalyzePlan` with the `spark_version` option, because it needs no plan:

```ocaml
let analyze t analyze =
  let req =
    P.Base.make_analyze_plan_request ~session_id:t.session_id
      ?client_observed_server_side_session_id:t.server_side_session_id
      ~user_context:(user_context t) ~client_type:t.client_type ~analyze ()
  in
  unary t ~method_:"AnalyzePlan" ~encode:P.Base.encode_pb_analyze_plan_request
    ~decode:P.Base.decode_pb_analyze_plan_response req
  >|= fun r -> observe t r.server_side_session_id; r

let version t =
  Client.analyze t.client B.Spark_version >|= fun r ->
  match r.result with Some (B.Spark_version v) -> v.version | _ -> failwith "unexpected response"
```

```text
server version: 4.2.0
```

Once that prints, the protobuf toolchain, the HTTP/2 stack, the gRPC framing and the session plumbing are all known good, and everything after it is vocabulary.

## Step 4: Build plans instead of running them

Plan building is the most clerical step of the seven. A `Relation` is a `common` block holding a `plan_id` plus a oneof of every operator the server understands: `Read`, `Project`, `Filter`, `Join`, `Aggregate`, `Sort`, `Limit`, `SetOp`, `Sample`, `Deduplicate`, `Range`, `Sql`, `LocalRelation`, and a long tail. A DataFrame method is a function that wraps the current relation in a new one, and that is the entire DataFrame API:

```ocaml
let of_rel_type client rel_type =
  { client;
    rel = R.make_relation ~common:(R.make_relation_common ~plan_id:(Client.fresh_plan_id client) ()) ~rel_type () }

let filter t cond = of_rel_type t.client (R.Filter (R.make_filter ~input:t.rel ~condition:cond ()))

let join ?(how = `Inner) t other ~on =
  of_rel_type t.client
    (R.Join (R.make_join ~left:t.rel ~right:other.rel ~join_condition:on ~join_type:(join_type_pb how) ()))
```

Expressions are the same idea one level down. A column reference is an `UnresolvedAttribute` holding a string; a literal is a `Literal` with a typed oneof; and every function *and every operator* is an `UnresolvedFunction` called by name, so `a + b` is the function `+` applied to two arguments and `a == b` is `==`. The client never resolves anything:

```ocaml
let fn ?(distinct = false) name args =
  of_expr_type (E.Unresolved_function
    (E.make_expression_unresolved_function ~function_name:name ~arguments:args ~is_distinct:distinct ()))

let add a b = fn "+" [ a; b ]
let eq a b = fn "==" [ a; b ]
let gt a b = fn ">" [ a; b ]
```

There is no analyzer in the client: `Column.col "nope"` is a string in a message until the server sees the plan, which is why a typo fails late under Connect. The client cannot check the name; it has no catalog to check it against.

The size of this layer depends on how much the server does, and the server does nearly everything. Each of the following is a server message rather than client code:

| What you'd expect to implement client-side           | What Connect actually does                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Rendering the table for `show()`                     | `ShowString` is a *relation*; the server formats the ASCII table and returns it as one string cell                                                                                               |
| `count()`                                            | an `Aggregate` with `count(1)`; the client reads back one row                                                                                                                                    |
| Schema, `printSchema()`, `explain()`                 | `AnalyzePlan` with `Schema`, `TreeString` or `Explain`; the server returns the type tree, the formatted text, or the plan string (the only way to see one, since Catalyst isn't on your machine) |
| `listTables()`, `currentDatabase()`, `tableExists()` | relations under the `Catalog` message; they execute like a query and return rows                                                                                                                 |
| `sql()` for DDL vs for a query                       | a `SqlCommand`; the server runs it eagerly and, for a query, hands back a relation to keep building on                                                                                           |
| Named and positional SQL parameters                  | literals attached to the `SqlCommand`; the server binds `:name` and `?`                                                                                                                          |
| Telling `a.id` from `b.id` in a self-join            | every relation carries a client-assigned `plan_id`, and an attribute can name the plan it belongs to                                                                                             |

The `plan_id` is the one piece of real design in this step. Because the client assigns `plan_id`s, it can mint a column reference bound to a particular DataFrame, and the server resolves it against that side of the join even when both sides have the same column names:

```ocaml
let col t name = Column.col_of_plan ~plan_id:(plan_id t) name

let a = Dataframe.alias people "a" and b = Dataframe.alias people "b" in
Dataframe.join a b ~on:Column.O.(Dataframe.col a "id" = Dataframe.col b "id" + Column.int 1)
```

## Step 5: Execute, and decode the Arrow that comes back

`ExecutePlan` takes a `Plan` (either a `Relation` to query or a `Command` to run) and returns a stream of `ExecutePlanResponse` messages. Each one has a `response_type` oneof: `arrow_batch` carries data, `sql_command_result` carries the relation a `SqlCommand` produced, `result_complete` is the end marker, and progress and metrics messages can be ignored at first. The collect loop is a fold over the stream:

```ocaml
let collect_arrow t =
  Client.execute t.client (root t) >>= fun stream ->
  let schema = ref None and batches = ref [] in
  Lwt_stream.iter
    (fun (r : B.execute_plan_response) ->
      match r.response_type with
      | Some (B.Arrow_batch ab) ->
          let sc, bs = Arrow_ipc.read_stream (Bytes.unsafe_to_string ab.data) in
          (match sc with Some s when !schema = None -> schema := Some s | _ -> ());
          batches := List.rev_append bs !batches
      | _ -> ())
    stream
  >|= fun () -> (!schema, List.rev !batches)
```

**Each `arrow_batch` in `ab.data` is a complete Arrow IPC stream**, a schema message followed by one record batch, not a bare batch sharing a schema across the response. So the decoder is a full IPC stream reader. In a language with an Arrow library this step is one function call. OCaml does not have one (the package on opam binds the C++ library, which defeats the point of a thin client), so this is where the project stopped being clerical.

An IPC stream is a sequence of messages, each framed as a continuation marker, a metadata length, a [FlatBuffers](https://flatbuffers.dev/) `Message`, and a body of raw buffers:

```text
FF FF FF FF  <int32 metadata length>  <FlatBuffer: Message{version, header type, header, bodyLength}>  <body>
```

The `Message` header is a `Schema` (a vector of `Field`s, each with a name, a nullability flag, a type union and child fields) or a `RecordBatch` (a row count, a vector of field *nodes* giving each column's length and null count, and a vector of *buffers* giving offsets into the body). Decoding a batch is a depth-first walk: for each field, take the next node, take its validity bitmap buffer, take its data buffer(s), and recurse into children for lists, structs and maps. FlatBuffers itself is a vtable-indirected binary format and reading it is a page or so of offset arithmetic. Then there is one decoder per type. The decoder is the largest file in the project not because Arrow is complicated but because Spark produces many Arrow types:

| Spark type                     | What arrives in the Arrow batch                                                                                   |
| ------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| tinyint, smallint, int, bigint | `Int` with bit width and signedness; a fixed-width buffer                                                         |
| float, double                  | `FloatingPoint` with precision                                                                                    |
| string, binary                 | `Utf8` / `Binary`: an offsets buffer plus a data buffer (and `Large` variants with 64-bit offsets)                |
| decimal(p, s)                  | `Decimal`: 128-bit (or 256-bit) little-endian two's complement, which needs a bignum-to-decimal-string conversion |
| date                           | `Date32`, days since the epoch                                                                                    |
| timestamp                      | `Timestamp` in microseconds, with the session time zone as a string                                               |
| timestamp_ntz                  | the same with no time zone                                                                                        |
| interval year to month         | `Interval(YEAR_MONTH)`                                                                                            |
| interval day to second         | `Duration(MICROSECOND)`                                                                                           |
| array, struct, map             | `List`, `Struct`, `Map`: child columns with their own nodes and validity bitmaps                                  |

Decimal decoding was the only algorithmic piece, and only because the natural answer (the `zarith` bignum library) is a C dependency I did not want in a client whose point is having none. Performance without tuning was acceptable: a two-column projection over three million rows (a bigint and a SHA-1 string) came back and decoded in 1.63 seconds on localhost, with the client building a boxed value per cell, the least efficient representation available. The server's time dominates.

## Step 6: Sending data to the server

`createDataFrame` has to send rows *to* the server, and Connect's `LocalRelation` message carries them as, again, an Arrow IPC stream. A client that builds a DataFrame from local values therefore needs an Arrow *writer*, including a FlatBuffers *builder* for the schema and record batch metadata:

```ocaml
let create_dataframe ?schema t ~columns rows =
  let data = Arrow_writer.encode ?schema ~columns rows in
  of_rel_type t (R.Local_relation (R.make_local_relation ~data:(Bytes.unsafe_of_string data) ()))
```

The builder is the fiddly half. FlatBuffers are written back to front with vtables, alignment padding and forward offsets, and a byte out of place produces a Java stack trace on the server rather than anything that points at the byte. So the acceptance test for the writer was not the Spark server, which is forgiving, but `pyarrow`'s `validate(full=True)`, which is not. The stream passed with every Spark type the decoder reads, including nested lists, structs and decimals. The server infers the Spark schema from the Arrow schema, so a local table of `Value.Int`, `Value.String` and `Value.Float` cells comes up as `bigint`, `string` and `double` with no DDL string needed (a DDL string can be passed for narrower types).

Every official client carries both halves of this codec; they borrow them from an Arrow library the language already had.

## Step 7: Errors, the way Spark sends them

The `grpc-status-details-bin` trailer is base64 of a `google.rpc.Status`, whose `details` is a list of `Any`. Spark puts a `google.rpc.ErrorInfo` in it, and the `metadata` map on that is where everything useful lives: `classes` (the JVM exception class chain as a JSON array), `sqlState`, `errorId`, and `messageParameters`. The error id goes to `FetchErrorDetails` for the server-side stack trace and query context.

```ocaml
let status = P.Status.decode_pb_status (Pbrt.Decoder.of_string raw) in
let info =
  List.find_map
    (fun (a : P.Any.any) ->
      if ends_with ~suffix:"google.rpc.ErrorInfo" a.type_url then
        Some (P.Error_details.decode_pb_error_info (Pbrt.Decoder.of_string (Bytes.to_string a.value)))
      else None)
    status.details
in
(* info.metadata: ("classes", "[...]"), ("sqlState", "42P01"), ("errorId", "..."), ... *)
```

The Spark error condition itself is not a separate field; it is the bracketed prefix of the message, so a client lifts it with a trivial parse. The OCaml client's output for a query on a table that does not exist, with no string matching beyond that bracket:

```text
Spark error INTERNAL (org.apache.spark.sql.catalyst.ExtendedAnalysisException):
[TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND] The table or view `nope` cannot be found. ...
SQLSTATE: 42P01; line 1 pos 14;
'Project [*]
+- 'UnresolvedRelation [nope], [], false
```

`error_class = TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND`, `sql_state = 42P01`, and the exception classes as a list. The server supplies all of it; the client's job is to keep it.

## Putting it together

With those seven pieces the client reads like every other Connect client, because they all converge on the proto's shape:

```ocaml
open Lwt.Infix
open Spark_connect

let () =
  Lwt_main.run begin
    Session.connect "sc://localhost:15002" >>= fun spark ->
    let people = Session.create_dataframe spark ~columns:[ "id"; "name" ]
      [ [ Value.Int 1; Value.String "ann" ]; [ Value.Int 2; Value.String "bob" ] ] in
    let orders = Session.create_dataframe spark ~columns:[ "pid"; "amount" ]
      [ [ Value.Int 1; Value.Float 10.0 ]; [ Value.Int 1; Value.Float 5.5 ] ] in
    let per_person =
      Dataframe.join people orders ~on:Column.O.(Column.col "id" = Column.col "pid")
      |> fun df -> Dataframe.group_by df [ Column.col "name" ]
      |> fun g -> Dataframe.Grouped.agg g [ Column.alias (F.sum (Column.col "amount")) "total" ] in
    Dataframe.show per_person >>= fun () ->
    Session.close spark
  end
```

```text
+----+-----+
|name|total|
+----+-----+
| ann| 15.5|
+----+-----+
```

The two local tables went up inside the plan as `LocalRelation`s, the join and aggregate went up as relation nodes around them, the server formatted the table and returned it as a one-cell Arrow batch, and the whole exchange was a single `ExecutePlan` call, since nothing before `show` touches the server. Pointed at a Databricks endpoint with `sc://host:443/;token=...`, the same client turns TLS on because the token is present, which is what the connection string spec asks for and what every client reimplements.

The SQL path is the only one with a wrinkle: `sql()` sends a `SqlCommand` and executes eagerly, so `CREATE TABLE` runs right away, and for a query the reply carries a `sql_command_result` relation that the client wraps as the DataFrame to keep building on. Config is a unary call with get/set/unset operations, the catalog is relations, writers are `WriteOperation` (v1, with save modes) and `WriteOperationV2` (create/replace/append) commands, and `persist` is an `AnalyzePlan` option.

## Testing its Production Readiness

So, here begets the real question: is this actually usable? Well, maybe. As much as I'd love Jane Street to plug this in and hire me to maintain it (though, I'm pretty happy at Databricks right now), there's still some coverage issues, particularly around UDFs which are highly variable anyways.
 
 For my own due diligence, I tested the client two ways: every message it can build, exercised against more than one Spark release, and execution on a real cluster of the kind of work I naively imagine someone at Jane Street would reach for OCaml to do.

### Every message, tested against three Spark releases

Coverage is precisely measurable for a Connect client, because the protocol is a finite list of protobuf messages. The repo has a script that reads the generated bindings, finds which relations, expressions, commands, catalog calls and analyze requests the client builds, follows each one back to the public function that builds it, and checks whether a test calls that function. Its output is [docs/protocol-coverage.md](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-connect-ocaml/blob/main/docs/protocol-coverage.md), regenerated rather than maintained by hand:

| Protocol area                    | Implemented | Of those, tested |
| -------------------------------- | ----------- | ---------------- |
| Relations (DataFrame operations) | 33 of 61    | all              |
| Expressions                      | 14 of 22    | all              |
| Literal types                    | 18 of 22    | all              |
| Catalog                          | 21 of 36    | all              |
| AnalyzePlan requests             | 11 of 14    | all              |
| Config operations                | 7 of 7      | all              |
| Commands                         | 4 of 20     | all              |

The same suite passes against Spark 4.1.3, 4.2.0 and 4.3.0-rc1. The unimplemented messages are mostly the runtime half of the protocol (streaming, UDFs, ML, pipelines), plus a tail of statistics relations like `crosstab` and `approx_quantile` that I have not needed yet.

The tests found bugs that a demo doesn't make obvious. `na_fill` sent whole numbers as 32-bit integer literals, which the server's fill rejects outright (PySpark always sends longs, so it never meets this). Sort orders without an explicit null ordering went up as "unspecified", so an ascending sort put nulls last where Spark and PySpark put them first. And `show()` did not end with a newline, so two tables printed in a row ran together. The suite also had a bug of its own: it compared a `TIMESTAMP` literal without pinning the session time zone, so it passed on every server running in UTC (all of my Docker ones) and failed on the one running natively on my machine.

### Case Study: A small options desk

OCaml's best-known home outside academia is finance, where trading firms write their pricing and risk code in it, wirh the same firms keep their market history in data lakes that Spark reads. OCaml and Spark here have historically met through Python or a SQL string.

So my E2E is a small options desk with one question: **should 30-day index options be priced off realized volatility, measured from recent prices, or off the VIX, the market's implied volatility?**

The pricing code is borrowed. It is the closed-form Black-Scholes module from Case Ollila's [option-pricing-model-comparison](https://github.com/crollila/option-pricing-model-comparison) (MIT), typed OCaml with Greeks in trader units and every numeric routine written from scratch, vendored unchanged into the example. The market data is public: daily S&P 500, Nasdaq Composite and Dow Jones closes, the VIX, and the 3-month Treasury yield, all from [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/). The whole thing runs as one OCaml program, [`spark-demos/demos/08_spark_connect_ocaml`](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-demos/tree/main/demos/08_spark_connect_ocaml), against a standalone Spark 4.2 cluster with Delta Lake:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  classDef you fill:#9a7b00,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#9a7b00,color:#ffffff
  classDef srv fill:#c0661a,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#c0661a,color:#ffffff
  classDef ex fill:#3a5f96,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#3a5f96,color:#ffffff
  classDef data fill:#6b4a9b,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#6b4a9b,color:#ffffff
  A["options_desk.exe<br/>OCaml client +<br/>option_pricer"]:::you -->|"sc://, gRPC"| B["Spark Connect server<br/>Delta Lake"]:::srv
  B -->|"tasks"| W1["worker 1<br/>executor + Python"]:::ex
  B -->|"tasks"| W2["worker 2<br/>executor + Python"]:::ex
  W1 -->|"pyspark_fred"| F[("FRED<br/>daily series")]:::data
  W2 --> F
  W1 <--> D[("Delta warehouse<br/>prices · daily · book")]:::data
  W2 <--> D
```

The program is a pipeline, and each step that can check itself does so against an independent calculation:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  classDef step fill:#3a5f96,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#3a5f96,color:#ffffff
  classDef oc fill:#9a7b00,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#9a7b00,color:#ffffff
  S1["1 ingest<br/>Python adapter → Delta"]:::step --> S2["2 analytics<br/>returns · realized vol ·<br/>drawdowns"]:::step
  S2 --> S3["3 pricing<br/>Black-Scholes in OCaml"]:::oc
  S3 --> S4["4 risk layer<br/>metric view"]:::step
  S4 --> S5["5 next day<br/>MERGE · time travel"]:::step
```

**1. Market data through a Python adapter.** The adapter is a short [Python data source](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-demos/blob/main/demos/08_spark_connect_ocaml/pyspark_fred/__init__.py) that downloads FRED series, one partition per series, installed on every node as a `pyspark_fred` package so Spark discovers it with no per-session registration. From OCaml the adapter is a format name:

```ocaml
let fred spark series =
  Session.read spark |> fun r ->
  Session.Reader.format r "fred" |> fun r ->
  Session.Reader.option r "series" (String.concat "," series) |> fun r -> Session.Reader.load r
```

The client never learns that Python is involved: it sends a `Read` relation naming a format, the executors run the adapter, and the same Arrow batches come back that the decoder reads for any query. The ingest lands ten years of closes in a Delta table (ten years because that is what FRED's agreement with S&P Dow Jones Indices lets it publish for their series, and the job trims the Nasdaq to the same window):

```text
+---------+--------+----------+----------+
|   series|count(1)| min(date)| max(date)|
+---------+--------+----------+----------+
|     DJIA|    2514|2016-10-10|2026-10-09|
|NASDAQCOM|    2515|2016-10-10|2026-10-09|
|    SP500|    2514|2016-10-10|2026-10-09|
+---------+--------+----------+----------+
```

**2. The heavy part, in Spark.** Daily log returns come from a `lag` over each series, realized volatility is the standard deviation of the last 21 returns annualized by the square root of 252 trading days, and drawdown is each close against the running maximum, all window functions built in OCaml and evaluated on the cluster:

```ocaml
let by_day = Column.Window.partition_by [ col "series" ] |> fun w -> Column.Window.with_order_by w [ col "date" ] in
let last_21 = Column.Window.rows_between by_day (Column.Window.Value (Column.int (-20))) Column.Window.current_row in
let daily =
  Dataframe.with_columns prices [ ("ret", F.log Column.O.(col "value" / Column.over (F.lag (col "value")) by_day)) ]
  |> fun d -> Dataframe.with_column d "rv21" Column.O.(Column.over (F.stddev (col "ret")) last_21 * F.sqrt (Column.int 252))
```

```text
+---------+----------+--------+--------+------------+----------------+-------------+
|   series|      date|    spot|rv21_pct|avg_rv21_pct|max_drawdown_pct|worst_day_pct|
+---------+----------+--------+--------+------------+----------------+-------------+
|     DJIA|2026-10-09|51654.95|    10.2|        14.3|           -37.1|        -13.8|
|NASDAQCOM|2026-10-09|27366.17|    14.2|        19.4|           -36.4|        -13.1|
|    SP500|2026-10-09| 7811.54|    10.0|        15.0|           -33.9|        -12.8|
+---------+----------+--------+--------+------------+----------------+-------------+
```

The worst single day for all three is 16 March 2020. The deepest drawdown is March 2020 for the S&P 500 and the Dow, but December 2022 for the Nasdaq, whose 2022 bear market went further than the Covid crash. Joining the S&P 500's trailing realized volatility to the VIX day by day answers half the desk's question: over the decade the VIX sat above realized volatility on 86.1% of trading days, by 3.7 volatility points on average. That gap is a rough measure of the volatility risk premium, the price the market charges for insurance.

**3. Pricing, in OCaml.** The program pulls the latest close and realized volatility for each index, plus the current VIX and T-bill yield, and hands them to the pricer as its author intended (I set the dividend yield to zero to keep the example small):

```ocaml
let m = { T.spot; strike = spot; ttm = 30. /. 365.; rate; div_yield = 0.0; vol = rv series } in
let g = BS.greeks kind m in
(BS.price kind m, g.delta, BS.vega_per_point g.vega, BS.theta_per_day g.theta)
```

```text
  risk-free (3m T-bill) 4.23%, VIX 15.4
  index      kind contracts     strike    vol  premium   delta   vega/pt theta/day
  SP500      call        20    7811.54  10.0%   103.40   0.554      8.85     -1.96
  SP500      put        -10    7811.54  10.0%    76.28  -0.446      8.85     -1.06
  NASDAQCOM  call         5   27366.17  14.2%   492.76   0.542     31.13     -9.03
  DJIA       put          8   51654.95  10.2%   516.15  -0.447     58.56     -7.22
  SP500 30-day ATM call: 103.40 at realized vol (10.0%), 151.41 at VIX (15.4%)
```

The same at-the-money S&P call is worth 103.40 at realized volatility and 151.41 at the VIX, 46% more, which is the volatility risk premium expressed in dollars. Put-call parity, the pricer's own check that its calls and puts are consistent with each other, holds for every index to within 5e-13. The priced book then goes back to Spark the other way, as a `LocalRelation` built from OCaml values and written as a Delta table.

**4. The risk layer, as a metric view.** Spark 4.2 added metric views ([SPARK-54403](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-54403), [SPARK-54405](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-54405)): a view defined in YAML as a source, dimensions, and measures, where each measure is an aggregate defined once and queried with `measure()` under whatever grouping the query asks for. A risk layer has the same shape, so the desk's exposures are defined once:

```yaml
version: "0.1"
source: desk_book
dimensions:
  - name: index_name
    expr: index_name
  - name: kind
    expr: kind
measures:
  - name: premium_usd
    expr: cast(round(sum(premium * contracts * 100)) as bigint)
  - name: dollar_delta
    expr: cast(round(sum(delta * contracts * 100 * spot)) as bigint)
  - name: vega_usd_per_pt
    expr: cast(round(sum(vega_pt * contracts * 100)) as bigint)
  - name: theta_usd_per_day
    expr: cast(round(sum(theta_day * contracts * 100)) as bigint)
```

The client has no code for metric views at all. Defining one is a SQL statement, and querying one from the DataFrame API is a function call, because `measure` is a function the server resolves:

```ocaml
Dataframe.group_by (Session.table spark "desk_risk") [ col "index_name" ] |> fun g ->
Dataframe.Grouped.agg g (List.map (fun m -> Column.alias (Column.fn "measure" [ col m ]) m)
                           [ "premium_usd"; "dollar_delta"; "vega_usd_per_pt"; "theta_usd_per_day" ])
```

```text
+----------+-----------+------------+---------------+-----------------+
|index_name|premium_usd|dollar_delta|vega_usd_per_pt|theta_usd_per_day|
+----------+-----------+------------+---------------+-----------------+
|      DJIA|     412920|   -18467411|          46844|            -5775|
| NASDAQCOM|     246379|     7417769|          15563|            -4514|
|     SP500|     130507|    12138611|           8853|            -2867|
+----------+-----------+------------+---------------+-----------------+
```

The check computes the same four sums directly from the book table and compares them row by row. They match.

**5. The next day.** The desk adds to its S&P calls and closes the Nasdaq position, as a `MERGE` from a DataFrame of fills built in OCaml. Delta keeps the previous book, and `VERSION AS OF` reads it back:

```text
  yesterday: [DJIA, put, 8] [NASDAQCOM, call, 5] [SP500, call, 20] [SP500, put, -10]
  today:     [DJIA, put, 8] [SP500, call, 25] [SP500, put, -10]
```

| Check | Compared against | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Put-call parity, each index | the pricer's own arbitrage identity | pass |
| Priced book written to Delta | the number of positions sent | pass |
| Risk measures from the metric view | the same aggregation on the book table | pass |
| Time travel to yesterday's book | the book before the `MERGE` | pass |

On the cluster, every Spark job succeeded, with the tasks split close to evenly between the two workers' executors.

## What's left on my to do list, and where the official clients spend their time

What this client does not do is also a map of where Connect stops being a plan-and-Arrow protocol and starts being a runtime:

- **Reattachable execution.** The official clients use `ReattachExecute` and `ReleaseExecute` so a dropped connection can resume a long query from the last response it saw. This one uses plain `ExecutePlan`, which Spark 4 servers fully support, but a flaky network on an hour-long query loses the query. It is the first thing to add.
- **User-defined functions.** A UDF in Connect is serialized *code* shipped to the server: pickled Python, or a Scala closure with its JARs uploaded through `AddArtifacts`. It only works when the server can run the client's language, and there is no OCaml runtime on a Spark executor. **This client will never have UDFs**; it has the whole SQL function library and higher-order functions with lambdas. Code that already lives on the server is a different matter: the desk's market-data adapter is Python installed on the executors, and any client can call it by name.
- **Streaming, MLlib and pipeline commands.** The messages are generated and reachable, but each is a stateful API rather than a plan.
- **Dictionary-encoded or compressed Arrow batches.** Spark does not send them by default; the decoder raises if it ever meets one.

Each item is either resilience or a place where the client has to be a runtime instead of a plan builder. The line between those halves is the line Connect draws. The first half is small enough to build in a language the Spark project will never target. The second half is where the Go, Swift and Rust clients are spending their effort, and it is the half to check before building on any of them.

## Further reading

- [Spark Connect overview](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/spark-connect-overview.html) and the [protobuf definitions](https://github.com/apache/spark/tree/master/sql/connect/common/src/main/protobuf/spark/connect) that are the real spec
- [gRPC over HTTP/2](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/master/doc/PROTOCOL-HTTP2.md), the framing and trailer rules from step 2
- [Arrow IPC streaming format](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/Columnar.html#serialization-and-interprocess-communication-ipc) and the [FlatBuffers schema](https://github.com/apache/arrow/tree/main/format) it's described in
- [spark-connect-ocaml](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-connect-ocaml), the client this post walks through, and the official [Go](https://github.com/apache/spark-connect-go), [Rust](https://github.com/apache/spark-connect-rust) and [Swift](https://github.com/apache/spark-connect-swift) clients to compare it against

---

# All About Iceberg's File Format API: simplifying the engine/format interface and Parquet's multimodal future

URL: https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/iceberg-file-format-api
Republished at: https://openlakehouse.io/blog/iceberg/iceberg-file-format-api
Original publisher: systems/null
Date: 2026-10-12
Category: Iceberg

*Originally published on [systems/null](https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/iceberg-file-format-api).*

## What is the file format API?

Apache Iceberg traditionally exposed its data files through three libraries, one each for Parquet, Avro and ORC, and until this year every engine that spoke Iceberg had its own way of calling them. Spark had `SparkParquetReaders`, Flink had `FlinkParquetReaders`, the generic Java API had `GenericParquetReaders`, and each engine chose its own path through the format's read options, filter pushdown, split handling, encryption and metrics. The practical effect was that a feature added to one format for one engine (a new v3 type, a default value, a shredded variant column) tended to arrive for the other engines later or not at all, because the work had to be redone per engine. 

The File Format API, which shipped in 1.11.0 and was [announced](https://iceberg.apache.org/blog/apache-iceberg-file-format-api/) in February, is the project's attempt to streamline all this: a single registry of "format models," each one the pairing of a file format with an engine's in-memory row type, and a single set of builders (`ReadBuilder`, `FileWriterBuilder` and its delete-file siblings) that every engine now goes through. It was also originally framed as the way to try out newer formats such as Vortex and Lance, which are fundamentally designed very differently than Parquet and meant specifically for vector work and multimodal data storage. 

Note for Rust/Python users: this is a Java API. The registry lives in `iceberg-core`, so it reaches exactly the engines that link that jar and reuse its readers (Spark, Flink, Hive, the plain Java `Record` path). DuckDB, DataFusion via iceberg-rust, PyIceberg and Polars each implement the Iceberg spec with their own readers and leverage Arrow readers instead. For Trino, which is Java, it instead uses Iceberg's core for metadata and its own Parquet and ORC readers for data. DuckDB, DataFusion, Polars and PyIceberg all read into Arrow or something Arrow can hand over without copying, so the row-type axis collapses to one and a new format just needs an Arrow reader (Lance and Vortex both ship one). Java implementations have three row types and no shared memory format, which is why it needed a registry to play the role Arrow plays everywhere else.

| Engine                             | Language | Reads Iceberg data files with                                    | Goes through the registry? |
| ---------------------------------- | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| Spark, Flink, Hive, plain Java API | Java     | Iceberg's own readers from `iceberg-core` and the format modules | yes                        |
| Trino                              | Java     | its own Parquet and ORC readers; Iceberg core for metadata only  | no                         |
| PyIceberg                          | Python   | its own readers on PyArrow                                       | no                         |
| DataFusion (via iceberg-rust)      | Rust     | its own Arrow-based Parquet reader                               | no                         |
| DuckDB                             | C++      | its own Parquet reader                                           | no                         |
| Polars                             | Rust     | Arrow                                                            | no                         |

*Table 1. Which engines the File Format API actually reaches.*

## Reducing Format Model x Reader Complexity

A **file format** is how bytes are laid out on disk: Parquet, Avro and ORC each have their own encoding, compression, statistics and footer, and Iceberg doesn't care which one a given data file uses as long as it can read it. An **engine in-memory row type**, which the project calls the *object model*, is how one row looks in memory once it's been read, and that depends on the engine, not the file: Spark wants an `InternalRow`, Flink a `RowData`, the plain Java API an Iceberg `Record`. The same Parquet file can be read into any of them, and the same `InternalRow` can be written out as Parquet or ORC. A format model is one cell in that grid: one format, one row type.

Here is the grid as it stands at 1.12.0, with a mark wherever a format model exists:

| Row type (object model) | Parquet | Avro | ORC |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Record` (plain Java API) | yes | yes | yes |
| `InternalRow` (Spark, row at a time) | yes | yes | yes |
| `ColumnarBatch` (Spark, vectorized) | read only | no | read only |
| `ColumnarBatch` (Arrow) | read only | no | no |
| `RowData` (Flink) | yes | yes | yes |

*Table 2. The format-by-row-type grid. Each "yes" is one registered format model.*

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  classDef fmt fill:#c0661a,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#c0661a,color:#ffffff
  classDef eng fill:#3a5f96,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#3a5f96,color:#ffffff
  P["one Parquet file<br/>(bytes on disk)"]:::fmt --> M1["format model<br/>(PARQUET, InternalRow)"] --> S["InternalRow<br/>in Spark's memory"]:::eng
  P --> M2["format model<br/>(PARQUET, RowData)"] --> F["RowData<br/>in Flink's memory"]:::eng
  P --> M3["format model<br/>(PARQUET, Record)"] --> G["Record<br/>in the Java API"]:::eng
```

Scale this complexity further, per engine and per format:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  classDef eng fill:#3a5f96,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#3a5f96,color:#ffffff
  classDef fmt fill:#c0661a,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#c0661a,color:#ffffff
  S["Spark"]:::eng --> SP["SparkParquetReaders"] --> P["Parquet"]:::fmt
  S --> SA["SparkAvroReader"] --> A["Avro"]:::fmt
  S --> SO["SparkOrcReader"] --> O["ORC"]:::fmt
  F["Flink"]:::eng --> FP["FlinkParquetReaders"] --> P
  F --> FA["FlinkAvroReader"] --> A
  F --> FO["FlinkOrcReader"] --> O
  G["Java API"]:::eng --> GP["GenericParquetReaders"] --> P
  G --> GA["..."] --> A
  G --> GO["..."] --> O
```

After, through the File Format API's registry:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  classDef eng fill:#3a5f96,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#3a5f96,color:#ffffff
  classDef reg fill:#6b4a9b,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#6b4a9b,color:#ffffff
  classDef fmt fill:#c0661a,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#c0661a,color:#ffffff
  S["Spark"]:::eng --> R["FormatModelRegistry<br/>readBuilder(format, rowType, file)"]:::reg
  F["Flink"]:::eng --> R
  G["Java API"]:::eng --> R
  R --> P["ParquetFormatModel"]:::fmt
  R --> A["AvroFormatModel"]:::fmt
  R --> O["ORCFormatModel"]:::fmt
```

**The API makes the engine's row type pluggable over a fixed list of file formats, such that any engine can register its own representation and read every Iceberg table through the shared builders, while a new format remains a change inside the Iceberg project; and because the formats are fixed, multimodal support is arriving as new column types defined on the Parquet side (see FILE type that was shipped in parquet-format 2.14.0, VECTOR type currently in proposal stage) and mirrored into the next table spec.

## Into the weeds 

Everything in the API is built on one map, which makes it the ideal place to start digging into in the codebase to gain a better understanding. If you only want to read and write files through the registry, skip ahead to "Usage." Read this section to understand *why* the API behaves the way it does, and come back to it when something in a later section needs the detail.

### The registry key

A *map* here is the ordinary programming kind: a lookup table from a key to a value. In `FormatModelRegistry`, the key is a pair (which file format, which row type) and the value is a *format model*, the object that knows how to read and write that one combination. Here is the method that puts entries into the map:

```java
// core/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/formats/FormatModelRegistry.java (1.12.0)
public static synchronized void register(FormatModel<?, ?> formatModel) {
  Pair<FileFormat, Class<?>> key = Pair.of(formatModel.format(), formatModel.type());
  ...
  MODELS.put(key, formatModel);
}
```

The second half of the key, `Class<?>`, is the Java class of the row the engine wants back. For the plain Java API it is Iceberg's own `Record`; for Spark it is `InternalRow` (one row at a time) or `ColumnarBatch` (a block of rows); for Flink it is `RowData`. The Iceberg project calls this the *object model*.

> **Object model versus schema**
> The object model is the engine's in-memory shape for a row. It says nothing about the file and nothing about the table's schema. The *schema* says which columns a table has; the *object model* says what Java class a row of that table becomes once it is read.

The first half of the key, `FileFormat`, is an *enum*: a type whose allowed values are a fixed list written into the source code. You cannot add a value at runtime. This enum lives in `iceberg-api`, the module that holds Iceberg's public interfaces:

```java
// api/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/FileFormat.java (1.12.0)
public enum FileFormat {
  PUFFIN("puffin", false),
  ORC("orc", true),
  PARQUET("parquet", true),
  AVRO("avro", true),
  METADATA("metadata.json", false);
  ...
}
```

Puffin and metadata appear because the enum names every kind of file Iceberg writes, not only data files. Puffin files hold statistics and deletion vectors; `metadata.json` is the table's root file. The three data formats are the ones in the middle: ORC, Parquet and Avro.

The two halves of the key are not the same kind of thing, and that difference organizes the rest of this post:

| Half of the key | Type | Allowed values | Who can add one |
|---|---|---|---|
| Format | `FileFormat` enum in `iceberg-api` | the five names above | the Iceberg project, by changing the enum |
| Row type | any `Class<?>` | anything | any engine, by calling `register()` |

*Table 3. The two halves of the registry key.*

The announcement says the registry "decouples engines from specific formats and allows new formats to be added without modifying engine code." That is true as far as engine code goes. What a new format has to modify is `iceberg-api`, the enum itself.

### What happens on a read

A *scan task* is Iceberg's description of one file to read, including which format it is in. From the task to the rows, a read goes like this:

1. The engine asks the registry for a read builder, passing the task's format, its own row type, and the file.
2. The registry looks up the (format, row type) pair.
3. If the pair is registered, the model returns a builder. The engine sets the columns it wants, a filter, and the byte range of the file it was assigned, then calls `build()`.
4. If the pair is not registered, the registry throws an error that names the pair it could not find.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    T["scan task<br/>file.format() = PARQUET"] --> R["FormatModelRegistry.readBuilder(<br/>PARQUET, InternalRow.class, inputFile)"]
    R --> K{"(PARQUET, InternalRow)<br/>in MODELS?"}
    K -->|yes| M["ParquetFormatModel<br/>registered by SparkFormatModels"]
    M --> B["ReadBuilder: project, filter,<br/>split, partition constants"]
    B --> I["CloseableIterable&lt;InternalRow&gt;"]
    K -->|no| E["IllegalArgumentException:<br/>Format model is not registered<br/>for format PARQUET and type ..."]
    F["FileFormat enum<br/>PUFFIN, ORC, PARQUET, AVRO, METADATA"] -.->|"format: one of these"| K
    C["Class&lt;?&gt;<br/>Record, InternalRow, ColumnarBatch, RowData, ..."] -.->|"type: anything"| K
```

The dotted lines draw the open-versus-closed distinction: one input to the lookup comes from a fixed list, the other is whatever the engine says it is.

### How models get registered

When the registry class is first loaded, it tries to call a `register()` method on four classes by name: the generic models, and the Arrow, Flink and Spark ones. If one of those classes, or something it depends on, is not on the *classpath* (the set of jars the program was started with), the registry logs a line and moves on. The practical consequence is that the contents of the map depend on which Iceberg jars you ship. You will see this directly in the "Usage" section. Everything the project registers at 1.12.0 is an engine's row type against a format Iceberg already had (Table 2); none of it is a new format.

## Usage

It would be a terrible user experience to construct format models yourself; so instead you'll ask the registry for a builder and configure it. A *builder* is an object you set options on one at a time and then finish with `build()`. The registry exposes two of them, and together they are the whole surface an engine touches:

| Call | You pass | You set | You get back |
|---|---|---|---|
| `readBuilder(format, rowType, inputFile)` | the file's format, your row type, the file | columns to project, a filter, a byte range (split) | something you can iterate over, yielding rows of your type |
| `dataWriteBuilder(format, rowType, outputFile)` | the format to write, your row type, the output | the schema and partition spec | a writer; closing it yields a `DataFile`, the record Iceberg stores in its manifests, with column statistics already filled in |

*Table 4. The two registry calls an engine uses.*

### Where this code lives

If your experience of Iceberg so far is `spark.sql("SELECT * FROM demo.orders")` or a REST catalog behind a `/v1/namespaces` endpoint, the first question is where code like this even goes. It goes nowhere near either of those. There are three different places you can stand when you use Iceberg, and the File Format API only exists at the lowest one:

| Where you stand | What you type | What Iceberg does for you | Sees the Format API? |
|---|---|---|---|
| An engine (Spark SQL, Flink SQL, Trino) | `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `MERGE` | catalog lookup, planning, file reads and writes, commits | No. The engine calls it for you. |
| A catalog client (the REST catalog, PyIceberg, a Spark catalog config) | load a table, list snapshots, commit metadata | metadata only; no data files are opened | No. Files are not touched at this level. |
| The Java library directly (`iceberg-core`, `iceberg-data`, `iceberg-parquet` on a classpath) | Java against `Table`, `Schema`, `FormatModelRegistry` | only what you call | Yes. This is where the registry is a public class you can call. |

*Table 5. Three levels of using Iceberg. The Format API is reachable only from the bottom one.*

The program below is a plain Java `main` method with the Iceberg jars as dependencies. It is not a Spark job, it is not submitted to anything, and it does not need a catalog or even a table. It writes one Parquet file with Iceberg's own writer and reads it back with Iceberg's own reader, which is the single step every engine performs thousands of times per query and the only step the Format API is responsible for.

You would never run something like this in production. You run it when you want to see what the registry contains on a given classpath, or when you are writing a new format model and want the shortest possible loop between a change and a result. Here is the whole setup:

1. Make an empty directory with two files in it: `pom.xml` and `src/main/java/demo/Main.java`.
2. In `pom.xml` (Maven is Java's package manager, and this is its dependency list), declare the Iceberg modules you want on the classpath. The set is deliberately minimal: `iceberg-api`, `iceberg-core`, `iceberg-data` and `iceberg-parquet`, plus the Hadoop client jars Parquet needs and a logger. There is no `iceberg-orc`, and no Spark.
3. Run `mvn -q compile exec:java`. Maven downloads the jars from Maven Central, compiles `Main.java`, and runs it on the JVM in your terminal. The output below is what it prints.

### The program

I ran this against Iceberg 1.12.0 from Maven Central on Java 17, with nothing timed. The program does four things:

1. Prints the `FileFormat` enum.
2. Reaches into the registry and prints what is in the map.
3. Writes three records through the write builder, then reads them back through the read builder.
4. Asks for a (format, row type) pair that cannot be there.

```java
package demo;

import java.io.File;
import java.lang.reflect.Method;
import java.util.Map;
import org.apache.iceberg.DataFile;
import org.apache.iceberg.FileFormat;
import org.apache.iceberg.Files;
import org.apache.iceberg.PartitionSpec;
import org.apache.iceberg.Schema;
import org.apache.iceberg.data.GenericRecord;
import org.apache.iceberg.data.Record;
import org.apache.iceberg.encryption.EncryptionUtil;
import org.apache.iceberg.formats.FormatModelRegistry;
import org.apache.iceberg.io.CloseableIterable;
import org.apache.iceberg.io.DataWriter;
import org.apache.iceberg.types.Types;

public class Main {
  public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {

    // 1. The format half of the key: a fixed list, nothing is added at runtime.
    System.out.println("== FileFormat enum values");
    for (FileFormat f : FileFormat.values()) {
      System.out.println("  " + f + " splittable=" + f.isSplittable());
    }

    // 2. Peek inside the registry (reflection, since the map is private).
    //    Shows what the jars on the classpath registered before main() ran.
    System.out.println("== registered format models on this classpath (core + data + parquet)");
    Method models = FormatModelRegistry.class.getDeclaredMethod("models");
    models.setAccessible(true);
    Map<?, ?> m = (Map<?, ?>) models.invoke(null);
    m.keySet().stream().map(Object::toString).sorted().forEach(k -> System.out.println("  " + k));

    // An Iceberg schema. Columns are matched by the numeric field id, not by name.
    Schema schema = new Schema(
        Types.NestedField.required(1, "id", Types.LongType.get()),
        Types.NestedField.optional(2, "name", Types.StringType.get()));

    // A local file to write to; an engine would get an object store path from FileIO.
    File out = new File(args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "/tmp/ffa-demo.parquet");
    out.delete();

    // 3a. Write. (PARQUET, Record.class) is the registry key; build() does the lookup
    //     and hands back the Parquet model's writer, or throws if the pair is missing.
    System.out.println("== write via FormatModelRegistry.dataWriteBuilder(PARQUET, Record.class, ...)");
    DataWriter<Record> writer =
        FormatModelRegistry.<Record, Object>dataWriteBuilder(
                FileFormat.PARQUET, Record.class,
                EncryptionUtil.plainAsEncryptedOutput(Files.localOutput(out)))
            .schema(schema)
            .spec(PartitionSpec.unpartitioned())  // required even without partitioning
            .overwrite()
            .build();

    // Record is Iceberg's generic row type; copy(name, value, ...) makes a row.
    GenericRecord rec = GenericRecord.create(schema);
    for (long i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
      writer.write(rec.copy("id", i, "name", "row-" + i));
    }
    writer.close();

    // toDataFile() returns the manifest entry an engine would commit, statistics included.
    DataFile df = writer.toDataFile();
    System.out.println("  wrote " + df.path() + " format=" + df.format() + " records=" + df.recordCount()
        + " bytes=" + df.fileSizeInBytes() + " valueCounts=" + df.valueCounts());

    // 3b. Read. Same key, other direction. An engine would also set a filter and a split.
    System.out.println("== read via FormatModelRegistry.readBuilder(PARQUET, Record.class, ...)");
    try (CloseableIterable<Record> rows =
        FormatModelRegistry.<Record, Object>readBuilder(
                FileFormat.PARQUET, Record.class, Files.localInput(out))
            .project(schema)
            .build()) {
      for (Record r : rows) {
        System.out.println("  " + r);
      }
    }

    // 4. A valid format and a valid row type, but iceberg-orc is not on the
    //    classpath, so nobody registered the pair. The error names it.
    System.out.println("== ask for a model that is not registered (ORC with generic Record, no iceberg-orc on classpath)");
    try {
      FormatModelRegistry.readBuilder(FileFormat.ORC, Record.class, Files.localInput(out));
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
      System.out.println("  " + e.getMessage());
    }
  }
}
```

And its output:

```text
== FileFormat enum values
  PUFFIN splittable=false
  ORC splittable=true
  PARQUET splittable=true
  AVRO splittable=true
  METADATA splittable=false
== registered format models on this classpath (core + data + parquet)
  (AVRO, class org.apache.iceberg.deletes.PositionDelete)
  (AVRO, interface org.apache.iceberg.data.Record)
  (PARQUET, class org.apache.iceberg.deletes.PositionDelete)
  (PARQUET, interface org.apache.iceberg.data.Record)
== write via FormatModelRegistry.dataWriteBuilder(PARQUET, Record.class, ...)
  wrote .../out.parquet format=PARQUET records=3 bytes=684 valueCounts={1=3, 2=3}
== read via FormatModelRegistry.readBuilder(PARQUET, Record.class, ...)
  Record(1, row-1)
  Record(2, row-2)
  Record(3, row-3)
== ask for a model that is not registered (ORC with generic Record, no iceberg-orc on classpath)
  Format model is not registered for format ORC and type interface org.apache.iceberg.data.Record
```

Reading the output top to bottom:

- **The map holds Parquet and Avro**, each paired with the generic `Record` and with the position-delete row type, and nothing else.
- **Avro is present without being asked for**, because its model ships inside `iceberg-core`.
- **ORC is absent** because the `iceberg-orc` jar is not on the classpath, and the error names the exact pair the registry could not find.
- **The write returned `valueCounts`**: the writer filled in the `DataFile` statistics without the program doing anything.
- **One thing the program cannot express at all** is a request for a format outside the five names. There is no `FileFormat.LANCE` to pass, and converting the string `"lance"` to a `FileFormat` throws "Invalid file format: lance" before the registry is ever reached.

The row-type side is open. The format side is closed.

### The same call, from Spark

To connect this back to the level you already know: when you run `spark.read.table("demo.orders").show()` with the Iceberg connector, Spark loads the table through the catalog, plans which data files each task should scan, and then, for every file, makes exactly the call the program made by hand. Here is the Spark connector's version at 1.12.0, from `BaseRowReader` in the `iceberg-spark` module:

```java
// Same call as the program above, with Spark's row type and all the options set.
ReadBuilder<InternalRow, ?> reader =
    FormatModelRegistry.readBuilder(format, InternalRow.class, file);
return reader
    .project(projection)          // columns the query asked for
    .idToConstant(idToConstant)   // partition values, not stored in the file
    .reuseContainers()
    .split(start, length)         // this task's byte range
    .caseSensitive(caseSensitive())
    .filter(residual)             // what is left of the WHERE clause
    .withNameMapping(nameMapping())
    .build();
```

The `format` variable is the `FileFormat` recorded in the manifest entry for that file, and `InternalRow.class` is the row type Spark registered for itself in `SparkFormatModels` at startup. The query you type at the top level becomes, at the bottom level, one registry lookup per file. Everything between the two is planning.

## Exploring pluggability

The extension point is relatively easy to grokk and doesn't take a ton of code. This section covers what an engine supplies, what the format model owns, and what "pluggable" therefore means in practice.

Here is how the generic Parquet model is registered, with each argument labeled:

```java
// data/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/data/GenericFormatModels.java (1.12.0)
FormatModelRegistry.register(
    ParquetFormatModel.create(
        Record.class,          // the row type
        Schema.class,          // the engine schema type
        (icebergSchema, fileSchema, engineSchema) ->              // how to write a Record
            GenericParquetWriter.create(icebergSchema, fileSchema),
        (icebergSchema, fileSchema, engineSchema, idToConstant) ->  // how to read one
            GenericParquetReaders.buildReader(icebergSchema, fileSchema, idToConstant),
        new RecordVariantShreddingAnalyzer(),                      // see below
        (Function<Schema, UnaryOperator<Record>>) ignored -> Record::copy));  // how to copy a row
```

The engine supplies two functions. The **writer function**, given a schema, builds something that writes a row's values into Parquet. The **reader function** builds something that reads values out of Parquet into a row; its `idToConstant` argument is a map from column ids to values that come from metadata rather than from the file, mostly partition columns. `ParquetFormatModel` wraps those two functions in the builders every caller uses, and everything else lives in the model, once, for every engine:

| The engine supplies | The format model owns |
|---|---|
| the row class and the engine schema type | *schema conversion* between Iceberg's schema and the file's |
| a writer function (row values into the file) | *filter pushdown*: skipping chunks of the file that cannot match |
| a reader function (file values into a row) | *splits*: reading one byte range of a large file |
| a shredding analyzer (which variant fields to shred) | encryption |
| a row-copy function | the statistics that end up in the `DataFile` |
| | the shredded write path itself |

*Table 6. Division of labour between an engine and a format model.*

The engine never touches anything in the right-hand column.

> **The analyzer argument**
> *Variant* is Iceberg's type for semi-structured data such as JSON. *Shredding* is Parquet's technique of storing some of a variant's fields as ordinary columns so they can be filtered and read quickly. The Parquet model owns the shredded write path; each engine supplies an analyzer that says which fields to shred for its row type. There is one for `Record` here, and a Spark one and a Flink one in their modules. It is a small example of how the labour divides: the format owns the mechanism, the engine owns the choice.

So if you maintain an engine, or anything with its own idea of a row, this is your plugin point, and it is a good one. Register your row type against Parquet, Avro and ORC, and your engine reads any Iceberg table through the same builders Spark uses, without changing anything in the Iceberg project.

And the engines really do all go through it now, which is the part of the announcement that is simply true. Every reader in the 1.12.0 source that opens a data file (in Spark, Flink, the generic Java path, the MapReduce input format and the Arrow reader) gets its reader from the registry; none of them calls the old per-format `Parquet.read`, `ORC.read` or `Avro.read` directly any more. One implementation per format, shared by every engine, chosen by (format, row type).

Put that next to the dotted lines in the read diagram and "pluggable" comes into focus. What was scattered and is now unified is the engine side. What was fixed and is still fixed is the format side. That is not a flaw so much as a boundary, and the next section is about what sits on the other side of it.

## Where formats come into play and the compatibility kit

This section answers two questions: how does a new file format get into Iceberg today, and what does it have to pass once it is there?

### Adding a format: the Vortex example

A new format enters Iceberg the way the project's own showcase does. *Vortex* is a newer columnar file format, and its integration ([issue 15416](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/issues/15416)) has a pull request ([#15915](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15915)) that shows every step.
