# An Idiot's Guide to Spark Connect Clients

URL: https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/idiots-guide-spark-connect-clients
Republished at: https://openlakehouse.io/blog/apache-spark/idiots-guide-spark-connect-clients
Original publisher: systems/null
Date: 2026-10-05
Category: Apache Spark

*Originally published on [systems/null](https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/idiots-guide-spark-connect-clients).*

[Spark Connect](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/spark-connect-overview.html) is a new concept for many of us, especially given the long history of how managing Spark clusters has traditionally worked. Spark Connect in a nutshell separates your application from Spark: your code becomes a small client, Spark runs as a server somewhere else, and the two talk over the network. The primary benefit of Connect for most users is getting rid of the headaches around `SparkContext`, installing a package from your notebook, your Python version not mattering, or a typo failing on the line you typed it, which Connect very kindly obfuscates for us. Honestly, it's a pretty overdue upgrade for Spark as an engine and a pretty intuitive direction: decouple client sessions from the server, and make the server and its configuration as dead easy as possible for your customers.

The mindset shift away from having your PySpark setup share the same process as your Spark driver is not a super hard jump, but it does mean there are some adjustments to make in how you set things like configurations or write jobs. This becomes even more intense once you get into the meat of Spark Connect, which is the language agnosticism and running multiple clients and servers, particularly for those of us dabbling in Rust or Go.

So this guide, written for idiots by an idiot, starts with a tour of how Spark itself works and how that changes with a Connect setup. From there it's practical: how to run a server, how to connect to it from Python and other languages, what changes in your code, and how to do some basic debugging. Note that after the inclusion of session tracing in 4.3, and hopefully an eventual Spark Connect Gateway, the latter will be much, much easier.

Every example comes from [spark-demos](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-demos/tree/main/demos/02_spark_connect), where each one is a runnable script, and I ran every snippet here against Spark 4.2.0, the current release.

## How Spark works

Spark lets you write code as if you were working with one table on one machine, and then runs it across however many machines you have; Connect's whole trick is moving part of the machinery that makes that possible somewhere else, so it's worth having a picture of that machinery first. A running Spark application has a [few kinds of pieces](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/cluster-overview.html):

- **The driver** is the brain. It holds your `SparkSession`, works out what your code actually means, decides how to run it, and coordinates everything else. Inside it:
  - the **analyzer**, which resolves the tables and columns you named, using the **catalog** (the registry of what tables exist and what's in them);
  - the **[Catalyst optimizer](https://www.databricks.com/glossary/catalyst-optimizer)**, which rewrites your query into a cheaper equivalent (skipping columns you never use, filtering before joining, and so on);
  - the **planner**, which turns the optimized query into physical operations;
  - the **schedulers**, which cut that physical plan into **stages** (at every point where data has to be reshuffled between machines) and each stage into **tasks**, one per slice (**partition**) of the data.
- **The cluster manager** hands out machines: Spark's own standalone master, YARN, or Kubernetes.
- **Workers** are the machines (or containers) the cluster manager gives you.
- **Executors** are the processes on those workers that actually run tasks, read and write data, hold cached data, and exchange data with each other during a shuffle.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  classDef drv fill:#c0661a,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#c0661a,color:#ffffff
  classDef cm fill:#6b4a9b,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#6b4a9b,color:#ffffff
  classDef ex fill:#3a5f96,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#3a5f96,color:#ffffff
  subgraph a1_D["driver"]
    a1_SS["SparkSession"]:::drv --> a1_AN["analyzer + catalog"]:::drv
    a1_AN --> a1_CAT["Catalyst optimizer"]:::drv
    a1_CAT --> a1_SCH["planner + schedulers"]:::drv
  end
  a1_SCH -->|"asks for resources"| a1_CM["cluster manager"]:::cm
  a1_SCH -->|"sends tasks"| a1_E1["executor<br/>(on a worker)"]:::ex
  a1_SCH -->|"sends tasks"| a1_E2["executor<br/>(on a worker)"]:::ex
  a1_E1 <-->|"shuffle"| a1_E2
```

Following one line of code through all of that:

```python
orders.filter(orders.total > 20).groupBy("region").count().show()
```

| Step | What happens | Where |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Your code describes the query: filter, group, count | your program |
| 2 | That becomes an *unresolved logical plan*: a tree of operations naming tables and columns that haven't been checked yet | the driver |
| 3 | The analyzer checks `orders`, `total` and `region` against the catalog and fills in types | the driver |
| 4 | Catalyst optimizes the plan (here it reads only the two columns it needs) | the driver |
| 5 | The planner picks physical operators and generates code for them | the driver |
| 6 | The schedulers split the work into stages (before and after the shuffle `groupBy` needs) and tasks | the driver |
| 7 | Executors run the tasks against their slices of the data | the executors |
| 8 | The counts come back to the driver, and on to you | the driver, then your program |

Nothing actually runs until step 8 is needed; until you call something that wants a result (`show()`, `count()`, writing a table), Spark is only building the plan, which is what people mean by lazy evaluation. Classic Spark does run step 3 straight away (it checks your names the moment you define a DataFrame), and that small difference ends up mattering a lot once Connect is involved, so keep it in your back pocket for the debugging section.

**The detail that matters most for this guide is where the driver runs.** In classic PySpark (in the default "client" mode) the driver runs inside your program: your Python process starts a Java virtual machine next to it and talks to it through a bridge called [Py4J](https://www.py4j.org/), and that JVM *is* the driver, with the analyzer, the catalog connection, Catalyst and the schedulers all living in it.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  classDef you fill:#9a7b00,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#9a7b00,color:#ffffff
  classDef drv fill:#c0661a,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#c0661a,color:#ffffff
  classDef ex fill:#3a5f96,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#3a5f96,color:#ffffff
  subgraph a2_P["your process"]
    a2_PY["your Python code"]:::you <-->|"Py4J"| a2_JVM["driver JVM<br/>analyzer · Catalyst ·<br/>schedulers"]:::drv
  end
  a2_JVM --> a2_E1["executor"]:::ex
  a2_JVM --> a2_E2["executor"]:::ex
```

Your code and Spark's brain share a process, a machine, a set of installed libraries, and a fate, such that if one of them crashes it takes the other down with it.

## What the shared driver costs you

Sharing a process is fine when it's one person on one laptop, and it causes a surprising number of problems as soon as more than one person (or more than one program) uses the same Spark:

- **You need Java and all of Spark on every machine that runs your code**, including your laptop, a CI runner, or a web service that just wants to run one query.
- **Your application and Spark are upgraded together.** Upgrading Spark means changing the environment every job runs in, whether the job was ready or not.
- **Everyone's code shares the driver.** One badly behaved notebook can take the driver down for everyone attached to it.
- **Only JVM languages and Python can talk to Spark**, because they're the ones that can live inside or next to the JVM.
- **Credentials go everywhere the driver goes**, so catalog passwords and storage keys end up on every machine that runs a job.

Spark Connect fixes all of these with one change, which is that **it splits the driver in two.** The part you write against, the DataFrame API, stays in your program; everything that thinks (the session, the analyzer, the catalog, Catalyst, the schedulers) moves into a long-running **Spark Connect server**, with a network connection in between. Your program builds step 2, the unresolved plan, as a small [protobuf](https://protobuf.dev/) message, sends it over [gRPC](https://grpc.io/) and gets results back as [Arrow](https://arrow.apache.org/), and steps 3 to 8 all happen on the server.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  classDef you fill:#9a7b00,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#9a7b00,color:#ffffff
  classDef drv fill:#c0661a,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#c0661a,color:#ffffff
  classDef ex fill:#3a5f96,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#3a5f96,color:#ffffff
  subgraph a3_C["client"]
    a3_APP["your code<br/>DataFrame API"]:::you
  end
  subgraph a3_S["server"]
    a3_DRV["driver<br/>session · analyzer ·<br/>Catalyst · schedulers"]:::drv
  end
  a3_APP -->|"plan over gRPC"| a3_DRV
  a3_DRV -->|"Arrow"| a3_APP
  a3_DRV --> a3_E1["executor"]:::ex
  a3_DRV --> a3_E2["executor"]:::ex
```

Piece by piece, this is what moves and what stays put:

| Piece | Classic PySpark | Spark Connect |
|---|---|---|
| Your code and the DataFrame API | your process | your process (the client) |
| Building the unresolved plan | the driver JVM, via Py4J | the client, as a protobuf message |
| `SparkSession` and its state (temp views, settings, artifacts) | the driver, in your process | the server |
| Analyzer and catalog connection | the driver, in your process | the server |
| Catalyst, physical planning, code generation | the driver, in your process | the server |
| Stage and task scheduling | the driver, in your process | the server |
| Cluster manager, workers, executors | the cluster | the cluster, **unchanged** |
| Results | Py4J and a local socket into your process | Arrow batches over gRPC |
| Catalog and storage credentials | wherever the driver runs | the server only |

The cluster itself doesn't change at all, and executors run tasks exactly as they did before. What changes is that your program no longer contains a driver, so it doesn't need Java, it can be written in any language that speaks gRPC and Arrow, and it can be upgraded on its own schedule rather than the server's. Connect first appeared in Spark 3.4, and since 4.0 the server has shipped in the standard Spark download.

**Pretty much every confusing thing about Connect is this split showing up somewhere you didn't expect it.** `explain()` shows you a plan your laptop didn't make, because Catalyst is on the server; a typo in a column name fails late, because the analyzer is on the server and only sees your plan once you ask for a result; `sparkContext` is gone, because it belonged to the driver. Anything that used to live in your program (the JVM, your files, your Python version, your credentials) now lives on the other side of a network connection, and most of the rest of this guide is working through the consequences of that.

## Connecting from Python

From Python it's two steps: install the thin client ([`pyspark-client`](https://pypi.org/project/pyspark-client/)),

```bash
pip install pyspark-client
```

and create your session with `.remote(...)` instead of `.master(...)`:

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

spark = SparkSession.builder.remote("sc://localhost:15002").getOrCreate()
print(spark.version)            # the *server's* Spark version

orders = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("metro", "pizza", 24.0), ("metro", "sushi", 40.0), ("urban", "pizza", 18.0)],
    "region string, item string, total double",
)
orders.groupBy("region").agg(F.round(F.avg("total"), 2).alias("avg_ticket")).show()
```

Everything after the session line is ordinary PySpark, the same code you'd run in classic mode. Your program builds the plan and the server optimizes and runs it, so if you call `.explain()` you're reading the server's plan (your laptop doesn't have an optimizer anymore).

### Before and after: setting up a session

A real classic session usually does a lot more than pick a master; it pulls in packages, sets SQL extensions, turns on Hive support and quiets the logs. A typical one looks something like this:

```python
# Before: Spark Classic. Everything is configured by the program that runs the driver.
spark = (
    SparkSession.builder
    .master("spark://my-cluster:7077")
    .config("spark.jars.packages", "org.apache.spark:spark-sql-kafka-0-10_2.13:4.2.0")
    .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "64")
    .enableHiveSupport()
    .getOrCreate()
)
spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("WARN")
```

Under Connect that one block splits in two, because some of those settings describe the *driver*, and the driver isn't yours anymore. Anything the server reads once when it starts (packages and JARs, `spark.sql.extensions`, catalog implementations, Hive support) moves to the command that starts the server:

```bash
# After, part 1: the server owns its JVM, so it gets the packages and static settings.
./sbin/start-connect-server.sh \
  --master spark://my-cluster:7077 \
  --packages org.apache.spark:spark-sql-kafka-0-10_2.13:4.2.0
```

and the client keeps only what can change per session:

```python
# After, part 2: the client names the server and sets runtime options.
spark = (
    SparkSession.builder
    .remote("sc://localhost:15002")
    .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "64")   # runtime settings still work from the client
    .getOrCreate()
)
```

The log level moves to the server as well (its `conf/log4j2.properties`), since the logs are the server's now. The sneaky part is that Connect doesn't stop you from setting a startup-only setting from the client; it warns and carries on without it. Asking for a package from the client gets you this, and no package:

```text
UserWarning: Failed to set spark.jars.packages to Some(org.apache.spark:spark-sql-kafka-0-10_2.13:4.2.0)
due to [CANNOT_MODIFY_CONFIG] Cannot modify the value of the Spark config ...
```

`enableHiveSupport()` does the same thing (with `CANNOT_MODIFY_STATIC_CONFIG`) and hands you a session without Hive, which you might not notice until a table you expected isn't there. The rule of thumb I've landed on is that if a setting describes how the server starts, it belongs wherever the server starts.

You can also leave the URL out of your code entirely by setting `SPARK_REMOTE`, and a plain `SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate()` will connect to it:

```bash
export SPARK_REMOTE="sc://localhost:15002"
```

### Before and after: the rest of your code

Most DataFrame code doesn't change at all. What does change is anything that reached into the driver, and accumulators are a good example:

```python
# Before: an accumulator, counted on the executors and read on the driver
bad_rows = spark.sparkContext.accumulator(0)
orders.foreach(lambda row: bad_rows.add(1) if row.total is None else None)
print(bad_rows.value)
```

```python
# After: an Observation, collected alongside a query you were running anyway
from pyspark.sql import Observation

obs = Observation("quality")
checked = orders.observe(obs, F.count(F.when(F.col("total").isNull(), 1)).alias("bad_rows"))
checked.write.mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("orders_checked")
print(obs.get["bad_rows"])
```

I'd argue the [Observation](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/api/python/reference/pyspark.sql/api/pyspark.sql.Observation.html) is the better pattern anyway, since the metric rides along with a write you were already doing instead of needing its own pass over the data. The rest of the common swaps, side by side:

| Before (Classic) | After (Connect) |
|---|---|
| `spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("WARN")` | set the level in the server's `conf/log4j2.properties` |
| `df.rdd.zipWithIndex()` | `df.zipWithIndex()` (4.2+) |
| `spark.read.json(rdd_of_strings)` | `spark.read.json(df)` on a string column (4.2+) |
| `sc.accumulator(0)` | `df.observe(Observation(...), ...)` |
| `sc.addPyFile("lib/geo.py")` | `spark.addArtifact("lib/geo.py", pyfile=True)` |
| `sc.broadcast(lookup)` | a broadcast join, `F.broadcast(lookup_df)`, or a literal column |
| `spark.newSession()` | `SparkSession.builder.remote(url).create()` |
| `spark-submit job.py` | `python job.py` with `SPARK_REMOTE` set |

All of that assumes there's a server sitting at `localhost:15002`, which brings us to running one.

## Running a Connect server

There are three ways to get one, roughly in order of effort.

**1. Inside your own Python process, for trying things out.** Full PySpark can start a Connect server in-process:

```python
spark = SparkSession.builder.remote("local[*]").getOrCreate()
```

This needs full `pyspark` (not `pyspark-client`) and Java installed, because the server still has to run somewhere; it's the Connect code path without a separate server, which makes it great for tests and for learning.

**2. From a Spark download, on your machine or a server.** Download Spark from [spark.apache.org](https://spark.apache.org/downloads.html) (you'll need Java 17 or newer) and start the server that ships with it:

```bash
./sbin/start-connect-server.sh        # listens on port 15002
./sbin/stop-connect-server.sh         # when you're done
```

By default it runs Spark locally on that one machine; to have it run jobs on a cluster instead, point it at the cluster's master:

```bash
./sbin/start-connect-server.sh --master spark://my-cluster:7077
```

One thing that surprised me is that **by default the server listens on every network interface**, so anything that can reach your machine can reach the server the moment it starts. On a laptop on shared Wi-Fi, restrict it with `--conf spark.connect.grpc.binding.address=127.0.0.1`. (You'll see `spark.connect.grpc.binding.host` in plenty of examples, including some of mine; it isn't a real setting, and Spark silently ignores it.)

**3. In Docker.** The official [`apache/spark`](https://hub.docker.com/r/apache/spark) image includes Spark, Java and Python; add PyArrow and pandas on top, since Python UDFs use Arrow by default as of Spark 4.2:

```dockerfile
FROM apache/spark:4.2.0-scala2.13-java21-python3-ubuntu
USER root
RUN python3 -m pip install --no-cache-dir pyarrow pandas
USER spark
```

Then start the server with `--wait`, which keeps it in the foreground (what a container needs):

```yaml
services:
  spark-connect:
    build: .
    entrypoint:
      - /opt/spark/sbin/start-connect-server.sh
      - --wait
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:15002:15002"   # Spark Connect
      - "127.0.0.1:4040:4040"     # Spark UI
```

The image's Python is 3.10, which matters for your client (more on that below).

For production, Connect servers also run on Kubernetes (the [Apache Spark Kubernetes Operator](https://github.com/apache/spark-kubernetes-operator) deploys one as an ordinary Spark application) and, since Spark 4.2, inside YARN. The repo's [topology guide](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-demos/blob/main/demos/02_spark_connect/setup/TOPOLOGIES.md) walks through six ways to deploy one and when each makes sense.

Before you share a server with other people, know that **a single server holds many sessions**, each isolated from the others but all sharing the server's memory and executors; if people need stronger isolation than that, they need separate servers.

## Running a job

There's no separate "submit" step for a Connect job, because **your program is the job**, and running it sends the work:

```bash
export SPARK_REMOTE="sc://localhost:15002"
python my_pipeline.py
```

(`SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate()` picks up `SPARK_REMOTE` from the environment, so the same script runs against whichever server the variable names.) A few other routes are worth knowing about.

**An existing job, almost unchanged.** `spark.api.mode` switches a classic job to Connect: Spark starts a Connect server for the job and runs your code as its client. Set it in the session builder and keep your existing `master`:

```python
spark = (SparkSession.builder
         .master("spark://my-cluster:7077")
         .config("spark.api.mode", "connect")
         .getOrCreate())
```

This is the gentlest way to try Connect on real work, since you can move one job, watch it, and move it back if something breaks. The documentation also shows passing it to `spark-submit` as `--conf spark.api.mode=connect`; on 4.2.0 that failed for me with `TypeError: 'JavaPackage' object is not callable` while the builder setting worked, so for now, set it in code.

**A [declarative pipeline](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/declarative-pipelines-programming-guide.html).** Tell the `spark-pipelines` CLI which server to use with `--remote`:

```bash
spark-pipelines run --spec spark-pipeline.yml --remote sc://localhost:15002
```

Don't rely on `SPARK_REMOTE` here; the CLI ignores it and quietly starts a local server of its own. The `spark-pipelines` command comes with full PySpark, and with only the thin client it's the other way round: run `python -m pyspark.pipelines.cli run --spec spark-pipeline.yml`, which has no `--remote` option and connects to whatever `SPARK_REMOTE` names.

**Code your job depends on.** If your functions import your own modules, the server doesn't have them, so ship them with the session using [`addArtifact`](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/api/python/reference/pyspark.sql/api/pyspark.sql.SparkSession.addArtifact.html):

```python
spark.addArtifact("lib/geo.py", pyfile=True)        # importable by your UDFs
spark.addArtifact("model.tar.gz", archive=True)     # unpacked on the executors
spark.addArtifact("lookup.csv", file=True)          # copied as is
```

JARs for catalogs and extensions are the exception; those have to be installed on the server.

## What you need locally

Much less than before, which is kind of the point:

| You need | Why |
|---|---|
| Python, **the same minor version as the server's** | Python functions you send run in the server's Python. The 4.2 client needs Python 3.10 or newer |
| `pyspark-client` | The thin client |
| Its dependencies: pyarrow, pandas, numpy, grpcio | They come with it; this is most of the install |
| **No** Java, no Spark download, no `SPARK_HOME` | That all lives on the server |

The thing actually worth getting right is which package you install, because there are four with nearly identical names:

| Package | What you actually get | Java needed locally? |
|---|---|---|
| `pyspark` | Full PySpark: about 470 MB, most of it some 280 JAR files | yes |
| `pyspark[connect]` | Full PySpark plus the Connect extras | yes |
| `pyspark-connect` | **A tiny package that installs full `pyspark`** (and makes Connect its default) | yes |
| `pyspark-client` | The thin client: about 15 MB, no JARs | no |

`pyspark-connect` sounds like the Connect client and isn't; the thin client is `pyspark-client`. Don't judge by the size of your environment either: with its dependencies a `pyspark-client` environment is about 330 MB against about 780 MB for `pyspark[connect]`, because pyarrow, pandas and numpy are most of it, so **what the thin client really saves you is Java, not disk space.** To check which one you actually have:

```python
import importlib.util, pathlib, pyspark

print((pathlib.Path(pyspark.__file__).parent / "jars").exists())  # thin client: False
print(importlib.util.find_spec("py4j") is not None)               # thin client: False
```

If either prints `True`, you're on full PySpark. And if you have a full Spark installed elsewhere on the machine, clear `SPARK_HOME` and `PYTHONPATH` before you start, or they can quietly shadow the thin client.

## Clients in other languages

Because the client only has to build a plan and read Arrow, it doesn't have to be Python, or even a JVM language, and the same server takes all of these:

| Language | Client | Latest release |
|---|---|---|
| Python | `pyspark-client` (in `apache/spark`) | 4.2.0 |
| Scala and Java | `spark-connect-client-jvm` (in `apache/spark`) | 4.2.0 |
| Go | [`apache/spark-connect-go`](https://github.com/apache/spark-connect-go) | v0.1.0 |
| Swift | [`apache/spark-connect-swift`](https://github.com/apache/spark-connect-swift) | 0.7.0 |
| Rust | [`apache/spark-connect-rust`](https://github.com/apache/spark-connect-rust) | 4.2.0 |
| Anything with JDBC | `spark-connect-client-jdbc`, URL `jdbc:sc://host:15002` | since 4.1 |

They all start the same way, with a connection string. In Scala:

```scala
val spark = SparkSession.builder().remote("sc://localhost:15002").getOrCreate()
spark.range(10).filter("id % 2 = 0").show()
```

In Go:

```go
spark, err := sql.NewSessionBuilder().Remote("sc://localhost:15002").Build(ctx)
df, err := spark.Sql(ctx, "SELECT 'apple' AS word, 123 AS count")
df.Show(ctx, 100, false)
```

(At the time of writing, the Go client's only release, v0.1.0, can't be fetched with `go get` because of a module-path mismatch; `go get github.com/apache/spark-connect-go@master` works.)

Rust is where it gets fun for me, because results arrive as Arrow and can go straight into a native Rust tool. This program from the repo has Spark aggregate five million rows down to seven and then hands them to [Polars](https://pola.rs/) for local work:

```rust
let spark = SparkSession::builder().remote("sc://localhost:15002").get_or_create()?;
let e = |c: Column| c.expression().clone();   // aggregate expressions, unwrapped

let summary = spark
    .range(5_000_000)?
    .with_column("bucket", col("id") % lit(7))
    .group_by([col("bucket")])
    .agg(vec![e(f::count(col("id")).alias("n"))]);

let batches = summary.collect_record_batches()?;   // Arrow RecordBatches, ready for Polars
```

That division of labour, with Spark doing the part that needs a cluster and your language of choice doing the rest, is the part of Connect I find most interesting. The clients aren't equally complete yet, though (the Python and JVM ones cover the most, the newer ones less), so check that the one you pick supports what you need before you build on it.

## Debugging

Most Connect problems come from forgetting that there are now two sides, so when something goes wrong I work through these in roughly this order.

**1. Am I talking to the server I think I am?** Print `spark.version` first, every time, since nothing in `sc://localhost:15002` says which Spark is supposed to answer. I learned this one the hard way: an old Spark 4.1 server was still sitting on port 15002 on my machine when I pointed newer tools at it, and it answered, misunderstood a request it had never heard of, and gave me an error convincing enough that I wrote it up as a Spark bug. (The full story is in Hosting an Entire Open Lakehouse on Port 8080.) Two related traps:

```python
a = SparkSession.builder.remote("sc://server-a:15002").getOrCreate()
b = SparkSession.builder.remote("sc://server-b:15002").getOrCreate()
assert b is a    # getOrCreate() returned the existing session; use .create() for a new one
```

and connection strings that look fine but aren't; the part after the port has to be empty, and parameter values can't contain `/`:

```text
sc://localhost:15002/;user_agent=myapp/setup
PySparkValueError: [INVALID_CONNECT_URL] ... The path component '/;user_agent=myapp/setup' must be empty.
```

**2. Read the error's name.** Connect errors carry an [error class](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/sql-error-conditions.html) in square brackets, and a handful of them cover most of what you'll hit early on:

| Error | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `JVM_ATTRIBUTE_NOT_SUPPORTED` | You used something that lived in the local JVM: `spark.sparkContext` (and so everything reached through it, like `sparkContext.setLogLevel`), `_jvm`, `df.rdd` | Use the DataFrame replacement: `df.zipWithIndex()`, `spark.read.json(df)`, `df.observe(...)` for counters, `addArtifact` for files |
| `PYTHON_VERSION_MISMATCH` | Your Python and the server's differ (e.g. 3.12 vs 3.10) | Match your Python minor version to the server's |
| `ModuleNotFoundError` inside a UDF | The server's Python is missing a package your function needs | Ship it with `addArtifact`, or install it on the server |
| `UNSUPPORTED_LOCAL_CONNECTION_STRING` | You called `.create()` with `local[*]` | Use `.getOrCreate()` for local |
| `INVALID_CONNECT_URL` | The connection string is malformed | Empty path, no `/` in parameter values |

One that doesn't raise at all is `enableHiveSupport()`, which prints a warning and gives you a session without Hive, so read your warnings.

**3. Errors arrive late.** Classic Spark checks your DataFrame the moment you define it (that step 3 from earlier); Connect doesn't send anything to the server until it needs an answer, so a typo in a column name fails at the `show()` or `write` rather than on the line with the typo, and a `try`/`except` around the definition catches nothing. The same thing has two quieter consequences:

```python
a.createOrReplaceTempView("brands")
first = spark.table("brands")
b.createOrReplaceTempView("brands")
first.count()     # Classic: rows of a    Connect: rows of b
```

A DataFrame built on a temp view reads whatever the view points to *when it runs*, and a Python function that reads a variable sees that variable's value *when it runs*, so give temp views unique names and pass values into functions explicitly.

**4. Look at the server's side.** The server has the [Spark UI](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/web-ui.html) (port 4040 by default), where you can see the jobs your client triggered along with a **Connect** tab listing every client session and request, and it has its logs (in `logs/` under the Spark directory, or `docker logs` for a container). `df.explain()` shows you the plan the server actually built.

**5. Check your client isn't newer than your server.** The supported direction is an older client talking to a newer server, and the other way round can fail in odd ways: a 4.2 client can't even build a DataFrame from a three-row Python list on a 4.1 server, because the 4.1 server reports a size limit as `3221225472b` and the 4.2 client chokes on the `b`.

**6. Let a script check for you.** The repo includes a [doctor](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-demos/blob/main/demos/02_spark_connect/tools/doctor.py) that checks the client you installed, whether the server is reachable, its version, and whether Python functions actually run on it:

```bash
python tools/doctor.py --remote sc://localhost:15002 --expect-version 4.2
```

## The whole guide, on one page

- **Spark** splits big data work across many machines.
- **Spark Connect** moves the driver out of your program; your code becomes a client that sends plans to a server.
- **Use it** with `pip install pyspark-client` and `SparkSession.builder.remote("sc://host:15002")`.
- **Get a server** in-process with `local[*]`, from a Spark download with `start-connect-server.sh`, or from the `apache/spark` Docker image (plus PyArrow).
- **Send a job** by running your program; ship your own modules with `addArtifact`.
- **Locally** you need Python matching the server's version and `pyspark-client`, and nothing else.
- **Other languages** (Scala, Go, Rust, Swift, JDBC) use the same server and the same connection string.
- **When it breaks,** check which server answered, read the error's name, remember errors arrive late, and look at the server's side.

Nearly all of it comes back to the one change at the start, which is that the driver moved out of your program; once you know which side of the network a thing lives on, most of Connect stops being surprising.

---

# A Field Guide to Apache Iceberg 1.12

URL: https://datacircus.substack.com/p/a-field-guide-to-apache-iceberg-112
Republished at: https://openlakehouse.io/blog/iceberg/iceberg-1-12-field-guide
Original publisher: Distributed Thoughts
Date: 2026-10-01
Category: Iceberg

*Originally published on [Distributed Thoughts](https://datacircus.substack.com/p/a-field-guide-to-apache-iceberg-112), Scott Haines's Substack.*

Anyone who has lived through a home renovation knows the gap between what looks like progress and what actually is progress. There is scaffolding across the front of the house, a permit taped to the window, and framing going up for a new addition that won’t be ready until next year. Meanwhile, it seems that every week there is another unexpected roadblock or unknown unknown. The addition is what we tell people about. The work that went into it rarely is.

Apache Iceberg 1.12 is part of the Table Format V4 renovation. There is an enormous amount of visible framing going up with roughly forty pull requests touching V4 internals, but just like a renovation in progress, we simply can’t use any of it yet. The work that will actually change our lives is behind the scenes: a cluster of bugs that were returning wrong answers without telling anyone, a real solution to Flink’s equality-delete problem, and Variant finally gaining the speedup we all knew it was capable of.

So, without further ado, let’s take a look at the 1.12 release: what’s new, what’s been fixed, and, more specifically, what to upgrade for, what to check before we upgrade, and which features are releasing with a little bit of red tape.

## The Road to V4

There are roughly forty pull requests in this release touching V4 internals. `TrackedFile` is the unified manifest entry that collapses the `DataFile`/`DeleteFile` split that defined Iceberg until now. [Relative paths](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15630) land in the spec with [resolution in the V4 manifest reader](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17434), and for anyone who has ever wanted to simplify copying a table from one location to another, this is the light at the end of the V4 tunnel. [Content stats](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14234) were also merged, with a genuinely elegant compatibility bridge living within `ContentStatsBackedMap` that presents typed columnar stats to a decade of existing code as the legacy bounds map, lazily, allocating nothing on point reads.

So can we use V4? The short answer is “not at this point.” It is also worth pointing out that V4 and adaptive metadata trees are not synonymous.

The adaptive metadata tree (AMT) replaces manifest lists with a small root manifest, inlines small commits, and provides a tree shape that adapts to each workload. This work is in progress and isn’t ready for prime time: at the time of writing, the read path itself is still not wired into place, with the V4 scan task planner still sitting in an open pull request. The write-direction wrappers are also still open, with changes requested as recently as September. The spec itself says Version 4 is under active development and has not been formally adopted.

What 1.12 contains is the **vocabulary** of V4: the entry struct, typed statistics, relative paths, manifest encoding, and the compatibility bridges. What is missing is the adaptive metadata tree, a scan that can traverse it, and a committer that can build it. It is simply not a feature we can turn on at this point in time.

It is tempting to say V4 is safely gated off. It is not. On main, `TableMetadata` carries:

```java
static final int SUPPORTED_TABLE_FORMAT_VERSION = 4;
```

So this is accepted, not rejected:

```sql
-- Accepted in 1.12. But please don't use it yet.
ALTER TABLE db.my_table SET TBLPROPERTIES ('format-version' = '4');
```

We should treat `format-version=4` in 1.12 as untested territory and leave it unset. For now, we can watch V4 become something we can begin to test against, and treat it as something wonderful that is coming in the future.

## Formal expressions spec baselined

Also contributing to the V4 scaffolding, the expressions spec was baselined and will be leveraged by future V4 features like constraints and default value expressions.

> **Take a read through the [baselined expressions specification here](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16652).**

So why is this important? Iceberg has had ad-hoc expression serialization for years. The intention of this spec is to replace the ad-hoc implementations with a real recursive grammar, as defined in [expressions-spec.md](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/blob/main/format/expressions-spec.md).

Value expressions first:

```text
EXPR: LITERAL | REFERENCE | APPLY

REFERENCE: BOUND_REF | UNBOUND_REF
BOUND_REF:   { "type": "reference", "id": ID }
UNBOUND_REF: { "type": "reference", "name": NAME }

APPLY: { "type": "apply", "function": FUNC_REF, "arguments": [ FUNC_ARG* ] }
```

Then predicates compose them:

```text
PREDICATE: true | false
    | { "type": "not",      "child": PREDICATE }
    | { "type": BINARY_OP,  "left": PREDICATE, "right": PREDICATE }
    | { "type": UNARY_OP,   "child": EXPR }
    | { "type": CMP_OP,     "left": EXPR, "right": EXPR }
    | { "type": SET_OP,     "child": EXPR, "values": LITERALS }
    | DEPRECATED_PREDICATE

BINARY_OP: "and" | "or"
UNARY_OP:  "is-null" | "not-null" | "is-nan" | "not-nan"
CMP_OP:    "lt" | "lt-eq" | "gt" | "gt-eq" | "eq" | "not-eq"
         | "starts-with" | "not-starts-with"
SET_OP:    "in" | "not-in"
```

Why does this matter enough to call out? Server-side scan planning means shipping predicates to a catalog for push-down. Without a standard serialization, every implementation invents its own, and that is how we end up with a protocol that works only between two vendors who happened to test against each other.

The implementation detail worth remembering is the **reference**. It either serializes **by field id** or **by name**, and that encodes _when_ a column’s identity gets decided. Stored expressions like `CHECK` constraints use ids, so a rename cannot orphan them; query filters use names, resolved against the current schema on every run. The spec is explicit that _server-side planning uses unbound named references_, so the client half of scan planning sends names, not ids. Older term-based forms still parse, so clients and catalog servers can each move on their own schedule rather than having to cut over together.

> We’ll keep you posted on the expressions spec as we continue to watch the progress being made on the road to V4.

## Variant grows up

V3 gave us the Variant type. 1.11 gave us shredded writes in Spark. 1.12 is where Variant really takes center stage, and the reason is [vectorized Parquet reads](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16292).

> Note: This support is available today for unshredded Variant, with shredded support still pending as of the 1.12 release.

Before this, a single Variant column forced the _entire table_ into row-at-a-time reads. Not the column, but the entire table. If we adopted Variant in 1.11 and concluded that semi-structured data on Iceberg was slow, this is why, and the fix comes in 1.12. Arrow readers now compose over the metadata and value children with per-file shredded detection.

The best part of this change is that there is zero additional config to enable it. It is on by default for non-shredded Variant columns, with transparent fallback to row-based reads for shredded files or when the metrics mode is `none` or `counts`. No new table property or flag to flip. Just upgrade and watch the performance of Variant scans take off.

Shredding on the write side does have a knob, though, and it remains opt-in for 1.12:

```sql
ALTER TABLE db.my_table SET TBLPROPERTIES (
  'write.parquet.shred-variants' = 'true'
);
```

Around that headline sit roughly eighteen changes: [Flink can write shredded Variant](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15596), [Kafka Connect and generic Record writes](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17520) gain shredding, and a stack of allocation work — [reduced allocation in construction](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16818), [caching of adjacent identical metadata](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16852), [precomputed sorted entries](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17114). There is also [hardening against malformed Variant binary](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16568), which matters more than it sounds if we are ingesting semi-structured data from anywhere we do not fully control.

## Function endpoints arrive

Alongside it, REST catalog **function endpoints** arrive in the IRC specification:

```http
GET /v1/{prefix}/namespaces/{namespace}/functions
GET /v1/{prefix}/namespaces/{namespace}/functions/{name}
```

[Those endpoints are defined](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15180), but what ships is the OpenAPI specification and generated models. Iceberg’s own Java catalog implementations do **not** implement the function endpoints in this release.

Remote signing also becomes complete rather than half-specified. [The `remote-signing-config` object](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16822) on `LoadTableResult` is joined by [the client implementation](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17709), which also removes the legacy `s3.signer.*` properties. Signing configuration moves from our client config to whatever the catalog hands back, which is a migration item, and we will come back to it.

## Flink finally gets an answer to equality deletes

Anyone running Flink upsert at volume can understand the pain of equality deletes. Equality deletes are cheap to write and expensive to read. Every query has to join data files against delete files to work out what is actually gone. On a continuously upserting table, that compounds until read latency is dominated by delete resolution and nobody can explain to the analytics team why the dashboard got slow.

1.12 ships `ConvertEqualityDeletes`, a maintenance task that rewrites those equality deletes into deletion vectors. It landed across six pull requests — [data model and key serialization](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16831), [the reader and primary-key index](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16844), [the DV writer](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16858), [the committer](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16874), [the planner](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16889), and [the public API](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16948) — which shows the level of effort it takes to come up with a battle-hardened solution for something this delicate.

There are two ways to run it, and the choice matters more than it looks.

The explicit route wires the task into a `TableMaintenance` pipeline:

```java
TableMaintenance.forTable(env, tableLoader)
    .add(
        ConvertEqualityDeletes.builder()
            .stagingBranch("staging")
            .targetBranch("main")
            .equalityFieldColumns(ImmutableList.of("id"))
            .scheduleOnEqDeleteFileCount(10)
            .parallelism(4))
    .append();
```

Walking that through:

1. We begin by binding the maintenance pipeline to a table, handing it the Flink execution environment and a `TableLoader` (the same loader our sink already uses).
2. We then stage conversion work on a separate branch. The staging branch is where the converter accumulates its work before it lands, which keeps partially converted state away from readers on `main`.
3. We name the target branch the conversion commits to. It defaults to `SnapshotRef.MAIN_BRANCH`, so leaving it off gives us in-place conversion.
4. We declare the equality field columns. **These must match what the writer is actually using** or this operation will fail.
5. We give it a trigger. Here the task fires once ten equality delete files have accumulated; `scheduleOnCommitCount(int)` and `scheduleOnInterval(Duration)` are the alternatives.
6. Finally, we set parallelism and append the task to the pipeline.

The second route is easier because it removes step four’s failure mode entirely. [The `IcebergSink` integration](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17142) derives the equality fields from the sink’s own resolved equality field identifiers, so they _cannot_ drift out of sync with the writer:

```java
IcebergSink.forRowData(stream)
    .tableLoader(tableLoader)
    .equalityFieldColumns(ImmutableList.of("id"))
    .convertEqualityDeletes()   // equality fields derived from the sink
    .append();
```

Or, if we configure through SQL or table properties rather than code:

| Property | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `flink-maintenance.convert-equality-deletes.enabled` | Enable converting equality deletes to deletion vectors (requires equality fields and format version >= 3) | `false` |
| `flink-maintenance.convert-equality-deletes.target-branch` | Branch the converted deletion vectors are committed to | not set (in place) |
| `flink-maintenance.convert-equality-deletes.schedule.commit-count` | Trigger after N commits | `1` |
| `flink-maintenance.convert-equality-deletes.schedule.interval-second` | Trigger after a time interval, in seconds | not set |

Before we turn any of this on, the constraints deserve a careful read. There are three, and two of them are disqualifying rather than inconvenient. The table must be **format version 3 or higher**, validated at job startup. And **row lineage is not preserved** through conversion, so if we depend on `_row_id` or `_last_updated_sequence_number`, this feature is not for us yet. The third is the inconvenient one: every partition column must also be an equality field. Row lineage is the red tape I’d put in front of the team before anyone gets excited.

There is a correctness fix here worth naming, because it was open until quite recently and caused real growing pains: [deleted rows could reappear after a failed conversion cycle](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17630). Resolving an equality delete consumes index entries, and a cycle that failed _after_ resolving one never restored them, because the target branch never moved, _but the task still reported success_. Silent resurrection of deleted rows with a green task checkmark is a big reason to upgrade.

While we are in Flink, two duplicate-row bugs got fixed that have nothing to do with the new feature and everything to do with everyday upsert. In [RANGE distribution](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17276), Iceberg consulted `schema.identifierFieldIds()` instead of the equality fields we actually configured, so explicitly configured equality fields on a schema without identifier fields were simply ignored. In [HASH mode](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16243), identifier-only records were round-robined while the writer still emitted equality deletes. Both are the same underlying failure: records sharing an equality key reached different writers, so the delete never suppressed the old row and the duplicate survived. If we run Flink upsert with explicitly configured equality fields, these two are the reason to upgrade.

One more that will save somebody a very bad afternoon: [savepoint restore was impossible](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17210) for jobs using `TableMaintenance`, because the builder derived its operator ID suffix from a random UUID. Operator IDs changed on every submission, so no savepoint could ever be restored. It is now derived from the table name.

> Expect a one-time operator ID change on upgrade, and plan for it rather than discovering it.

Lastly, [reading Iceberg views from Flink SQL](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17859) arrives here too, [backported](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18104) across 2.2, 2.1, and 1.20.

## Correctness fixes and squashed bugs

Most release notes lead with features. This one shouldn’t, because 1.12 fixes a cluster of bugs that produced _silently wrong results_. Not exceptions, not failed jobs, just answers that were confidently incorrect. If you were thinking about skipping the 1.12 release, the following are really good reasons to upgrade instead.

### Deletion vector indexes

There was a bug with [deletion vector indexing](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17497) that is now resolved in 1.12. The problem was that scan planning indexes deletion vectors (DVs) by data file location alone, but a single Puffin file can hold DVs for many data files. Every DV in that file resolves to the _last_ index. So if we run DVs at any scale (and after 1.11, many of us do), this meant incorrect rows were returned, or deleted rows quietly came back to life.

### Metadata table query filtering

Adjacent to the DV bug, [metadata table queries filtering on `data_file.content`](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17440) pruned delete manifests they shouldn’t have, because a single delete manifest could store both positional and equality deletes. So even if you were auditing your tables, any tooling built to support runtime checks for your tables could also have been returning incomplete answers (depending on the table and whether it used deletes). In the same family, [negated filters on `all_manifests`](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17346) pruned every snapshot and returned zero rows even when matching delete manifests existed. The query that bit people looks completely innocent:

```sql
-- Spark parses this as Not(EqualTo), which pruned every snapshot.
-- Before 1.12 this returned zero rows even when delete manifests existed.
SELECT * FROM db.my_table.all_manifests WHERE content != 0;
```

An empty result set looks a lot like “nothing to worry about,” which is exactly the problem.

### Time travel on tables with clock skew

`SnapshotUtil` assumed the snapshot log was in chronological order. The spec makes no such promise and explicitly allows skew, so `AS OF` queries against write-audit-publish (WAP) or cherry-pick workflows could read the wrong snapshot entirely. The [fix for time travel on tables with clock skew](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17360) looks for the entry with the maximum timestamp &lt;= the requested timestamp, rather than taking the last entry’s timestamp.

### Fixed resource leaks

Resource leaks are traditionally challenging to find in large distributed systems, and they are the kind that degrade a long-running service rather than failing immediately. Both the [`HadoopCatalog` and `HiveCatalog` leaked `FileIO` on every `close()`, while the `BigQueryMetastoreCatalog` had no `close()` at all](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16862). This results in slow-motion resource exhaustion for any service that creates catalogs.

[Vectorized row-lineage reads never released their off-heap Arrow vectors](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17296), which is direct-memory exhaustion in long-running Spark and Flink scans.

If we take one thing from this section, it’s that the resource leaks alone justify this upgrade, before we look at a single feature.

### Issues that the upgrade won’t fix automatically

Let’s assume that a fixed writer can never repair what a broken writer already wrote. Mitigating that is always left to the data engineering teams, or to agents.

Three of the fixes in 1.12 correct _metrics bounds_, which are the min/max values stored in the manifest metadata that drive predicate pushdown and file skipping. Bounds are written once and persist. Upgrading corrects the code that writes them going forward. It does absolutely nothing about the bounds already sitting in our manifests. And because those bounds decide which files a query can safely skip, a wrong bound means a query silently skips a file that _does_ contain matching rows.

The specifics are narrow, and that is the good news:

- [Variant BINARY fields](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16880) with values over 16 bytes, where the stored upper bound could come out _smaller_ than a value actually in the file. Written badly by 1.9.0, 1.10.0, and 1.11.0.
- [Variant STRING fields](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17397), where bounds were merged using Java string ordering rather than UTF-8 byte order, so bounds could invert on non-BMP characters — emoji being the obvious case. Written badly by 1.10.0 and 1.11.0.
- [ORC `timestamp_ns`](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16922), where statistics were converted to microseconds while bounds serialize as nanoseconds, making bounds roughly 1000x too small. The affected version range is not stated on the pull request, and I could not determine it.

Both Variant fixes were backported to 1.9.x, 1.10.x, and 1.11.x, which tells us how seriously the community took them. Non-Variant binary and string columns were never affected, since the standard path used the right comparator.

So what do we actually do? The first step is fairly simple: find out whether we are exposed to the problem in the first place. Most teams won’t be.

```sql
-- Step 1: does this table even have an at-risk column type?
DESCRIBE TABLE db.my_table;
-- Looking for: VARIANT columns (binary or string fields inside them),
-- or TIMESTAMP_NS columns on ORC-backed tables.

-- Step 2: which Iceberg versions have written to this table?
-- Snapshot summaries carry the writer's environment context.
SELECT snapshot_id, committed_at, summary
FROM db.my_table.snapshots
ORDER BY committed_at;
```

For the second query, reading writer provenance out of snapshot summaries is an _approach_, but it isn’t a documented recipe (so there may be better ways to find this information within your setup). What keys appear in `summary` depends on what the writing engine populated, so treat this as a starting point for investigation rather than a reliable filter. If the schema check from step one comes back clean, none of this matters and we can move on with a clear conscience.

If we _are_ exposed, the remediation is to rewrite the affected files so metrics get recomputed:

```sql
-- Rewriting recomputes metrics, which replaces the bad bounds.
CALL system.rewrite_data_files(
  table => 'db.my_table',
  options => map('rewrite-all', 'true')
);
```

> Note: zero pull requests in this release propose a repair path. Not one mentions rewriting manifests, rewriting data files, or a bounds escape hatch. Rewriting the affected files is an available approach given how metrics are computed, but remember to test and validate. Until the affected files are rewritten, treat query results over those columns as untrustworthy.

For contrast, [nanosecond timestamp pushdown in Parquet](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16619), where a `timestamp_ns` predicate matched every row, is read-side only. Nothing bad actually persisted, and upgrading fully fixes it. _Remember to always think about where a bug lives: is it in code or on disk?_

## Kafka Connect

Through August, the Kafka Connect sink carried two open data-integrity issues that would have been big red flags. The first was a data-loss path that triggered on _default configuration_: a coordinator could enter a zombie state — thread alive, partitions revoked — and keep re-committing a stale control-topic offset. Nothing errored. The task looked healthy. When that offset eventually aged out of the control topic’s retention, a newly elected coordinator sought to an offset that no longer existed and, because the reset policy defaults to `latest`, skipped every record in between.

The second was duplicate file commits after task restart.

```java
// Before — an unconditional put let the tracked position move BACKWARDS
// when a control topic partition was re-read.
controlTopicOffsets.put(record.partition(), record.offset() + 1);

// After — keep the highest position ever seen.
// kafka-connect/.../connect/channel/Channel.java
controlTopicOffsets.merge(record.partition(), record.offset() + 1, Long::max);
```

That map feeds the snapshot’s `kafka.connect.offsets` watermark. Once the watermark regressed, replayed `DataWritten` envelopes passed the minimum-offset filter and the same data files got committed again — and `distinctByKey` only deduplicates within a single commit, so nothing downstream caught it. The production report behind [the fix](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17933) is worth looking at for scale: 149 double-referenced files and roughly 112,000 duplicated rows.

[The zombie-coordinator path](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17552) is closed too, by making the coordinator commit offsets only when they are greater than existing ones.

Worth knowing: the duplicate-commit fix explicitly does _not_ include the content-level backstop that was discussed — a bounded set of recently committed file locations — which was left for a follow-up. So the mechanism that caused the regression is fixed; a second, independent check against the same class of problem is not there yet.

## Upgrading to 1.12

Every consolidation release has a gotcha, and this one is mostly a deprecation purge that has been coming for a while.

### We say goodbye to Spark 3.4

Spark 3.4 is removed entirely. The `spark/v3.4` module is deleted and `iceberg-spark-runtime-3.4_2.12` will not be published. Supported versions move to 3.5.9, 4.0.4, and 4.1.3. There is no path here except upgrading Spark.

`SparkFilters` **is gone** across Spark 3.5, 4.0, and 4.1 and is replaced with `SparkV2Filters`:

```java
// Before — removed in 1.12
import org.apache.iceberg.spark.SparkFilters;

// After — DSv2 Predicate[] instead of the old Filter API
import org.apache.iceberg.spark.SparkV2Filters;
```

**The core removals** are the ones with the widest blast radius. Here is the migration table:

| Removed | Replacement |
| --- | --- |
| `SystemProperties` (class) | `SystemConfigs` |
| `ThreadPools.newWorkerPool(String)`, `newWorkerPool(String, int)` | `newExitingWorkerPool` for long-lived pools, `newFixedThreadPool` for short-lived |
| `SnapshotUtil.newFiles`, `newFilesBetween` | `SnapshotChanges` with `ancestorsBetween` |
| `TableScanUtil.hasDeletes(CombinedScanTask)`, `hasEqDeletes(CombinedScanTask)` | the `FileScanTask` overloads |
| `BaseScan.io()` | `table().io()` |

That `ThreadPools` split is the one most likely to be waved through in review, because the old call site still reads fine in the diff:

```java
// Before
ExecutorService pool = ThreadPools.newWorkerPool("my-pool", 8);

// After — pick based on lifetime, which is the point of the split
ExecutorService longLived  = ThreadPools.newExitingWorkerPool("my-pool", 8);
ExecutorService shortLived = ThreadPools.newFixedThreadPool("my-pool", 8);
```

### Writing position deletes with row data is no longer supported

This sounds more alarming than it is: [writes are rejected while reads are preserved](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17706), so it is not a compatibility break for existing tables. Concretely, `buildPositionWriter()` in Avro, ORC, and Parquet now throws `UnsupportedOperationException` when a row schema is set, `PositionDelete.set(CharSequence, long, R)` and the `row()` getter are removed, and Flink’s `FlinkAppenderFactory` — whose position delete path was built entirely on row data — is gone. The sharp edge is that maintenance operations encountering existing such files will now fail loudly rather than silently dropping the row column, which is the correct behavior and still a surprise if we hit it during a rewrite at 2 a.m.

### S3 remote signing

If we configure S3 remote signing, the `s3.signer.*` properties are removed and that configuration moves server-side, per the `remote-signing-config` work above.

### Performance improvements to Hive catalog table listings

That covers the breaking changes. On to the improvements, starting with a genuinely useful one: [Hive catalog table listing](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17317) no longer loads every table object into client memory. The old path timed out at roughly 46,000 tables even with a 900-second socket timeout. The same namespace now lists in about five seconds. If we run a large Hive Metastore, that is the number to bring to the upgrade conversation.

### Fix for unbounded row groups

Most of the performance work in 1.12 is opt-in, which means we get none of it by default. This one is worth opting into.

```sql
-- Enforce the row-group target against uncompressed size. Without this,
-- GZIP/ZSTD tables compare compressed bytes to an uncompressed target
-- and row groups grow unbounded.
ALTER TABLE db.my_table SET TBLPROPERTIES (
  'write.parquet.row-group-size-track-uncompressed' = 'true'
);
```

### Performance improvements for small-file and metadata-heavy workloads

For Parquet-based tables, the read path gets a huge improvement for free. Opening a Parquet file normally means several round trips: one for the footer length, one for the footer body, then one per row group. `EagerInputFile` collapses all those calls into a single fetch, and [it is now wired into the Parquet read path](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17284). This is especially important for small-file and metadata-heavy workloads, since compaction, manifest reads, scan planning, and streaming polls all pay that footer latency linearly in file count.

> This integration lives in the `parquet` module rather than in any engine tree, so **it is not a Spark thing or a Flink thing** — every engine reading Parquet through Iceberg gets it. There is also no property to tune. The threshold is a private constant:
>
> ```java
> // From parquet/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/parquet/Parquet.java
> private static final long EAGER_FETCH_THRESHOLD_BYTES = 1024 * 1024;   // 1 MB
>
> private static boolean canEagerFetch(long fileLength) {
>   return fileLength > 0 && fileLength <= EAGER_FETCH_THRESHOLD_BYTES;
> }
> ```
>
> So files at or below 1 MB are fetched eagerly and everything larger behaves as before. We do not opt in, and (at this point) we cannot tune it upward for a workload that might benefit from a larger window.

### Opting into Hilbert-curve clustering

Compaction gets a new option. [Hilbert-curve clustering](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16827) joins Z-order, preserving locality more consistently for multidimensional data (where points close together in space stay close along the curve, without the large jumps Z-order produces at certain boundaries):

```sql
CALL system.rewrite_data_files(
  table => 'db.tbl',
  strategy => 'sort',
  sort_order => 'hilbert(c1, c2)'
);
```

Because it is expressed as a sort order rather than a new strategy, adopting it is a one-line change to an existing rewrite rather than a new maintenance job.

### Flink version support changes

The `flink/v2.0` module is gone now, with **2.2 and 2.3 support added**. The matrix is now 1.20, 2.1, 2.2, and 2.3. If you were on 2.0, upgrading will make supporting equality deletes so much easier.

## Where that leaves us

1.12 is a consolidation release paving the way for V4. The V4 commits are numerous, visible, and not yet usable. The release is concentrated in four places: a cluster of correctness repairs, a real solution to Flink equality deletes, Variant becoming fast, and the arrival of a formal expressions specification that the REST catalog ecosystem is going to lean on for years.

As a side note, before we upgrade, one checklist item that nothing else will catch for us: if we have Variant binary or string columns, or ORC `timestamp_ns` columns, written by 1.9 through 1.11, those bounds are already wrong on disk and the upgrade will not repair them. A fixed writer never repairs what a broken writer already wrote.

---

Thanks to all the [Apache Iceberg contributors](https://iceberg.apache.org/releases/#1120-release) who helped make this release a success. Also, a shout-out to [Jason Reid](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jasonreid/), [Daniel Weeks](https://www.linkedin.com/in/daniel-weeks-a1946860/), and [Anoop Johnson](https://www.linkedin.com/in/anoopjohnson/) from [Databricks](https://www.linkedin.com/company/databricks/posts/?feedView=all), and to [Neelesh Salian](https://www.linkedin.com/in/neeleshsalian/), who all helped with the technical review of this post, and a special thanks to Neelesh, who was the release manager for 1.12.

---

*This post was originally published by Scott Haines as
[“A Field Guide to Apache Iceberg 1.12”](https://datacircus.substack.com/p/a-field-guide-to-apache-iceberg-112)
on [Distributed Thoughts](https://datacircus.substack.com/). Republished here with attribution to the original
source.*
