And Real-Time Mode in 4.3 gains stateful operators, but still can't run Python UDFs ([SPARK-57237](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-57237) is open).

Housekeeping to plan for: [4.2 raised the minimum PyArrow to 18.0.0 and dropped PyPy](https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/branch-4.3/python/docs/source/migration_guide/pyspark_upgrade.rst), and 4.3 drops Python 3.10 ([SPARK-56889](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-56889)).

---

I opened with a UDF that took 10 seconds at 100 million rows and was the fastest Python option at 100 thousand. The reason is the same one behind every change on this list: your function was never the expensive part.

The crossing was, and the best PySpark optimization is still the one that decides the data doesn't need to cross.

---

# Stop Blaming Serialization for Slow Python UDFs

URL: https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/pyspark-udf-showdown
Republished at: https://openlakehouse.io/blog/apache-spark/pyspark-udf-showdown
Original publisher: systems/null
Date: 2026-09-28
Category: Apache Spark

*Originally published on [systems/null](https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/pyspark-udf-showdown).*

## The benchmark that tested the wrong Arrow

Earlier this year I built a benchmark to answer a question that comes up constantly: if you need custom Python logic in Spark, which kind of UDF should you write, and what does it cost? It compared seven options across three workloads (trivial arithmetic, a string transform, and a normal CDF) at scales from 100K to 100M rows.

The result my write-up leaned on hardest was a pair of rows that came out almost identical: a plain `@udf` ran at 48.5x the cost of the equivalent built-in function at 50M rows, and the same `@udf` "with Arrow turned on" ran at 48.9x (69.2x against 69.0x at 100M). I called it the key insight: switching transport from pickle to Arrow buys nothing when your function still executes one row at a time.

The conclusion about per-row execution is right, but the evidence wasn't what I thought. This is the setting the benchmark toggled:

```python
# What my benchmark flipped for its "@udf + Arrow" case:
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled", "true")
# ...which only governs DataFrame.toPandas() and createDataFrame(pandas_df).
# It never touches Python UDFs.

# What actually moves a regular Python UDF onto Arrow:
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.execution.pythonUDF.arrow.enabled", "true")   # session-wide
@udf(DoubleType(), useArrow=True)                                        # or per UDF
def f(x): ...
```

[The PySpark documentation](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/api/python/tutorial/sql/arrow_pandas.html) is explicit that `arrow.pyspark.enabled` controls pandas conversions. So my two nearly identical rows were the same pickled UDF measured twice, and the gap between them (under 1%) is just how much two runs of the same thing vary.

I had built an A/A test by accident, in a benchmark that existed precisely because Spark's "Arrow" naming is easy to confuse.

That mistake is the best evidence I have for the actual thesis: **the cost of a Python UDF is decided far more by what your function receives (a single value, a pandas Series, or an Arrow array) than by whether Arrow carries the bytes, and because "Arrow" names several different mechanisms, it's easy to flip the switch that sounds right and optimize nothing.** Here is what each of them actually does:

| What you set | What it controls | Affects your UDF? |
|---|---|---|
| `spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled` | `toPandas()` and `createDataFrame(pandas_df)` conversions | No |
| `@udf(useArrow=True)` or `spark.sql.execution.pythonUDF.arrow.enabled` | Moves a regular UDF to Arrow batches (`ArrowEvalPython`); your function still gets one scalar per call. On by default since Spark 4.2 | Yes, 1.4x to 2.4x |
| `@pandas_udf` | Arrow batches; your function gets a `pandas.Series` per call | Yes, vectorized |
| `@arrow_udf` (Spark 4.1+, SPARK-53014) | Arrow batches; your function gets a `pyarrow.Array` per call | Yes, vectorized, no pandas |

## Three choices hiding behind every decorator

Every Python UDF call makes three independent choices: how data crosses from the JVM to the Python worker (transport), which physical operator Spark plans (`BatchEvalPython` or `ArrowEvalPython`), and what your function receives once the data arrives (the execution model). **The last one determines how many times Python has to be entered.**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    JVM["JVM executor<br/>(Spark rows)"]
    JVM -->|"@udf (default)<br/>pickle, BatchEvalPython"| R1["your function called<br/>once per ROW<br/>(Python scalars)"]
    JVM -->|"@udf(useArrow=True)<br/>Arrow batches, ArrowEvalPython"| R2["batch unpacked,<br/>function called<br/>once per ROW"]
    JVM -->|"@pandas_udf<br/>Arrow batches, ArrowEvalPython"| B1["function called<br/>once per BATCH<br/>(pandas.Series)"]
    JVM -->|"@arrow_udf<br/>Arrow batches, ArrowEvalPython"| B2["function called<br/>once per BATCH<br/>(pyarrow.Array)"]
```

| UDF type | Operator | Transport | Calls into your Python | Receives |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `@udf` (default, pre-4.2) | `BatchEvalPython` | pickle | once per row | scalar |
| `@udf(useArrow=True)` | `ArrowEvalPython` | Arrow | once per row | scalar |
| `@pandas_udf` | `ArrowEvalPython` | Arrow | once per batch | `pandas.Series` |
| `@arrow_udf` | `ArrowEvalPython` | Arrow | once per batch | `pyarrow.Array` |

This is the exact code the benchmark ran for the arithmetic workload (`x * 2 + 1`):

```python
@udf(DoubleType())                    # once per row, pickle
def py_arith(x):
    return float(x) * 2 + 1 if x is not None else None

@udf(DoubleType(), useArrow=True)     # once per row, Arrow batches
def use_arrow_arith(x):
    return float(x) * 2 + 1 if x is not None else None

@pandas_udf(DoubleType())             # once per batch, pandas.Series
def pandas_arith(x):
    return x * 2 + 1

@arrow_udf(DoubleType())              # once per batch, pyarrow.Array
def arrow_arith(x: pa.Array) -> pa.Array:
    return pc.add(pc.multiply(x, 2), 1)
```

And for the string workload (`upper(x) + '_SUFFIX'`), where the two vectorized options separate:

```python
@pandas_udf(StringType())
def pandas_string(x):
    return x.str.upper() + "_SUFFIX"

@arrow_udf(StringType())
def arrow_string(x: pa.Array) -> pa.Array:
    upper = pc.utf8_upper(x)
    suffix = pa.array(["_SUFFIX"] * len(upper), type=pa.string())   # see note below
    return pc.binary_join_element_wise(upper, suffix, "")
```

## What the measurements show

Median wall-clock seconds at 50M rows, with the multiple of the built-in time in parentheses (the mislabeled "Arrow config" row is omitted, since it was a second run of the default `@udf`):

| | arithmetic | string | normal CDF |
|---|---|---|---|
| built-in functions | 0.107 | 0.486 | 0.176 |
| SQL UDF | 0.095 (0.9x) | 0.477 (1.0x) | n/a |
| `@arrow_udf` | 0.725 (6.8x) | 1.545 (3.2x) | 0.762 (4.3x) |
| `@pandas_udf` | 0.789 (7.4x) | 2.512 (5.2x) | 0.819 (4.7x) |
| `@udf(useArrow=True)` | 2.228 (20.8x) | 4.430 (9.1x) | 2.942 (16.7x) |
| `@udf` (default, pickle) | 5.199 (48.5x) | 6.216 (12.8x) | 6.183 (35.1x) |

And at 100M rows:

| | arithmetic | string | normal CDF |
|---|---|---|---|
| built-in functions | 0.147 | 0.910 | 0.267 |
| `@arrow_udf` | 1.332 | 2.904 | 1.333 |
| `@pandas_udf` | 1.400 | 4.743 | 1.449 |
| `@udf(useArrow=True)` | 4.188 | 8.735 | 5.658 |
| `@udf` (default, pickle) | 10.139 | 12.212 | 12.060 |

Three things stand out, and each one follows from the execution model rather than the transport.

**Arrow batching helps a row-at-a-time UDF, but only about 2x.** `useArrow=True` took arithmetic from 5.20s to 2.23s and the CDF from 6.18s to 2.94s, because `ArrowEvalPython` moves data in efficient batches instead of pickling rows. It still calls your function once per value, though, and that per-call cost is a hard ceiling: across every workload and scale, the row-at-a-time UDFs topped out at roughly 8 to 10 million rows per second (50M rows in 5.2s; 100M in 10.1s), which is about the rate at which CPython can be entered and exited no matter what's computed inside.

The vectorized UDFs cross into Python once per batch instead, and they were about 3x faster again than `useArrow=True` on arithmetic.

**Between the vectorized options, the gap is almost entirely strings.**

| `@arrow_udf` speedup over `@pandas_udf` | arithmetic | string | CDF |
|---|---|---|---|
| 50M rows | 1.09x | 1.63x | 1.07x |
| 100M rows | 1.05x | 1.63x | 1.09x |

That split is what you'd expect from how the two libraries lay out data. A numeric pandas Series is a NumPy array underneath, so converting from Arrow is cheap and the arithmetic is the same vectorized arithmetic either way. Strings are different; pandas has traditionally stored them as an array of Python objects, each its own heap allocation, while Arrow keeps them in one contiguous buffer plus an array of offsets. Converting to pandas means building millions of Python objects, and every operation afterwards walks memory scattered across the heap.

If anything the benchmark understates the gap, because my `@arrow_udf` string function builds a Python list of suffixes the length of every batch before joining them, which is exactly the per-element Python work `pyarrow.compute` exists to avoid. The CDF case is close for the opposite reason: `pyarrow.compute` has no `erf`, so my "Arrow" CDF converts to NumPy and calls SciPy, just like the pandas version does.

**Scale changes which choice matters.** Arithmetic workload, median seconds (the `@arrow_udf` column is blank below 50M because it wasn't a separate case in those earlier runs):

| rows | built-in | `@arrow_udf` | `@pandas_udf` | `useArrow=True` | `@udf` (pickle) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100K | 0.073 | | 0.181 | 0.212 | 0.161 |
| 1M | 0.077 | | 0.200 | 0.248 | 0.258 |
| 10M | 0.074 | | 0.299 | 0.568 | 1.092 |
| 50M | 0.107 | 0.725 | 0.789 | 2.228 | 5.199 |
| 100M | 0.147 | 1.332 | 1.400 | 4.188 | 10.139 |

At 100K rows every Python UDF was within 2x to 6x of the built-ins, and the plain pickled `@udf` was actually the fastest Python option on arithmetic, because fixed costs (starting Python workers, setting up batches) dominate everything at that size. The tiers only separate cleanly somewhere around 10M rows.

If your job processes a few hundred thousand rows, UDF type is unlikely to be what's making it slow.

## Why I'd trust the seconds over the multipliers

There's a second correction to my own write-up, and it applies to almost any benchmark reported as "Nx slower." My report said row-at-a-time UDFs showed superlinear growth, from 48.5x at 50M to 69.2x at 100M. **That's true of the ratio and false of the thing you care about:**

| default `@udf`, arithmetic | 50M | 100M | growth for 2x rows |
|---|---|---|---|
| `@udf` absolute time | 5.199s | 10.139s | 1.95x (linear) |
| built-in absolute time | 0.107s | 0.147s | 1.37x |
| ratio | 48.5x | 69.2x | "superlinear" |

The ratio grew because its denominator grew slowly; the built-in at this scale is mostly fixed overhead.

The baseline has another problem I can't fully explain away. SQL UDFs, which compile to the same plan as built-ins, came out slightly faster than them at every scale (0.64x to 0.98x). The likeliest cause is ordering: the built-in case always ran first in each workload and may have absorbed start-up cost despite the warmup. If so, every multiplier here is somewhat inflated. An earlier set of my own 50M runs, before I raised driver memory, had the built-in at 0.25s and the pickled `@udf` at about 22x, while the `@udf`'s own time moved only about 10%.

The headline multiplier more than doubled on the strength of the baseline alone.

## What has changed, and what I didn't measure

Spark 4.2 [turns Arrow optimization on by default](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/api/python/tutorial/sql/arrow_pandas.html) for regular Python UDFs, after an attempt to do the same for 4.0 was reverted ([SPARK-48516](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-48516)). On 4.2 a plain `@udf` should therefore behave like my `useArrow=True` rows, a free 2x for anyone who never touches the setting; I haven't rerun the benchmark on 4.2, so **that's an expectation, not a measurement**.

I also only benchmarked scalar UDFs. The partition-level APIs `mapInPandas` and `mapInArrow`, and the grouped `applyInPandas` and `applyInArrow`, follow the same logic about what your function receives (the Arrow variants skip pandas conversion entirely), and they're the right tools when you need to change the number of rows or see a whole partition or group at once. I have no measurements for them, and I'd rather say so than borrow numbers.

The benchmark's own limits:

- One machine, `local[*]`, via Spark Connect; hardware not recorded.
- Synthetic, low-cardinality data (`spark.range` plus two derived columns, short strings), cached in memory before timing.
- Each case materialized with a count, not written anywhere.
- One warmup, median of three timed runs, no variance recorded.
- The 100K to 10M runs predate the 32GB driver setting and the separate `@arrow_udf` case, so there's no genuine `@arrow_udf` data below 50M.

None of this changes the ordering, which held everywhere, but the exact multipliers are specific to this setup.

## Choosing, based on what was measured

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Need custom logic"] --> B{"Expressible with built-in<br/>functions or a SQL UDF?"}
    B -->|yes| C["Use that.<br/>~1x: nothing in Python came close"]
    B -->|no| D{"Can your function<br/>work on a whole batch?"}
    D -->|yes| E{"Maps onto pyarrow.compute,<br/>especially strings?"}
    E -->|yes| F["@arrow_udf<br/>fastest; 1.6x over pandas on strings"]
    E -->|"needs pandas / NumPy / SciPy"| G["@pandas_udf<br/>within ~5-9% on numeric work"]
    D -->|"no, needs one value at a time"| H["@udf(useArrow=True)<br/>or the default on Spark 4.2<br/>1.4-2.4x over pickle"]
```

**Whichever you choose, check which "Arrow" your setting actually refers to.** Mine didn't, and I wrote a benchmark about exactly this.

## Further reading

- [SPARK-53014](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-53014): Arrow UDF public API (`@arrow_udf`).
- [SPARK-40307](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-40307): Arrow-optimized Python UDFs (`useArrow`), Spark 3.5.0.
- Benchmark code and raw results: `spark-udf-benchmark` (Spark 4.1.0, Spark Connect, `local[*]`).

# AUTO_CDC: Turning an event log into current state with Spark Declarative Pipelines

URL: https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/auto-cdc-declarative-pipelines
Republished at: https://openlakehouse.io/blog/apache-spark/auto-cdc-declarative-pipelines
Original publisher: systems/null
Date: 2026-09-28
Category: Apache Spark

*Originally published on [systems/null](https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/auto-cdc-declarative-pipelines).*

## The question an event log can't answer cheaply

The dataset I use for most of my pipeline demos is a simulated ghost kitchen (a delivery-only restaurant operation), and like most operational data it arrives as an append-only log. Every order produces a lifecycle of events, each stamped with a time and a per-order sequence number, and a day of it is about a million events. The generator deliberately injects a few percent of late and duplicated events, because real streams do that.

Logs like this are excellent at answering what happened and awkward at answering what operations people actually ask: which orders are live right now, and where is each one?

The usual answer is to recompute it. Group the whole history by order, take the latest event for each, drop the cancelled ones, and repeat on every refresh, paying for the entire history every time and getting it subtly wrong whenever "latest" means latest to arrive rather than latest to happen.

The better answer depends on noticing something that sounds obvious once it's said: **an append-only lifecycle log is already a change data capture feed.** Each event is a change to the current state of one entity (the order), keyed by order id, sequenced by when it happened, and a cancellation is simply a delete.

Here is an illustrative order (simplified; the real sequence is described below), first as the lifecycle log records it, then as the change feed it implies:

| seq | event_type | as a change to `orders_live` |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `order_created` | UPSERT order 1042, status = `order_created` |
| 2 | `kitchen_started` | UPSERT order 1042, status = `kitchen_started` |
| 3 | `order_ready` | UPSERT order 1042, status = `order_ready` |
| 4 | `driver_picked_up` | UPSERT order 1042, status = `driver_picked_up` |
| 5 | `driver_ping` | UPSERT order 1042, status = `driver_ping` |
| 6 | `delivered` | UPSERT order 1042, status = `delivered` |

An order that ends in `order_cancelled` produces a DELETE as its last change instead, and disappears from the table. Once the log is seen this way, "current status of every order" stops being an aggregation problem and becomes the problem of applying a change feed to a table, which is exactly what AUTO CDC was built to do.

My argument is that AUTO CDC is worth adopting less because it saves code (though it does, a lot) than because it moves the hard parts of change application into the engine, and leaves you with a small, explicit contract: **a sequence column that is unique and never null, a target that genuinely supports row-level operations, and deletes expressed as events.** Most of what goes wrong with hand-rolled CDC is the engine's side of that contract done badly; most of what can still go wrong with AUTO CDC is your side of it.

## What AUTO CDC is, and where it stands

AUTO CDC began as `APPLY CHANGES` in Databricks' Delta Live Tables and was contributed to Apache Spark under its own SPIP ([SPARK-56249](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-56249)), as part of [Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-51727). In Python it's `create_auto_cdc_flow`.

| Release | AUTO CDC status |
|---|---|
| Spark 4.2.0 (July 2026) | Shipped. SCD Type 1 via the Python / Spark Connect API |
| Spark 4.3.0 (release candidate) | Adds SCD Type 2 (history with validity ranges) |
| main branch (5.0.0-SNAPSHOT) | Ongoing work under SPARK-56249 |

Everything I tested was *SCD Type 1* (the target holds only the current state per key, and updates overwrite in place), on a build of the main branch from late May 2026, before [4.2 was released](https://spark.apache.org/news/).

Applying a change feed correctly means doing several things at once:

- matching each change to its row by key
- keeping the version with the highest sequence per key, not the last to arrive
- honouring deletes, but only when the delete is the latest thing that happened to that key
- staying idempotent when a streaming source redelivers after a failure

The hand-rolled version is usually a `foreachBatch` with windowed deduplication feeding a `MERGE`, and **it tends to get the cross-batch cases wrong without throwing errors**. A late update that lands in the micro-batch after a newer one quietly overwrites it, and nobody notices until the numbers disagree with something else.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    LOG["order_events<br/>(append-only lifecycle log)"] --> PROJ["projection<br/>op = UPSERT / DELETE<br/>seq = unique per order"]
    PROJ --> SRC["streaming source<br/>@dp.table"]
    SRC --> FLOW["create_auto_cdc_flow<br/>keys = order_id<br/>sequence_by = seq"]
    FLOW --> TGT["gold.orders_live<br/>(Iceberg, one row per live order)"]
    FLOW <--> AUX["__spark_autocdc_aux_state_...<br/>latest seq per key, across runs"]
    LOG -.->|"naive alternative:<br/>re-aggregate all history every refresh"| NAIVE["latest-event-per-order<br/>full recompute"]
```

## The code

The projection from lifecycle log to change feed is ordinary Spark. This is the core of what my test harness does: every event becomes an UPSERT of the order's current status, a cancellation becomes a DELETE, and the sequence is made unique per order.

```python
feed = events.select(
    F.col("order_id"),
    F.col("event_type").alias("status"),
    F.col("location_id").cast("int").alias("location_id"),
    F.col("ts_seconds").alias("event_ts"),
    F.when(F.col("event_type") == "order_cancelled", F.lit("DELETE"))
     .otherwise(F.lit("UPSERT")).alias("op"),
    # unique per-key ordering: event time, broken by per-order sequence
    (F.col("ts_seconds") * F.lit(100) + F.col("sequence")).alias("seq"),
)
```

Then the pipeline itself is three declarations: a streaming source, a target streaming table, and the flow.

```python
from pyspark import pipelines as dp

@dp.table(name="order_cdc_source")
def order_cdc_source():
    return spark.readStream.schema(ORDER_SCHEMA).json("file:///data/order_cdc/*.json")

dp.create_streaming_table("ice.gold.orders_live")

dp.create_auto_cdc_flow(
    target="ice.gold.orders_live",
    source="order_cdc_source",
    keys=["order_id"],                  # how a change finds its row
    sequence_by="seq",                  # highest sequence per key wins, whatever the arrival order
    apply_as_deletes="op = 'DELETE'",   # which events delete the row
    except_column_list=["op", "seq"],   # bookkeeping columns to leave out of the target
    stored_as_scd_type=1,
)
```

The engine handles what the hand-rolled version gets wrong: deduplication across micro-batches by `sequence_by`, the generated upsert and delete, exactly-once checkpointing, and the auxiliary state table that remembers the latest sequence per key across runs.

That table is what lets a late event arriving in a later batch resolve correctly.

| | Recompute from the log | AUTO CDC |
|---|---|---|
| Cost per refresh | re-aggregates the entire history | processes only new events |
| Out-of-order events | "latest" by arrival is wrong | resolved by `sequence_by` |
| Cancellations | a row every query must remember to filter | the row is deleted |
| Code | bespoke `foreachBatch` + dedup + `MERGE` | three declarations |

## Running it on messy data

I ran the order-status projection on a sample of the ghost-kitchen stream: a little under five thousand orders and roughly 125,000 of their lifecycle events, including the injected late and duplicate ones. AUTO CDC collapsed them into one row per live order:

| `gold.orders_live` | rows |
|---|---|
| `delivered` | 4,601 |
| `driver_ping` (mid-delivery) | 84 |
| `order_ready` | 3 |
| `order_created` | 1 |
| `kitchen_started` | 1 |
| `driver_picked_up` | 1 |
| **total live orders** | **4,691** |
| cancelled orders removed by `apply_as_deletes` | 308 |

To check it, I recomputed the same table from scratch the naive way and compared the two in both directions:

```python
w = Window.partitionBy("order_id").orderBy(F.desc("seq"))
naive = (feed.withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(w)).filter("rn = 1")
             .filter("op != 'DELETE'").select("order_id", "status"))
pairs = spark.table("ice.gold.orders_live").select("order_id", "status")
match = naive.subtract(pairs).count() == 0 and pairs.subtract(naive).count() == 0
# match = True
```

They matched exactly.

It's worth being precise about what that proves: it compares the two columns the table exists to answer, as sets, rather than every column byte for byte.

Two details of the run also deserve honesty, because they're the kind of thing that makes a demo look cleaner than it was. The sample was drawn by sorting order ids and taking the first five thousand, and because the raw data contains events with a null order id (which Spark sorts first), the sample was really 4,999 orders.

And the projection joined each event to its order's creation event, so orders with duplicated creation events fanned out into duplicate rows in the feed. AUTO CDC handled both without complaint, since duplicate copies of an event carry the same sequence value and resolve to the same row, but a pipeline that quietly processes inputs it wasn't meant to receive is a reminder to **look at your inputs before trusting your outputs**.

The second scenario was the textbook one: keeping a dimension current as kitchens relocate, rename, and close. These are the exact changes streamed into `silver.dim_locations_current`, on top of an initial load of four locations at sequence 1:

```python
changes = [
    {"id": 2, "city": "Los Angeles - Arts District", "op": "UPSERT", "seq": 5},
    {"id": 1, "city": "San Francisco - SoMa",        "op": "UPSERT", "seq": 4},
    {"id": 3, "city": "Chicago",                      "op": "DELETE", "seq": 6},   # kitchen closed
    {"id": 2, "city": "Los Angeles (STALE)",          "op": "UPSERT", "seq": 3},   # arrives late, older
]
```

| id | after AUTO CDC | why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | San Francisco - SoMa | rename at seq 4 applied |
| 2 | Los Angeles - Arts District | rename at seq 5 kept; the stale seq 3 edit ignored |
| 3 | (no row) | closure at seq 6 deleted it |
| 4 | Austin | unchanged |

A nightly full reload would eventually reach the same names, but it copies every unchanged row to get there and has no way at all to express that a location no longer exists.

That's the more general lesson: an append-only or aggregate pipeline can only add facts, so "this was cancelled" becomes another row every downstream query has to remember to filter. **In a CDC pipeline a terminal business event can be the delete itself**, and the same mechanism propagates hard deletes for compliance.

## Edge cases, and how Type 1 resolves them

I put SCD Type 1 through a battery of adversarial cases, and it behaved correctly in every one. The behaviours are worth knowing precisely, because this is where intuition tends to be wrong. These are the cases from my stress harness, with the events in arrival order; `|` separates micro-batches.

| Case | Events for one key | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Upsert to a key that never existed | UPSERT@1 | row inserted |
| Delete of a key that never existed | DELETE@1 | no-op |
| Several updates in one batch | UPSERT@1, UPSERT@2, UPSERT@3 | row has the @3 values |
| Stale delete | UPSERT@1 \| UPSERT@3 \| DELETE@2 | row stays, with the @3 values; the update is newer |
| Stale insert after a delete | UPSERT@3 \| DELETE@5 \| UPSERT@2 | row stays deleted |
| Delete arrives before an older insert | DELETE@5 \| UPSERT@2 | row stays deleted |
| Resurrection | UPSERT@1 \| DELETE@2 \| UPSERT@3 | row present, with the @3 values |
| Volume, out of order | 500 keys, each UPSERT@1, @3, @2 shuffled across 5 batches, plus DELETE@5 for 100 of them | exactly 400 rows, all with the @3 values |
| Tie (probe, not pass/fail) | UPSERT@5 "Boston", UPSERT@5 "Denver" in one batch | one of them, chosen arbitrarily |

## Your side of the contract

**The sequence.** A null in the `sequence_by` column fails the micro-batch with `AUTOCDC_MICROBATCH_VALIDATION.NULL_SEQUENCE` rather than guessing, which is the right behaviour, and means the column has to be non-null by construction.

Ties are worse, because they don't fail: two changes to the same key with the same sequence in one micro-batch are resolved arbitrarily, as [the programming guide](https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/master/docs/declarative-pipelines-programming-guide.md) itself warns. A coarse timestamp is the classic way to produce ties, so **sequence on something strictly increasing per key**, like a log offset or commit LSN. My composite of timestamp times 100 plus the per-order sequence works only because no order in this data has more than 99 events; it's a local trick, not a general recipe. The ties that did occur in my data were all injected exact duplicates, the one case where an arbitrary choice is harmless.

**The target.** AUTO CDC needs a connector that implements Spark's DataSource V2 row-level operation interface (`SupportsRowLevelOperations`), and *"supports MERGE"* is not the same thing:

| Target | Result in my testing |
|---|---|
| Plain Parquet | rejected immediately: `AUTOCDC_TARGET_DOES_NOT_SUPPORT_MERGE` |
| Delta | did not work: Delta's table implementation doesn't expose `SupportsRowLevelOperations`, despite supporting MERGE elsewhere |
| Iceberg, Hadoop catalog | worked |
| Iceberg, JDBC (Postgres) catalog | worked |
| Iceberg, Hive Metastore catalog | worked |
| Iceberg, Gravitino REST catalog | worked |
| Iceberg, Glue catalog (emulated) | worked |
| Iceberg, Unity Catalog OSS REST | failed: the catalog is read-only |
| Any ephemeral / in-memory catalog | unsuitable: the aux state table must persist across restarts |

Two smaller surprises: the target carries a hidden `__spark_autocdc_metadata` column that shows up in `SELECT *`, and Iceberg's own changelog is batch-only in open-source Spark for now, so you can't stream one Iceberg table's changes straight into AUTO CDC as a source.

**A correction.** I originally reported that running an AUTO CDC pipeline through the `spark-pipelines` CLI failed at registration with `InvalidPlanInput: RELTYPE_NOT_SET`, and called it a bug. It wasn't.

The CLI connects to the default Spark Connect endpoint, and an old Spark 4.1 Connect server was still listening there, so my pipeline was being sent to a server that had never heard of AUTO CDC. Against a server of the right version the CLI works correctly. If you see that error, **check what's actually listening on `sc://localhost:15002` before anything else.**

## What changes

With a hand-rolled pipeline, the question you're left with is whether you've correctly implemented cross-batch deduplication, sequenced deletes, and idempotent merges, and the honest answer is usually that you won't know until something disagrees. With AUTO CDC that part belongs to the engine, which is tested against exactly the cases people get wrong.

The question becomes whether you've given it a sequence that is unique and never null, a target that really supports row-level operations, and a delete for everything that should be allowed to disappear. That's a much better question to be left with, and the first step is often not a new data source at all; it's noticing that **the event log you already have has been a change feed all along**.

## Further reading

- Test harnesses and results: `lakehouse-stack/scripts/pipelines/autocdc-scd1` (Spark main branch, 5.0.0-SNAPSHOT at 06ffa273, with an Iceberg runtime ported to Spark 5.0).

# From Pickle to Arrow: A Decade of Moving Data Between Spark's JVM and Python

URL: https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/arrow-and-spark
Republished at: https://openlakehouse.io/blog/apache-spark/arrow-and-spark
Original publisher: systems/null
Date: 2026-09-28
Category: Apache Spark

*Originally published on [systems/null](https://systemsnull.net/posts/data-engineering-ai/arrow-and-spark).*

**Arrow's real contribution to PySpark isn't speed at any one API but a shared memory format at every boundary between the JVM and Python; each release removed one conversion at one boundary, what each one left behind explains the next, and the conversion that remains now lives inside Spark's own engine rather than at the Python edge.** 

That crossing is the oldest problem in PySpark, and the most persistent attempt to fix it started in February 2016, when Wes McKinney (the creator of pandas) filed a Spark ticket with a modest title: [SPARK-13534](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-13534), "Implement Apache Arrow serializer for Spark DataFrame for use in DataFrame.toPandas." It asked for one method to stop using pickle.

It took two years to ship. And over the decade that followed, the same idea went through every other door between Spark's JVM and Python: UDFs, partition-level APIs, the network protocol of Spark Connect, custom data sources, until in Spark 4.1 a Python function could receive Spark's data as an Arrow array and never touch pandas at all, and in Spark 4.2 the Arrow paths [finally became the defaults](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/api/python/tutorial/sql/arrow_pandas.html).

---

## The wall

PySpark is not a Python reimplementation of Spark. It's a Python client for a JVM engine. When you write `df.filter(col("x") > 5).groupBy("y").count()`, Python builds a query plan and hands it to the JVM, which optimizes, distributes, and executes it; **Python never touches the data**, which is why DataFrame code runs at the same speed in PySpark and Scala.

The trouble starts the moment your own code needs the data: a UDF, `toPandas()`, `createDataFrame(pandas_df)`, a custom data source. Then data has to physically cross from the JVM into a Python process, and for most of Spark's history the only way across was pickle, one row at a time:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant J as JVM executor (Spark task)
    participant P as Python worker (your UDF)
    Note over J,P: TCP loopback socket, before Arrow
    loop once for every row in the partition
        J->>P: pickle(row)
        P->>P: unpickle, call your function, pickle the result
        P->>J: pickle(result)
        J->>J: unpickle(result)
    end
```

Every row pays four serialization steps and a function call. For a UDF like `return x * 1.1`, the arithmetic is nanoseconds and the machinery around it is microseconds, **three orders of magnitude of overhead wrapped around almost no work.**

That was PySpark from 2015 to 2018, and the same crossing existed at every door between the two runtimes, on both the driver and the executors:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  classDef jvm fill:#3a5f96,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#3a5f96,color:#ffffff
  classDef py fill:#6b4a9b,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#6b4a9b,color:#ffffff
  subgraph JVM["JVM"]
    DRV["driver"]:::jvm
    EX["executor tasks"]:::jvm
    EX2["executor tasks<br/>(scanning a Python source)"]:::jvm
    CS["Spark Connect server"]:::jvm
  end
  subgraph PY["Python"]
    PD["Python driver<br/>toPandas(), createDataFrame()"]:::py
    PW["Python workers<br/>UDFs, mapIn*, applyIn*"]:::py
    DS["Python data source<br/>reader"]:::py
    CC["Spark Connect client<br/>(remote, no JVM)"]:::py
  end
  DRV ---|"collected results,<br/>local DataFrames"| PD
  EX ---|"batches of rows,<br/>per task"| PW
  EX2 ---|"tuples or RecordBatches"| DS
  CS ---|"plans in, results out<br/>(gRPC)"| CC
```

## Why the fix was a memory format, not a faster pickle

Arrow was conceived in late 2015 by people who had hit the same wall from different directions. McKinney had spent years fighting pandas' memory model; his 2017 essay [*"Apache Arrow and the 10 Things I Hate About pandas"*](https://wesmckinney.com/blog/apache-arrow-pandas-internals/) lists the grievances, including a rule of thumb that pandas users needed "5 to 10 times as much RAM as the size of your dataset."

Jacques Nadeau, building a query engine at Dremio, saw every data system inventing its own internal format and paying to translate between them at every boundary. Marcel Kornacker, who created Impala at Cloudera, saw the same copying across the Hadoop ecosystem. [They met at Strata NYC](https://www.dremio.com/blog/origin-and-history-of-apache-arrow/) in September 2015, and Arrow was announced as an Apache top-level project in February 2016, skipping the incubator entirely, which is unusual and reflected how many companies wanted the same thing.

The idea was not a faster serializer. **It was to agree on the bytes themselves:** [a language-independent, columnar, in-memory layout](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/Columnar.html) specified down to byte alignment, null bitmaps, and buffer order, so that two Arrow-aware systems can hand each other data without converting it.

Within a process, or with shared memory, that's genuinely *zero-copy*; across a socket it's still a copy, but with no per-row decoding on either side, because the bytes on the wire are already the bytes in memory.

Columnar mattered as much as standard. In a row layout, values from one column are interleaved with everything else in the row:

```
row layout:     [id=1, name="Alice", age=30] [id=2, name="Bob", age=25] [id=3, name="Carol", age=35]
columnar:       id:   [1, 2, 3]
                name: ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol"]
                age:  [30, 25, 35]
```

With columns stored contiguously, a 64-byte cache line holds eight useful `int64` values instead of one row's mixed fields, and SIMD instructions can process a run of values at once.

The database literature had already shown what this buys: the [MonetDB/X100 work](https://www.cidrdb.org/cidr2005/papers/P19.pdf) (CIDR 2005) argued that pushing batches of around a thousand column values through each operator, instead of one row at a time, is an order of magnitude or two faster. Arrow's batch-oriented design was built around exactly that model.

---

## Boundary one: the driver (2018)

The first door was the smallest. `DataFrame.toPandas()` collected results to the driver by pickling every row and rebuilding each one as Python objects before pandas could wrap them, and it was notoriously slow. [McKinney's ticket](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-13534), filed on February 28, 2016, three weeks after the first commit to the Arrow repository, asked to replace that path. It stayed open for over a year. Bryan Cutler, at IBM's Spark Technology Center, resolved it on June 23, 2017, and it reached users in Spark 2.3.0 in February 2018.

Two years, for one method.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef jvm fill:#3a5f96,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#3a5f96,color:#ffffff
    classDef py fill:#6b4a9b,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#6b4a9b,color:#ffffff
    subgraph JVM["JVM driver"]
        A["InternalRow batches"]:::jvm --> B["Arrow RecordBatches"]:::jvm
    end
    subgraph PY["Python driver"]
        C["pyarrow reads RecordBatches<br/>(a copy across processes,<br/>no per-row decoding)"]:::py --> D["Table.to_pandas()<br/>(zero-copy for many<br/>numeric types)"]:::py
    end
    B -->|"Arrow IPC stream"| C
```

```python
# Spark 2.3 name, later renamed; on by default since Spark 4.2
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled", "true")
```

The reverse direction, `createDataFrame(pandas_df)`, got the same treatment ([SPARK-20791](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-20791)). What made this matter wasn't the one method; it was [the plumbing Cutler built](https://arrow.apache.org/blog/2017/07/26/spark-arrow/) to do it (Arrow converters on the JVM side, pyarrow integration on the Python side), **which every later boundary reused**.

**What it removed:** pickle for collecting data to the driver. **What it left:** everything that happens on executors. UDFs still crossed row by row.

## Boundary two: UDFs, in batches (2018)

The second door was the one that mattered for performance, and it came from outside Databricks. The proposal, [SPARK-21190](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-21190) ("SPIP: Vectorized UDFs in Python"), was filed by Reynold Xin, but most of the implementation was done by Li Jin, an engineer at the quantitative investment firm Two Sigma and an Arrow committer, on top of Cutler's serializer. It shipped in the same Spark 2.3.0 release. Instead of calling your function once per row, Spark would send a batch of rows (10,000 by default, `spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch`) as an Arrow RecordBatch and call your function once per batch, with a pandas Series:

```python
# Before: once per row, pickle both ways
@udf(returnType="double")
def add_tax(price):
    return price * 1.1 if price else None

# After: once per batch, a pandas Series in and out
@pandas_udf("double")
def add_tax(price: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    return price * 1.1
```

[Li Jin's post introducing the feature](https://www.databricks.com/blog/2017/10/30/introducing-vectorized-udfs-for-pyspark.html) in October 2017 reported speedups from around 3x on simple arithmetic to around 100x on a cumulative-probability function, and the spread is the point: **the simpler the function, the more of its cost was the crossing**, and the more complex the function, the more it also benefits from running as vectorized NumPy instead of Python bytecode.

My own measurements, eight years and many releases later, land in the same shape. At 50 million rows, a pandas UDF did the arithmetic workload in 0.79 seconds against 5.20 for a pickled UDF, and a normal CDF in 0.82 against 6.18; on a string transform the gap was narrower, 2.51 against 6.22, for a reason that turns out to matter later.

**What it removed:** per-row serialization and per-row function calls. **What it left:** a rewrite (your function had to speak pandas), and a conversion. Every batch arrived as Arrow and was turned into pandas before your code saw it, and the result was turned back:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  classDef jvm fill:#3a5f96,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#3a5f96,color:#ffffff
  classDef py fill:#6b4a9b,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#6b4a9b,color:#ffffff
  classDef conv fill:#c0661a,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#c0661a,color:#ffffff
  A["JVM: batch of<br/>10,000 rows"]:::jvm -->|"Arrow IPC"| B["pyarrow<br/>RecordBatch"]:::py
  B -->|"Arrow to pandas,<br/>per batch"| C["pandas.Series"]:::conv
  C --> D["your function,<br/>once per batch"]:::py
  D --> E["pandas.Series"]:::conv
  E -->|"pandas to Arrow,<br/>per batch"| F["pyarrow<br/>RecordBatch"]:::py
  F -->|"Arrow IPC"| G["JVM: rows"]:::jvm
```

## What actually crosses the socket

Every boundary from here on sends the same thing over the socket: [Arrow's IPC stream format](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/python/ipc.html), a schema message followed by record-batch messages, each framed like this:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Continuation indicator: 0xFFFFFFFF (4 bytes)                │
│ Metadata length (4 bytes, little-endian int32)              │
│ Flatbuffer metadata (Message type, schema or batch header)  │
│ Padding to 8-byte boundary                                  │
│ Message body (data buffers, padded to 8-byte multiple)      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Inside the body, each column is a set of plain buffers: a validity bitmap with one bit per value, the values themselves as a contiguous typed array, and, for variable-length types like strings, an offsets array into one contiguous UTF-8 buffer. For four rows of `(name: string, age: int32)`:

```
Validity bitmap (age):  [1, 1, 0, 1]      → 0b1011 (bit-packed)
Data buffer (age):      [30, 25, 0, 35]   → 16 bytes (4 × int32)
Offsets (name):         [0, 5, 8, 13, 18] → 5 × int32
Data buffer (name):     "AliceBobCarolDavid" (contiguous UTF-8)
```

No per-value type tags, no escaping, no framing between values.

Strings are where Arrow and pandas differ most: **in Arrow, a million strings are one buffer and an array of offsets**, while in traditional pandas they're a million separate Python objects.

---

## Boundary three: letting code see Arrow (2022 to 2025)

For four years, every batch API in PySpark handed you pandas, whether you wanted pandas or not.

The first API that let user code see Arrow directly was `mapInArrow`, added by Hyukjin Kwon, a long-time PySpark maintainer at Databricks ([SPARK-37227](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-37227), with the Python side in [SPARK-37228](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-37228)), in Spark 3.3.0 in June 2022. It passes whole partitions as an iterator of `pyarrow.RecordBatch` objects, and your function yields RecordBatches back:

```python
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.compute as pc

def add_tax_arrow(batches):
    for batch in batches:
        taxed = pc.multiply(batch.column("price"), pa.scalar(1.1))
        yield pa.RecordBatch.from_arrays([batch.column("id"), taxed],
                                         names=["id", "price_with_tax"])

df.mapInArrow(add_tax_arrow, schema="id long, price_with_tax double")
```

Grouped operations were the obvious remaining gap, and Enrico Minack closed it with `applyInArrow` ([SPARK-40559](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-40559)), which shipped in Spark 4.0.0 in May 2025. Where `applyInPandas` turns each group into a pandas DataFrame, `applyInArrow` hands you the group as a `pyarrow.Table`:

```python
def normalize(table: pa.Table) -> pa.Table:
    totals = table.column("total")
    mean, std = pc.mean(totals).as_py(), pc.stddev(totals).as_py()
    normalized = (pa.array([0.0] * len(totals)) if not std
                  else pc.divide(pc.subtract(totals, pa.scalar(mean)), pa.scalar(std)))
    return pa.Table.from_arrays([table.column("order_id"), totals, normalized],
                                names=["order_id", "total", "normalized"])

orders.groupBy("location_id").applyInArrow(
    normalize, schema="order_id long, total double, normalized double")
```

The same idea reached the other direction in 4.0 too: the new Python Data Source API ([SPARK-44076](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-44076)) lets a custom source written in Python yield `pyarrow.RecordBatch` objects instead of tuples ([SPARK-48493](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-48493)), so data read by Python code can enter Spark as Arrow instead of being built up one Python tuple at a time.

I haven't benchmarked the grouped or data-source paths myself, so there are no numbers for them here; the mechanism is the same as everywhere else, and the benefit should be largest where the pandas conversion is most expensive, which is strings.

**What it removed:** the forced detour through pandas, for anyone willing to write Arrow code. **What it left:** that condition. Most PySpark code is plain `@udf` functions that nobody is going to rewrite.

## Boundary four: the network (2023)

Spark Connect started as a proposal from Martin Grund at Databricks in June 2022 ([SPARK-39375](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-39375)): separate the client from the server, so an application talks to Spark over gRPC instead of living inside the driver's JVM. Once there's a network between you and the engine, **the format results travel in stops being an optimization and becomes the protocol**.

The answer was Arrow.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef jvm fill:#3a5f96,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#3a5f96,color:#ffffff
    classDef py fill:#6b4a9b,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#6b4a9b,color:#ffffff
    subgraph Client["Spark Connect client (no JVM)"]
        C1["Python app builds<br/>a logical plan"]:::py
        C2["Receives the Arrow stream,<br/>reconstructs the DataFrame"]:::py
    end
    subgraph Server["Spark Connect server (full Spark runtime)"]
        S1["Catalyst optimizer,<br/>physical execution"]:::jvm
        S2["Results converted to<br/>Arrow RecordBatches"]:::jvm
    end
    C1 -->|"unresolved plan<br/>(Protobuf over gRPC)"| S1 --> S2 -->|"Arrow IPC over gRPC"| C2
```

The client sends unresolved logical plans as Protocol Buffers; the server optimizes and runs them and streams the results back as Arrow record batches over the same channel. That's what makes a JVM-free Python client possible at all: the `pyspark-client` package is a 1.6 MB wheel of pure Python. The same columnar format that moves data between executors and Python workers now moves data between a remote cluster and a laptop.

## Boundary five: the UDFs nobody rewrote (2023 to 2026)

Every boundary so far helped people who changed their code. Arrow-optimized Python UDFs ([SPARK-40307](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-40307), Spark 3.5.0, September 2023) took the opposite approach: keep your plain `@udf` exactly as written, and swap the transport underneath it. Batches cross as Arrow; Python unpacks each batch and still calls your function once per value.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef old fill:#4b5563,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#4b5563,color:#ffffff
    classDef new fill:#d97706,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#d97706,color:#ffffff
    subgraph Before["Pickle @udf"]
        A1["JVM: each row"]:::old --> A2["pickle(value)"]:::old --> A3["socket"]:::old --> A4["Python: unpickle"]:::old --> A5["call function"]:::old
    end
    subgraph After["Arrow-optimized @udf"]
        B1["JVM: batch of rows"]:::new --> B2["Arrow RecordBatch"]:::new --> B3["socket"]:::new --> B4["Python: unpack batch"]:::new --> B5["call function per value"]:::old
    end
```

[Xinrong Meng's 2023 Databricks post](https://www.databricks.com/blog/arrow-optimized-python-udfs-apache-sparktm-35) measured about 1.6x over pickle for a single UDF and 1.9x for three chained ones on a 32 GB dataset, and my benchmark agrees in spirit: `useArrow=True` took the arithmetic workload from 5.20 to 2.23 seconds and the CDF from 6.18 to 2.94. Real, and cheap to get, but nothing like the pandas UDF numbers, because the per-row function call is still there.

That call is my benchmark's ceiling.

Turning this on by default took two tries. It was merged for Spark 4.0 ([SPARK-48516](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-48516)) and reverted in March 2025 before the release; it finally shipped as the default in Spark 4.2, along with Arrow for `toPandas()` and for Python UDTFs, and [a minimum PyArrow of 18.0](https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/branch-4.3/python/docs/source/migration_guide/pyspark_upgrade.rst). On 4.2, then, every existing `@udf` gets Arrow transport without anyone touching it.

It's also where I made the mistake that best illustrates how confusing this boundary is. My benchmark's "Arrow" variant of the plain UDF flipped `spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled`, which governs `toPandas()` and `createDataFrame()` and has nothing to do with UDFs. The setting that actually moves a UDF onto Arrow is `spark.sql.execution.pythonUDF.arrow.enabled`, or `useArrow=True` on the decorator. So my "Arrow" row was the pickled UDF measured twice, and its near-identical result was an accidental A/A test.

**Three settings are named for Arrow, and they control three different boundaries.**

**What it removed:** pickle, for everyone, with no code changes. **What it left:** the function call per row, which is the part no transport format can fix.

## Boundary six: Arrow as the execution format (2025)

The last step turned Arrow from the way data travels into the way your code computes. Ruifeng Zheng's [SPARK-53014](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-53014), "Make Arrow UDF public," shipped in Spark 4.1.0 on December 16, 2025, almost ten years after McKinney's ticket. An Arrow UDF receives `pyarrow.Array` values and returns one, and it's meant to be written with `pyarrow.compute`, whose functions are [C++ kernels operating directly on Arrow buffers](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/python/compute.html):

```python
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.compute as pc
from pyspark.sql.functions import arrow_udf

@arrow_udf("double")
def add_tax(price: pa.Array) -> pa.Array:
    return pc.multiply(price, pa.scalar(1.1))

@arrow_udf("string")
def clean_email(email: pa.Array) -> pa.Array:
    return pc.utf8_trim(pc.utf8_lower(email))
```

The four UDF types differ only in where the data changes format:

| UDF type | Data path | Format conversions |
|---|---|---|
| Pickle `@udf` | JVM → pickle → Python value → pickle → JVM | pickle both ways, per row |
| Arrow-optimized `@udf` | JVM → Arrow → Python value → Arrow → JVM | Arrow ↔ Python objects, per row |
| `@pandas_udf` | JVM → Arrow → pandas → Arrow → JVM | Arrow ↔ pandas, per batch |
| `@arrow_udf` | JVM → Arrow → your function → Arrow → JVM | none on the Python side |

In my benchmark, `@arrow_udf` was the fastest Python option everywhere, but **the margin over pandas UDFs depended almost entirely on the data type**. On arithmetic and the CDF it was only 5 to 9% faster; on the string transform it was 1.6x faster at both 50M and 100M rows (1.55 seconds against 2.51 at 50M).

The split comes down to strings. A numeric pandas Series is a NumPy array underneath, so converting from Arrow is cheap; a string column in traditional pandas is an array of Python objects, so converting means building millions of them. `pyarrow.compute` skips all of that and works on the one contiguous buffer.

**What it removed:** the last conversion on the Python side. **What it left:** Spark's side.

Taken together, the choice today comes down to what your function can receive:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    classDef best fill:#d97706,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#d97706,color:#ffffff
    classDef ok fill:#3a5f96,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#3a5f96,color:#ffffff
    classDef last fill:#4b5563,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#4b5563,color:#ffffff
    Q1{"Expressible with built-in<br/>Spark functions or SQL?"} -->|yes| A1["Use those. Nothing in Python came close."]:::best
    Q1 -->|no| Q3{"Expressible with<br/>pyarrow.compute?"}
    Q3 -->|yes| A3["@arrow_udf<br/>(largest win on strings)"]:::ok
    Q3 -->|no| Q4{"Needs pandas / NumPy / SciPy?"}
    Q4 -->|yes| A4["@pandas_udf"]:::ok
    Q4 -->|no| A5["plain @udf: Arrow transport<br/>by default on Spark 4.2"]:::last
```

## The pipe itself

Everything above changes what goes through the socket. Hyukjin Kwon's [SPARK-51688](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-51688), shipped in Spark 4.1.0, changes the socket: instead of TCP over loopback, which runs every byte through the full TCP/IP stack even though it never leaves the machine, the JVM and Python workers can talk over a *Unix domain socket*, which goes straight through a kernel buffer.

It's opt-in (`spark.python.unix.domain.socket.enabled`, whose default comes from the `PYSPARK_UDS_MODE` environment variable) in 4.1 and 4.2, and that's unchanged on the 4.3 branch, which instead adds another transport option: [pipelined, asynchronous transfer of UDF batches](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-56642) between the JVM and Python (`spark.python.udf.pipelined.enabled`, off by default).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  classDef jvm fill:#3a5f96,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#3a5f96,color:#ffffff
  classDef py fill:#6b4a9b,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#6b4a9b,color:#ffffff
  classDef old fill:#4b5563,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#4b5563,color:#ffffff
  classDef new fill:#d97706,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#d97706,color:#ffffff
  subgraph TCP["TCP over loopback (default)"]
    J1["JVM executor"]:::jvm --> T1["TCP/IP stack<br/>(segments, ACKs, flow control)"]:::old --> L["loopback interface"]:::old --> T2["TCP/IP stack"]:::old --> P1["Python worker"]:::py
  end
  subgraph UDS["Unix domain socket (opt-in since 4.1)"]
    J2["JVM executor"]:::jvm --> K["kernel socket buffer"]:::new --> P2["Python worker"]:::py
  end
```

```
Spark 1.x:  pickle format  + TCP loopback        slow format over a slow pipe
Spark 2.3:  Arrow format   + TCP loopback        fast format over a slow pipe
Spark 4.1:  Arrow format   + Unix domain socket  fast format over a faster pipe (opt-in)
```

---

## One boundary at a time

```mermaid
timeline
    title Arrow in PySpark, one boundary at a time
    2016 : Apache Arrow launched : SPARK-13534 filed
    2018 : Spark 2.3 : Arrow-backed toPandas and createDataFrame : Pandas UDFs
    2022 : Spark 3.3 : mapInArrow
    2023 : Spark 3.4 : Spark Connect streams results as Arrow : Spark 3.5 : Arrow-optimized Python UDFs (opt-in)
    May 2025 : Spark 4.0 : applyInArrow : Python Data Source with Arrow batches
    Dec 2025 : Spark 4.1 : Arrow UDFs made public : Unix domain sockets (opt-in)
    Jul 2026 : Spark 4.2 : Arrow on by default for toPandas, Python UDFs, and UDTFs
```

As of Spark 4.2, Arrow is the format at every place data crosses between the JVM and Python:

| Boundary | Arrow's role | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `toPandas()` / `createDataFrame()` | replaces pickle for driver data collection | yes, since 4.2 |
| `@udf` (plain Python UDFs) | replaces pickle transport | yes, since 4.2 |
| `@pandas_udf`, `mapInPandas`, `applyInPandas` | batch transport, converted to pandas | always |
| `@arrow_udf`, `mapInArrow`, `applyInArrow` | transport and execution format | always |
| Spark Connect results | the result protocol | always |
| Python Data Source API | source data format | when the source yields RecordBatches |

## The last boundary

What's left is on Spark's side of the wall. Inside the JVM, Spark still executes on its own row format (UnsafeRow, from the Tungsten project), and Arrow exists at the edges, so **every crossing still begins and ends with a conversion** between Spark's rows and Arrow's columns. Engines like Velox and DataFusion show that a query engine can execute on Arrow-format data directly; Spark doesn't, and closing that gap is a much bigger change than any of the boundaries above.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  classDef jvm fill:#3a5f96,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#3a5f96,color:#ffffff
  classDef py fill:#6b4a9b,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#6b4a9b,color:#ffffff
  classDef conv fill:#c0661a,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#c0661a,color:#ffffff
  classDef new fill:#d97706,fill-opacity:0.72,stroke:#d97706,color:#ffffff
  subgraph Spark["Spark: rows inside, Arrow at the edge"]
    direction LR
    U["execution on UnsafeRow<br/>(Tungsten row format)"]:::jvm -->|"rows to columns"| C1["Arrow batch"]:::conv --> P["Python, Connect client,<br/>anything outside"]:::py --> C2["Arrow batch"]:::conv -->|"columns to rows"| U2["execution on UnsafeRow"]:::jvm
  end
  subgraph Native["DataFusion, Velox: columns all the way through"]
    direction LR
    N["execution on Arrow or<br/>Arrow-compatible columns"]:::new -->|"no conversion"| P2["anything that<br/>speaks Arrow"]:::py
  end
  Spark ~~~ Native
```

The 4.3 branch, which hasn't been released yet (its first release candidate [failed its vote on September 6](https://lists.apache.org/thread/6bhgq2w84zrv3sl4wr2zl8p23fvbsfrg), and a second, [put to a vote on October 13](https://lists.apache.org/thread/y7h0v7km0814xb5fg57ght5wtfptn9lt), drew -1 votes over critical fixes that still need backporting, so there's no date), has two small signs of movement at exactly this edge. One is an Arrow format for Spark's in-memory cache (`ArrowCachedBatchSerializer`, [SPARK-57268](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-57268)), part of a proposal to make Spark better on a single machine: the first time Arrow shows up as a storage format inside Spark itself rather than at a door.

The other goes around the boundary instead of through it: experimental transpilation of Python UDFs into Spark expressions (SPIP [SPARK-54783](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-54783)), so a simple enough Python function never has to cross into Python at all. It's off by default, classic-mode only, and requires ANSI mode, but it's the one approach that could get under my benchmark's ceiling, because **it removes the per-row Python call rather than making the trip to it cheaper**.

The pandas side is moving too, more slowly than you'd expect. [pandas 3.0, released in January 2026](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/v3.0.0.html), made a PyArrow-backed string type the default, which should shrink exactly the string-conversion cost that separates pandas UDFs from Arrow UDFs. But PySpark doesn't support pandas 3 yet, not even on the 4.3 branch: it still pins pandas below 3.0, and the umbrella ticket for supporting it ([SPARK-55139](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-55139)) is open.

When Wes McKinney filed SPARK-13534 in 2016, he was asking for one method to stop pickling. Ten years later, every door he could have named uses Arrow, the defaults finally say so, and the conversion that remains is the one Spark performs on itself, between its own rows and everything outside it.

That's the last boundary, and **it was never a Python problem.**

---

# Apache Iceberg 1.11.0 Release

URL: https://iceberg.apache.org/blog/apache-iceberg-1.11.0-release/
Republished at: https://openlakehouse.io/blog/iceberg/iceberg-1-11-0-release
Original publisher: Apache Iceberg
Date: 2026-06-16
Category: Iceberg

The Apache Iceberg community is pleased to announce the release of Apache Iceberg 1.11.0. This release is the result of over **1,000 commits** from **200+ contributors**. See the [release notes](https://iceberg.apache.org/releases/#1110-release) for the complete list of changes.

## Release Highlights

### REST Catalog: A More Complete Protocol

1.11.0 represents the most significant step forward for the REST catalog protocol since it was introduced.

[Remote scan planning](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/13400) allows catalog servers to plan table scans and stream back file scan tasks directly. Previously, every client had to fetch manifest lists and manifests itself to determine which files to read. With server-side planning, clients receive only the relevant scan tasks, reducing driver memory pressure and enabling server-side optimizations that are transparent to the query engine. This release extends remote scan planning to cover [incremental scans](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14661) for Structured Streaming workloads and [metadata tables](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14881) such as `history` and `snapshots`. A [per-table override](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15572) allows individual tables to opt out of catalog-level scan planning mode when needed.

[Freshness-aware table loading](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14398) adds ETag-based caching to table metadata. When a client loads a table it already has metadata for, the server can return a `304 Not Modified` response instead of re-sending the full metadata payload, cutting unnecessary round-trips in tight read loops and interactive workloads.

[Idempotency key support](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14740) introduces a standard `Idempotency-Key` header for mutating catalog operations. Retried writes — commits, creates, and drops — are now guaranteed not to execute twice, preventing duplicate snapshots and corrupted state from network timeouts.

[Register View](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14868) completes the view lifecycle in the REST catalog. Just as tables can be registered from their metadata location, views can now be [registered via the REST API](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14870) too — enabling cross-catalog migrations and re-attaching orphaned view metadata.

[Custom Table and View Operations](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14465) can now be injected into the REST catalog, allowing users to extend or override default `TableOperations` and `ViewOperations` behavior without forking the catalog implementation.

### OpenAPI Specification Updates

Several protocol-level additions land in the OpenAPI spec this release, tightening the contract between clients and catalog servers.

- **Namespace separator configurable by server**: [The server can now advertise a custom namespace separator](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14448) in the config endpoint, allowing catalogs that use separators other than `.` to communicate this to clients without out-of-band configuration.
- **Register view endpoint**: [A new `/register-view` REST endpoint](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14869) is added to the OpenAPI spec, enabling view registration as an independently authorized catalog capability.
- **ETag for `CommitTableResponse`**: [ETag support on commit responses](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14760) enables clients to detect whether a concurrent write changed the table between their load and commit.
- **S3 signing endpoint promoted to main spec**: [The S3 signing endpoint](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15450) moves from an extension into the main OpenAPI spec, making it an official part of the REST catalog protocol.
- **Partition statistics in `TableUpdate`**: [`SetPartitionStatisticsUpdate` and `RemovePartitionStatisticsUpdate`](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14957) are now included in the `TableUpdate` union type.
- **Storage credentials in scan planning responses**: [Storage credentials are now returned](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15524) in `PlanTableScanResponse` and `FetchPlanningResultResponse` when the `include-credentials` flag is set.

### Spec: SQL UDFs and Geospatial Types

The [SQL UDF Specification](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14117) introduces a new spec for storing SQL user-defined functions in Iceberg catalogs. UDFs are versioned, support multiple SQL dialects, and are portable across engines, bringing function management into the catalog layer for the first time.

[Geospatial bounding box types](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/12667) add native bounding box types and an `INTERSECTS` predicate to Iceberg's type system, enabling spatial partition pruning and file skipping for geospatial workloads directly on Iceberg tables. [Restrictions for geometry types in V3](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14250) are also clarified in this release.

Several smaller but meaningful spec additions round out the release:

- **`added-rows` in snapshot fields**: The [`added-rows` field is restored to snapshot metadata](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14048).
- **`referenced-by` in `loadTable` response**: [`loadTable` now returns a `referenced-by` field](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/13810) listing views and other objects that depend on the table.
- **`scan-planning-mode` in `LoadTableResult`**: [The server can now advertise its preferred scan planning mode](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14867).
- **404 for missing warehouse on config endpoint**: [The `/v1/config` endpoint now returns 404](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15746) when the requested warehouse does not exist.

### Performance and Reliability

[LIMIT pushdown to scan](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14615) stops scanning after enough rows are found when a query includes a `LIMIT` clause, rather than reading all matching files. For exploratory queries, this can reduce I/O by orders of magnitude.

Vectorized reads now cover additional Parquet encodings, eliminating the row-at-a-time fallback for [BYTE_STREAM_SPLIT](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15373), [DELTA_LENGTH_BYTE_ARRAY, and DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15362).

[Snapshot expiration cleanup modes](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14287) introduce a new `cleanupMode` API that gives finer control over what gets cleaned up when snapshots expire.

[Unique table locations](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/12892) via a new catalog property append a UUID to table storage paths, preventing a data loss scenario where `DeleteOrphanFiles` could remove files from a renamed table.

Scheduled credential refresh for [AWS S3FileIO](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15678) and [GCS FileIO](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15696) proactively rotates credentials before they expire, eliminating transient failures in long-running Spark and Flink jobs.

The [GCSAnalyticsCore library](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14333) is now integrated into GCSFileIO, bringing analytics-optimized I/O for Google Cloud Storage.

### Format V4 Foundations

1.11.0 begins laying the groundwork for Table Format V4.

New foundational types — [TrackedFile, TrackingInfo, ContentInfo, and ManifestStats](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15049) — are the building blocks for V4's adaptive metadata tree.

The new [FormatModel abstraction](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/12774) replaces hardcoded file format handling with a pluggable interface. [Parquet](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15253), [ORC](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15255), Avro, and Arrow each now implement a `FormatModel` contract.

### Encryption

1.11.0 makes table encryption available to Iceberg users. The [Encryption integration and test](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/13066) activates the encryption mechanism in Hive tables via a table property containing the ID of the table master key.

[Manifest list encryption](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/7770) extends Iceberg's encryption coverage to manifest list files. [Automatic key rotation](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14396) adds support for rotating key encryption keys without manual intervention.

[Cloud KMS support](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15272) now covers AWS, Azure, and GCP through a unified `encryption.kms-type` property.

### New APIs

The [Content Stats API](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/13933) introduces classes for file-level statistics — min/max values, null counts, and more — providing richer information for query planners.

The [Partition Stats Scan API](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14640) replaces the old single-shot partition stats reader with a composable, filterable interface consistent with the rest of Iceberg's Scan API.

### Engine Updates

#### Spark

[Spark 4.1](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14155) is now supported, with several notable additions:

- **MERGE INTO schema evolution**: [Initial support](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14970) for schema changes during merge writes
- **Shredded Variant writes**: [Support for writing shredded Variant data](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14297) in Iceberg-Spark
- **Async micro-batch planner**: [Reduces scheduling overhead](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15299) in Structured Streaming
- **Adaptive split sizing**: [Session config support](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16088) for tuning split sizes and parallelism

**[Spark 3.4 support is deprecated](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14099)** in this release.

#### Flink

[Flink 2.1](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/13714) is now supported and Flink 1.19 has been removed.

**Row lineage** readers for [`_row_id` and `_last_updated_sequence_number`](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14148) are now available in Flink, with [row lineage preserved through RewriteDataFiles](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14149).

The Flink Dynamic Sink receives major improvements:

- **Deletion vector support**: [Efficient row-level deletes](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14414) without rewriting data files
- **Variant type support**: [Variant is now supported in Flink 2.1](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15265)
- **Schema evolution**: [Support for dropping columns](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14728) and [case-insensitive field matching](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14729)
- **SQL-configurable options**: Dynamic Sink options are now configurable through [Flink SQL](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15279)
- **Post-commit maintenance**: [Arbitrary maintenance tasks can now be registered via the IcebergSink Builder](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15566)

[Nanosecond timestamp precision](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15475) is now supported, matching the full range of Iceberg's timestamp spec.

#### Kafka Connect

- **Variant type ingestion**: [Semi-structured JSON data](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15283) can now be ingested directly into Iceberg's Variant type
- **Table UUID validation on commit**: [Verifies table identity at commit time](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14979)
- **SMT offset tracking fix**: [Fixes a bug](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15880) where Single Message Transforms could cause duplicate records

### Cloud Integrations

**AWS**: The [KMS endpoint is now configurable](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14246), [chunked encoding for S3 requests is configurable](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15242), custom credential providers are [preferred over the default chain](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15249), and [retry policies now apply to Glue and DynamoDB clients](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15094).

**Azure**: A [KeyManagementClient implementation for Azure Key Vault](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/13186) adds native Azure KMS support, and [token credential provider support](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14136) enables flexible authentication including managed identity and service principal flows.

**GCP**: [Service account impersonation in BigQueryMetastoreCatalog](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14447), a new [`gcp.auth.credentials-key` property](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14713) for base64-encoded service account keys, and [ETag-based conflict detection on commit](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14940).

**Aliyun**: [RRSA authentication is now supported for OSS](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14443).

## Breaking Changes

- **Apache DataFusion Comet removed**: [The Comet integration has been removed](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15674) from the Spark module
- **Java 11 dropped**: [Java 11 support has been removed](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14400); Java 17 is now the minimum required version
- **Flink 1.19 removed**: [Flink 1.19 support has been removed](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/13714); upgrade to Flink 1.20 or 2.x

## Dependency Updates

Notable version changes in this release:

- **AWS SDK**: 2.33.0 → 2.44.4
- **Parquet**: 1.16.0 → 1.17.1
- **ORC**: 1.9.7 → 1.9.8
- **Avro**: 1.12.0 → 1.12.1
- **Nessie**: 0.104.5 → 0.107.5
- **Guava**: 33.4.8-jre → 33.6.0-jre
- **Hadoop**: 3.4.1 → 3.4.3
- **Jetty**: 11.0.26 → 12.1.8

New support added for Spark 4.1 (4.1.1) and Flink 2.1 (2.1.0).

## Getting Involved

Apache Iceberg is developed by a community of contributors. We use GitHub [issues](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/issues) for tracking work and the [Apache Iceberg Community Slack](https://iceberg.apache.org/community/#slack) for discussions.

The easiest way to get started is to:

1. Try Apache Iceberg with your workloads and report any issues you encounter
2. Review the [contributor guide](https://iceberg.apache.org/contribute/)
3. Look for [good first issues](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/contribute)

For more information, visit the [Apache Iceberg repository](https://github.com/apache/iceberg) or the [documentation](https://iceberg.apache.org/docs/latest/).
