# Installing Omnigent

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/learn/getting-started/omnigent-install
Date: 2026-06-17
Category: Getting Started

Get Omnigent running in a few minutes. Install the CLI, set up your credentials, and launch your first agent. Once it's running you can add the native macOS app for a full UI — it's the last step of this same flow.

## Requirements

- **Python 3.12+**
- **Node.js 22 LTS** and npm
- **tmux**

## Install Omnigent

<Tabs>
<Tab label="Installer">

```bash
curl -fsSL https://omnigent.ai/install.sh | sh
```

Run the same command to upgrade an existing installation.

</Tab>
<Tab label="uv">

```bash
uv tool install omnigent
```

</Tab>
<Tab label="pip">

```bash
pip install omnigent
```

</Tab>
<Tab label="Homebrew">

```bash
brew install omnigent
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Set up credentials

```bash
omni setup
```

The wizard detects credentials in your environment and prompts for any that are missing. See [Models & Credentials](https://omnigent.ai/docs/build/models#credentials) for the full reference.

## Launch Debby

Try your install with Debby, a built-in multi-AI agent that sends every question to both Claude and GPT and lets them debate.

```bash
omni debby
```

This launches a web UI and prints the server URL and port. Ask something like `What came first, the chicken or the egg?` and watch the models challenge each other. See the [Debby reference](https://omnigent.ai/docs/use/builtin-agents/debby) for more.

## Add the macOS app

Prefer a native experience? The macOS app gives you a full UI, session history, and the ability to connect to a local or remote server — on top of the install you just set up. It's optional; everything above already works from the terminal.

[Download macOS App](https://omnigent.ai/download/mac/v0.1.1)

Open the downloaded app — it will ask for a server URL. The `omni debby` command above prints that URL when it launches the web UI. By default it is `http://localhost:6767`. If port 6767 is already taken, the server uses the next available port, so check the web UI for the actual URL (e.g. `http://localhost:6768`). Paste that into the desktop app to connect.

Now your desktop app is ready to use. Pick **Debby** from the agent picker in the UI (along with the other agents we ship) and ask it anything.

## Next step

Now that Omnigent is installed, [get started with the coding agent](/learn/getting-started/omnigent) to see what it adds on top of Claude Code or Codex.

---

# Getting started with Omnigent

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/learn/getting-started/omnigent
Date: 2026-06-15
Category: Getting Started

Already using Claude Code or Codex? This tutorial shows you what Omnigent adds on top: a web UI with file editing and inline comments, mobile access, session sharing, and the ability to fork or switch agents mid-conversation. None of this is possible with a native coding agent alone.

**Time:** 5 minutes. **Everything runs locally.**

<Callout type="info" title="Prerequisite">
Get Omnigent running in a few minutes. [Install the CLI](/learn/getting-started/omnigent-install), set up your credentials, and launch your first agent. Once it's running you can add the native macOS app for a full UI — it's the last step of this same flow.
</Callout>

## 1. Start your coding agent

```bash
omni claude    # Claude Code
omni codex     # Codex
```

Pick whichever you already use. Either command launches the coding agent in your terminal and opens a web UI at `http://localhost:6767`. Both are connected to the same session and stream output in real time.

## 2. Give it a task

Ask it to do something in your project. For example:

```text
Write a Python function that reads a CSV file and returns the top 5 rows sorted by the second column.
```

Watch it work in the terminal. Then follow along in the web UI or the desktop app. Terminal, browser, and desktop app are three views of the same session: type in one, and the others update in real time.

<Tabs>
<Tab label="Web UI">

Open `http://localhost:6767` in your browser. The web UI shows your conversation on the left and a right panel with four tabs: **Files** (browse and edit files the agent created), **Agents** (sub-agents if any), **Shells** (running terminals), and **Todos**. Everything syncs with the terminal in real time.

</Tab>
<Tab label="Desktop App">

Install the native macOS app from the [install guide](/learn/getting-started/omnigent-install). It attaches to the same local session as the terminal and browser, giving you a polished native UI with the same files, agents, shells, and todos panels.

</Tab>
</Tabs>

## 3. Try native Omnigent features

Now that your agent has produced some output, try these features in the web UI:

### Comment on the agent's work

Click on a specific part of the agent's output and leave an inline comment like "make this more concise" or "use pandas instead". The agent sees exactly what you're referring to and revises it. No need to describe the location in chat.

### Edit files directly

Open any file the agent created in the built-in editor. Make changes yourself with syntax highlighting. The agent can see your edits and continue from there.

### Paste an image

Drag a screenshot, mockup, or diagram into the chat. The agent sees it alongside your text. Try pasting a screenshot of a UI bug or a design spec.

### Fork a session and switch agents

Fork your current session to try a different approach without affecting the original. The fork copies the full conversation history up to that point, so you can experiment freely.

Sessions in Omnigent belong to you, not to a specific agent, so a fork doesn't have to continue with the agent it started with. **Started in Claude Code? Fork the session and continue the fork with Codex (or vice versa).** The new agent picks up the full conversation history and keeps going, so you can compare how each one tackles the same problem from the same starting point.

## 4. Add a policy in plain language

Type this into the chat:

```text
Don't send any PII like emails or credit card numbers to the model. Ask me first if a message contains some.
```

The agent attaches Omnigent's built-in PII policy to the session. From now on, every outgoing model request is scanned, and anything containing PII is held for your approval before it leaves your machine. Try it: paste a log file with a fake email address and watch the policy step in. This is enforcement at the platform layer, something no coding agent can do on its own. Cost budgets, access controls, and more work the same way. See [Contextual Policies](https://omnigent.ai/docs/policies/overview).

## What's next

- [Try Polly](https://omnigent.ai/quickstart/polly) to see multi-agent coding orchestration in action.

---

# Getting started with Unity Catalog

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/learn/getting-started/unity-catalog
Date: 2026-06-03
Category: Getting Started

Unity Catalog is the open-source catalog for **every** asset in your lakehouse — tables, files,
functions, and AI models — with one shared permission model that travels across engines. In the above video, Developer Advocate's [Lisa Cao](https://www.linkedin.com/in/lisancao/) and [Scott Haines](https://www.linkedin.com/in/scotthaines/) cover what the catalog is, and also what it isn't.

## Why catalogs matter

Without a catalog, every engine reinvents discovery and permissions. With one, your tables
become first-class, shareable assets that any compatible engine — Spark, Trino, DuckDB,
Daft — can read with the same identity and the same governance rules.

<Callout type="tip" title="Mental model">
Catalog → Schema → Asset. Three levels, one namespace. Anything you can register fits
into that hierarchy: Delta tables, Iceberg tables, volumes (files), functions, AI models.
</Callout>

## Spin it up locally

<Steps>
  <Step title="Clone and start the server">
    The reference server is a single Java process. Clone the repo and start it — no external
    database required for local dev.

    ```bash
    git clone https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog
    cd unitycatalog
    bin/start-uc-server
    ```
  </Step>
  <Step title="List the seed assets">
    The server runs locally with a sample catalog so you can test the waters before heading out on your own.

    ```bash
    bin/uc table list --catalog unity --schema default
    ```
  </Step>
  <Step title="Create your first table">
    Register a Delta table that lives on local disk — the same API works against S3 / GCS / ADLS.

    ```bash
    bin/uc table create \
      --full_name unity.default.my_first_table \
      --columns "id INT, name STRING" \
      --storage_location file:///tmp/my_first_table
    ```
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Use it from your favorite LLM

Want to explore Unity Catalog further with Claude or ChatGPT? Copy this prompt:

<PromptBlock label="Prompt for your LLM">
You are helping me learn Unity Catalog. Given the following primitives:

- Catalogs, Schemas, Tables (Delta + Iceberg), Volumes, Functions, Models
- Grants on each level
- A REST API + CLI

Walk me through:
1. The minimal set of `uc` CLI commands to register a Delta table and grant SELECT
   to another user.
2. How those commands map to the underlying REST endpoints.
3. How an engine like Spark uses the catalog to resolve a table reference at
   query time.
</PromptBlock>

## Go Further, Jump into the Unity Catalog Playground
Head over to [unitycatalog-playground](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/unitycatalog-playground) in the open-lakehouse github organization. This project provides you with a simple way of getting started with Unity Catalog on your own terms. 


## What's next

- **Deep dive:** how the three-level namespace maps to storage.
- **Tutorial:** federate Unity Catalog with an Iceberg REST catalog.
- **Concepts:** lineage and audit trails via OpenLineage.

# Getting started with MLflow

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/learn/getting-started/mlflow
Date: 2026-06-03
Category: Getting Started

MLflow is the open standard for tracking experiments, packaging models, and shipping ML
and GenAI applications without locking you to a single vendor or framework.

## Set up the MLflow server

<Callout type="tip" title="MLflow Assistant">
Need help with this setup? Try <a href="https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/genai/getting-started/try-assistant" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">MLflow Assistant</a> — a powerful AI assistant that understands your codebase and can set up MLflow for you.
</Callout>

MLflow is open source, and you can set up the MLflow server using either `pip`, `uv`, or `docker`.
Before you can leverage MLflow for your LLM application and AI agent development, you must first
start the MLflow server.

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="Local (uv)">
    Install the Python package manager [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/)
    (which also installs the [`uvx` command](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/guides/tools/) for invoking
    Python tools without installing them).

    Then start an MLflow server locally:

    ```shell
    uvx mlflow server
    ```

    <Callout type="info">
      See <a href="https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/self-hosting/security/secure-installs" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">Secure Installs</a> to learn how to pin dependencies to known-good versions using hash checking and upload-time filtering.
    </Callout>
  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Local (pip)">
    **Python environment:** Python 3.10+

    Install the `mlflow` Python package via `pip` and start an MLflow server locally:

    ```shell
    pip install --upgrade mlflow
    mlflow server
    ```

    <Callout type="info">
      See <a href="https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/self-hosting/security/secure-installs" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">Secure Installs</a> to learn how to pin dependencies to known-good versions using hash checking and upload-time filtering.
    </Callout>
  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Local (docker)">
    MLflow provides a Docker Compose file to start a local MLflow server with a PostgreSQL database
    and a MinIO server.

    ```shell
    git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow.git
    cd mlflow
    git sparse-checkout set docker-compose
    cd docker-compose
    cp .env.dev.example .env
    docker compose up -d
    ```

    Refer to the [docker-compose README](https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/tree/master/docker-compose/README.md)
    for more details (e.g., overriding the default environment variables).
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

### Access the UI

Any of the options above will start the server on port 5000 on your local machine, and you can
access the MLflow web UI at [http://localhost:5000](http://localhost:5000).

If you are looking for more guidance about self-hosting the MLflow server, see the
[Self-Hosting Guide](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/self-hosting) for more details.

<Callout type="info">
If you are using MLflow on Databricks, visit the <a href="https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/getting-started/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">Databricks MLflow getting-started guide</a> for environment setup instructions specific to Databricks.
</Callout>

## Next step

Now that you have started the MLflow server, let's start tracing your LLM application or AI agent.
Follow [this quickstart](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/genai/tracing/quickstart) to send your
LLM application or AI agent traces to the MLflow server.

# Getting started with Delta Lake

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/learn/getting-started/delta-lake
Date: 2026-06-03
Category: Getting Started

This guide helps you quickly explore the [main features](https://docs.delta.io/latest/delta-intro.html)
of Delta Lake. It provides code snippets that show how to read from and write to Delta tables from
interactive, batch, and streaming queries. It also demonstrates table updates and time travel.

## Set up Apache Spark with Delta Lake

Follow these instructions to set up Delta Lake with Spark. You can run the steps in this guide on
your local machine in the following two ways:

1. **Run interactively:** Start the Spark shell (Scala or Python) with Delta Lake and run the code
   snippets interactively in the shell.
2. **Run as a project:** Set up a Maven or SBT project (Scala or Java) with Delta Lake, copy the
   code snippets into a source file, and run the project. Alternatively, you can use the
   [examples provided in the GitHub repository](https://github.com/delta-io/delta/tree/master/examples).

### Set up an interactive shell

To use Delta Lake interactively within the Spark Scala or Python shell, you need a local
installation of Apache Spark. Depending on whether you want to use Python or Scala, you can set up
either PySpark or the Spark shell, respectively. For all the instructions below, make sure you
install the correct version of Spark or PySpark that is compatible with Delta Lake 2.1.0. See the
release compatibility matrix for details.

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="PySpark shell">
    1. Install the PySpark version that is compatible with the Delta Lake version:

    ```shell
    pip install pyspark==4.1.0
    ```

    2. Run PySpark with the Delta Lake package and additional configurations:

    ```shell
    pyspark --packages io.delta:delta-spark_4.1_2.13:4.2.0 \
      --conf "spark.sql.extensions=io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension" \
      --conf "spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog=org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog"
    ```
  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Spark Scala shell">
    Download the compatible version of Apache Spark by following instructions from
    [Downloading Spark](https://spark.apache.org/downloads.html), either using `pip` or by
    downloading and extracting the archive and running `spark-shell` in the extracted directory.

    ```shell
    bin/spark-shell --packages io.delta:delta-spark_4.1_2.13:4.2.0 \
      --conf "spark.sql.extensions=io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension" \
      --conf "spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog=org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog"
    ```
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## Set up a project

If you want to build a project using Delta Lake binaries from Maven Central Repository, you can use
the following Maven coordinates.

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="Maven">
    You include Delta Lake in your Maven project by adding it as a dependency in your POM file.
    Delta Lake is compiled with Scala 2.12.

    ```xml
    <dependency>
      <groupId>io.delta</groupId>
      <artifactId>delta-spark_4.1_2.13</artifactId>
      <version>4.2.0</version>
    </dependency>
    ```
  </Tab>
  <Tab label="SBT">
    You include Delta Lake in your SBT project by adding the following line to your `build.sbt` file:

    ```scala
    libraryDependencies += "io.delta" %% "delta-spark" % "4.2.0"
    ```
  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Python">
    To set up a Python project (for example, for unit testing), you can install Delta Lake using
    `pip install delta-spark` and then configure the `SparkSession` with the
    `configure_spark_with_delta_pip()` utility function in Delta Lake:

    ```python
    from delta import *

    builder = pyspark.sql.SparkSession.builder.appName("MyApp") \
        .config("spark.sql.extensions", "io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension") \
        .config("spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog", "org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog")

    spark = configure_spark_with_delta_pip(builder).getOrCreate()
    ```
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## Create a table

To create a Delta table, write a DataFrame out in the `delta` format. You can use existing Spark
SQL code and change the format from `parquet`, `csv`, `json`, and so on, to `delta`.

```python
data = spark.range(0, 5)
data.write.format("delta").save("/tmp/delta-table")
```

These operations create a new Delta table using the schema that was _inferred_ from your DataFrame.
For the full set of options available when you create a new Delta table, see the
[Create a table](https://docs.delta.io/delta-batch/#create-a-table) and
[Write to a table](https://docs.delta.io/delta-batch/#write-to-table)
documentation articles.

<Callout type="info">
This guide uses local paths for Delta table locations. For configuring cloud storage for
Delta tables, see the <a href="https://docs.delta.io/latest/delta-storage.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">Storage configuration</a> documentation article.
</Callout>

## Read data

You read data in your Delta table by specifying the path to the files `"/tmp/delta-table"`:

```python
df = spark.read.format("delta").load("/tmp/delta-table")
df.show()
```

## Update table data

Delta Lake supports several operations to modify tables using standard DataFrame APIs. This example
runs a batch job to overwrite the data in the table:

### Overwrite

```python
data = spark.range(5, 10)
data.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").save("/tmp/delta-table")
```

If you read this table again, you should see only the values 5–9 you have added because you
overwrote the previous data.

### Conditional update without overwrite

Delta Lake provides programmatic APIs to conditionally update, delete, and merge (upsert) data into
tables. Here are a few examples:

```python
from delta.tables import *
from pyspark.sql.functions import *

deltaTable = DeltaTable.forPath(spark, "/tmp/delta-table")

# Update every even value by adding 100 to it
deltaTable.update(
  condition = expr("id % 2 == 0"),
  set = { "id": expr("id + 100") })

# Delete every even value
deltaTable.delete(condition = expr("id % 2 == 0"))

# Upsert (merge) new data
newData = spark.range(0, 20)

deltaTable.alias("oldData") \
  .merge(
    newData.alias("newData"),
    "oldData.id = newData.id") \
  .whenMatchedUpdate(set = { "id": col("newData.id") }) \
  .whenNotMatchedInsert(values = { "id": col("newData.id") }) \
  .execute()

deltaTable.toDF().show()
```

You should see that some of the existing rows have been updated and new rows have been inserted.

For more information on these operations, see the
[Table deletes, updates, and merges](https://docs.delta.io/latest/delta-update.html) documentation
article.

## Read older versions of data using time travel

You can query previous snapshots of your Delta table by using time travel. If you want to access
the data that you overwrote, you can query a snapshot of the table before you overwrote the first
set of data using the `versionAsOf` option.

```python
df = spark.read.format("delta") \
  .option("versionAsOf", 0) \
  .load("/tmp/delta-table")

df.show()
```

You should see the first set of data, from before you overwrote it. Time travel takes advantage of
the power of the Delta Lake transaction log to access data that is no longer in the table. Removing
the version 0 option (or specifying version 1) would let you see the newer data again. For more
information, see the
[Query an older snapshot of a table (time travel)](https://docs.delta.io/delta-batch/#query-an-older-snapshot-of-a-table-time-travel)
documentation article.

## Write a stream of data to a table

You can also write to a Delta table using Structured Streaming. The Delta Lake transaction log
guarantees exactly-once processing, even when there are other streams or batch queries running
concurrently against the table. By default, streams run in append mode, which adds new records to
the table:

```python
streamingDf = spark.readStream.format("rate").load()

stream = streamingDf \
  .selectExpr("value as id") \
  .writeStream.format("delta") \
  .option("checkpointLocation", "/tmp/checkpoint") \
  .start("/tmp/delta-table")
```

While the stream is running, you can read the table using the earlier commands.

<Callout type="tip">
If you're running this in a shell, you may see the streaming task progress, which makes it hard to
type commands in that shell. It may be useful to start another shell in a new terminal for querying
the table.
</Callout>

You can stop the stream by running `stream.stop()` in the same terminal that started the stream.

For more information about Delta Lake integration with Structured Streaming, see the
[Table streaming reads and writes](https://docs.delta.io/latest/delta-streaming.html) documentation
article.

## Read a stream of changes from a table

While the stream is writing to the Delta table, you can also read from that table as a streaming
source. For example, you can start another streaming query that prints all the changes made to the
Delta table. You can specify which version Structured Streaming should start from by providing the
`startingVersion` or `startingTimestamp` option to get changes from that point onwards. See the
[Structured Streaming](https://docs.delta.io/latest/delta-streaming.html#-specify-initial-position)
documentation article for details.

```python
stream2 = spark.readStream.format("delta") \
  .load("/tmp/delta-table") \
  .writeStream.format("console") \
  .start()
```

## Next steps

Here are some further resources for learning more about Delta Lake:

- [Delta FAQ](https://docs.delta.io/latest/delta-faq.html) for answers to common questions about Delta Lake
- [Delta Videos](https://lovable.dev/projects/b4d84797-7392-4fb5-9d57-04c5559c97cd) for videos about Delta Lake

---

# Getting started with Apache Spark

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/learn/getting-started/apache-spark
Date: 2026-06-03
Category: Getting Started

This tutorial provides a quick introduction to using Spark. We will first introduce the API through Spark's interactive shell (in Python or Scala), then show how to write applications in Java, Scala, and Python.

To follow along with this guide, first, download a packaged release of Spark from the [Spark website](https://spark.apache.org/downloads.html). Since we won't be using HDFS, you can download a package for any version of Hadoop.

<Callout type="info">
Before Spark 2.0, the main programming interface of Spark was the Resilient Distributed Dataset (RDD). After Spark 2.0, RDDs are replaced by Dataset, which is strongly-typed like an RDD, but with richer optimizations under the hood. The RDD interface is still supported, and you can get a more detailed reference at the [RDD programming guide](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/rdd-programming-guide.html). However, we highly recommend you to switch to use Dataset, which has better performance than RDD. See the [SQL programming guide](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/sql-programming-guide.html) to get more information about Dataset.
</Callout>

## Interactive Analysis with the Spark Shell

### Basics

Spark's shell provides a simple way to learn the API, as well as a powerful tool to analyze data interactively. It is available in either Scala (which runs on the Java VM and is thus a good way to use existing Java libraries) or Python. Start it by running the following in the Spark directory:

<Tabs>
<Tab label="Python">

```bash
./bin/pyspark
```

Or if PySpark is installed with pip in your current environment:

```bash
pyspark
```

Spark's primary abstraction is a distributed collection of items called a Dataset. Datasets can be created from Hadoop InputFormats (such as HDFS files) or by transforming other Datasets. Due to Python's dynamic nature, we don't need the Dataset to be strongly-typed in Python. As a result, all Datasets in Python are Dataset[Row], and we call it `DataFrame` to be consistent with the data frame concept in Pandas and R. Let's make a new DataFrame from the text of the README file in the Spark source directory:

```python
>>> textFile = spark.read.text("README.md")
```

You can get values from DataFrame directly, by calling some actions, or transform the DataFrame to get a new one. For more details, please read the [API doc](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/api/python/index.html#pyspark.sql.DataFrame).

```python
>>> textFile.count()  # Number of rows in this DataFrame
126

>>> textFile.first()  # First row in this DataFrame
Row(value=u'# Apache Spark')
```

Now let's transform this DataFrame to a new one. We call `filter` to return a new DataFrame with a subset of the lines in the file.

```python
>>> linesWithSpark = textFile.filter(textFile.value.contains("Spark"))
```

We can chain together transformations and actions:

```python
>>> textFile.filter(textFile.value.contains("Spark")).count()  # How many lines contain "Spark"?
15
```

</Tab>
<Tab label="Scala">

```bash
./bin/spark-shell
```

Spark's primary abstraction is a distributed collection of items called a Dataset. Datasets can be created from Hadoop InputFormats (such as HDFS files) or by transforming other Datasets. Let's make a new Dataset from the text of the README file in the Spark source directory:

```scala
scala> val textFile = spark.read.textFile("README.md")
textFile: org.apache.spark.sql.Dataset[String] = [value: string]
```

You can get values from Dataset directly, by calling some actions, or transform the Dataset to get a new one. For more details, please read the [API doc](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/api/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/Dataset.html).

```scala
scala> textFile.count() // Number of items in this Dataset
res0: Long = 126 // May be different from yours as README.md will change over time, similar to other outputs

scala> textFile.first() // First item in this Dataset
res1: String = # Apache Spark
```

Now let's transform this Dataset into a new one. We call `filter` to return a new Dataset with a subset of the items in the file.

```scala
scala> val linesWithSpark = textFile.filter(line => line.contains("Spark"))
linesWithSpark: org.apache.spark.sql.Dataset[String] = [value: string]
```

We can chain together transformations and actions:

```scala
scala> textFile.filter(line => line.contains("Spark")).count() // How many lines contain "Spark"?
res3: Long = 15
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

### More on Dataset Operations

Dataset actions and transformations can be used for more complex computations. Let's say we want to find the line with the most words:

<Tabs>
<Tab label="Python">

```python
>>> from pyspark.sql import functions as sf
>>> textFile.select(sf.size(sf.split(textFile.value, "\s+")).name("numWords")).agg(sf.max(sf.col("numWords"))).collect()
[Row(max(numWords)=15)]
```

This first maps a line to an integer value and aliases it as "numWords", creating a new DataFrame. `agg` is called on that DataFrame to find the largest word count. The arguments to `select` and `agg` are both [Column](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/api/python/index.html#pyspark.sql.Column), we can use `df.colName` to get a column from a DataFrame. We can also import pyspark.sql.functions, which provides a lot of convenient functions to build a new Column from an old one.

One common data flow pattern is MapReduce, as popularized by Hadoop. Spark can implement MapReduce flows easily:

```python
>>> wordCounts = textFile.select(sf.explode(sf.split(textFile.value, "\s+")).alias("word")).groupBy("word").count()
```

Here, we use the `explode` function in `select`, to transform a Dataset of lines to a Dataset of words, and then combine `groupBy` and `count` to compute the per-word counts in the file as a DataFrame of 2 columns: "word" and "count". To collect the word counts in our shell, we can call `collect`:

```python
>>> wordCounts.collect()
[Row(word=u'online', count=1), Row(word=u'graphs', count=1), ...]
```

</Tab>
<Tab label="Scala">

```scala
scala> textFile.map(line => line.split(" ").size).reduce((a, b) => if (a > b) a else b)
res4: Int = 15
```

This first maps a line to an integer value, creating a new Dataset. `reduce` is called on that Dataset to find the largest word count. The arguments to `map` and `reduce` are Scala function literals (closures), and can use any language feature or Scala/Java library. For example, we can easily call functions declared elsewhere. We'll use `Math.max()` function to make this code easier to understand:

```scala
scala> import java.lang.Math
import java.lang.Math

scala> textFile.map(line => line.split(" ").size).reduce((a, b) => Math.max(a, b))
res5: Int = 15
```

One common data flow pattern is MapReduce, as popularized by Hadoop. Spark can implement MapReduce flows easily:

```scala
scala> val wordCounts = textFile.flatMap(line => line.split(" ")).groupByKey(identity).count()
wordCounts: org.apache.spark.sql.Dataset[(String, Long)] = [value: string, count(1): bigint]
```

Here, we call `flatMap` to transform a Dataset of lines to a Dataset of words, and then combine `groupByKey` and `count` to compute the per-word counts in the file as a Dataset of (String, Long) pairs. To collect the word counts in our shell, we can call `collect`:

```scala
scala> wordCounts.collect()
res6: Array[(String, Int)] = Array((means,1), (under,2), (this,3), (Because,1), (Python,2), (agree,1), (cluster.,1), ...)
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

### Caching

Spark also supports pulling data sets into a cluster-wide in-memory cache. This is very useful when data is accessed repeatedly, such as when querying a small "hot" dataset or when running an iterative algorithm like PageRank. As a simple example, let's mark our `linesWithSpark` dataset to be cached:

<Tabs>
<Tab label="Python">

```python
>>> linesWithSpark.cache()

>>> linesWithSpark.count()
15

>>> linesWithSpark.count()
15
```

It may seem silly to use Spark to explore and cache a 100-line text file. The interesting part is that these same functions can be used on very large data sets, even when they are striped across tens or hundreds of nodes. You can also do this interactively by connecting `bin/pyspark` to a cluster, as described in the [RDD programming guide](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/rdd-programming-guide.html#using-the-shell).

</Tab>
<Tab label="Scala">

```scala
scala> linesWithSpark.cache()
res7: linesWithSpark.type = [value: string]

scala> linesWithSpark.count()
res8: Long = 15

scala> linesWithSpark.count()
res9: Long = 15
```

It may seem silly to use Spark to explore and cache a 100-line text file. The interesting part is that these same functions can be used on very large data sets, even when they are striped across tens or hundreds of nodes. You can also do this interactively by connecting `bin/spark-shell` to a cluster, as described in the [RDD programming guide](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/rdd-programming-guide.html#using-the-shell).

</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Self-Contained Applications

Suppose we wish to write a self-contained application using the Spark API. We will walk through a simple application in Scala (with sbt), Java (with Maven), and Python (pip).

<Tabs>
<Tab label="Python">

Now we will show how to write an application using the Python API (PySpark).

If you are building a packaged PySpark application or library you can add it to your setup.py file as:

```python
    install_requires=[
        'pyspark==4.1.2'
    ]
```

As an example, we'll create a simple Spark application, `SimpleApp.py`:

```python
"""SimpleApp.py"""
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

logFile = "YOUR_SPARK_HOME/README.md"  # Should be some file on your system
spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("SimpleApp").getOrCreate()
logData = spark.read.text(logFile).cache()

numAs = logData.filter(logData.value.contains('a')).count()
numBs = logData.filter(logData.value.contains('b')).count()

print("Lines with a: %i, lines with b: %i" % (numAs, numBs))

spark.stop()
```

This program just counts the number of lines containing 'a' and the number containing 'b' in a text file. Note that you'll need to replace YOUR_SPARK_HOME with the location where Spark is installed. As with the Scala and Java examples, we use a SparkSession to create Datasets. For applications that use custom classes or third-party libraries, we can also add code dependencies to `spark-submit` through its `--py-files` argument by packaging them into a .zip file (see `spark-submit --help` for details). `SimpleApp` is simple enough that we do not need to specify any code dependencies.

We can run this application using the `bin/spark-submit` script:

```bash
# Use spark-submit to run your application
$ YOUR_SPARK_HOME/bin/spark-submit \
  --master "local[4]" \
  SimpleApp.py
...
Lines with a: 46, Lines with b: 23
```

If you have PySpark pip installed into your environment (e.g., `pip install pyspark`), you can run your application with the regular Python interpreter or use the provided 'spark-submit' as you prefer.

```bash
# Use the Python interpreter to run your application
$ python SimpleApp.py
...
Lines with a: 46, Lines with b: 23
```

</Tab>
<Tab label="Scala">

We'll create a very simple Spark application in Scala–so simple, in fact, that it's named `SimpleApp.scala`:

```scala
/* SimpleApp.scala */
import org.apache.spark.sql.SparkSession

object SimpleApp {
  def main(args: Array[String]): Unit = {
    val logFile = "YOUR_SPARK_HOME/README.md" // Should be some file on your system
    val spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("Simple Application").getOrCreate()
    val logData = spark.read.textFile(logFile).cache()
    val numAs = logData.filter(line => line.contains("a")).count()
    val numBs = logData.filter(line => line.contains("b")).count()
    println(s"Lines with a: $numAs, Lines with b: $numBs")
    spark.stop()
  }
}
```

Note that applications should define a `main()` method instead of extending `scala.App`. Subclasses of `scala.App` may not work correctly.

This program just counts the number of lines containing 'a' and the number containing 'b' in the Spark README. Note that you'll need to replace YOUR_SPARK_HOME with the location where Spark is installed. Unlike the earlier examples with the Spark shell, which initializes its own SparkSession, we initialize a SparkSession as part of the program.

We call `SparkSession.builder` to construct a `SparkSession`, then set the application name, and finally call `getOrCreate` to get the `SparkSession` instance.

Our application depends on the Spark API, so we'll also include an sbt configuration file, `build.sbt`, which explains that Spark is a dependency. This file also adds a repository that Spark depends on:

```scala
name := "Simple Project"

version := "1.0"

scalaVersion := "2.13.17"

libraryDependencies += "org.apache.spark" %% "spark-sql" % "4.1.2"
```

For sbt to work correctly, we'll need to layout `SimpleApp.scala` and `build.sbt` according to the typical directory structure. Once that is in place, we can create a JAR package containing the application's code, then use the `spark-submit` script to run our program.

```bash
# Your directory layout should look like this
$ find .
.
./build.sbt
./src
./src/main
./src/main/scala
./src/main/scala/SimpleApp.scala

# Package a jar containing your application
$ sbt package
...
[info] Packaging {..}/{..}/target/scala-2.13/simple-project_2.13-1.0.jar

# Use spark-submit to run your application
$ YOUR_SPARK_HOME/bin/spark-submit \
  --class "SimpleApp" \
  --master "local[4]" \
  target/scala-2.13/simple-project_2.13-1.0.jar
...
Lines with a: 46, Lines with b: 23
```

</Tab>
<Tab label="Java">

This example will use Maven to compile an application JAR, but any similar build system will work.

We'll create a very simple Spark application, `SimpleApp.java`:

```java
/* SimpleApp.java */
import org.apache.spark.sql.SparkSession;
import org.apache.spark.sql.Dataset;

public class SimpleApp {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    String logFile = "YOUR_SPARK_HOME/README.md"; // Should be some file on your system
    SparkSession spark = SparkSession.builder().appName("Simple Application").getOrCreate();
    Dataset<String> logData = spark.read().textFile(logFile).cache();

    long numAs = logData.filter(s -> s.contains("a")).count();
    long numBs = logData.filter(s -> s.contains("b")).count();

    System.out.println("Lines with a: " + numAs + ", lines with b: " + numBs);

    spark.stop();
  }
}
```

This program just counts the number of lines containing 'a' and the number containing 'b' in the Spark README. Note that you'll need to replace YOUR_SPARK_HOME with the location where Spark is installed. Unlike the earlier examples with the Spark shell, which initializes its own SparkSession, we initialize a SparkSession as part of the program.

To build the program, we also write a Maven `pom.xml` file that lists Spark as a dependency. Note that Spark artifacts are tagged with a Scala version.

```xml
<project>
  <groupId>edu.berkeley</groupId>
  <artifactId>simple-project</artifactId>
  <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
  <name>Simple Project</name>
  <packaging>jar</packaging>
  <version>1.0</version>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.apache.spark</groupId>
      <artifactId>spark-sql_2.13</artifactId>
      <version>4.1.2</version>
      <scope>provided</scope>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</project>
```

We lay out these files according to the canonical Maven directory structure:

```bash
$ find .
./pom.xml
./src
./src/main
./src/main/java
./src/main/java/SimpleApp.java
```

Now, we can package the application using Maven and execute it with `./bin/spark-submit`.

```bash
# Package a JAR containing your application
$ mvn package
...
[INFO] Building jar: {..}/{..}/target/simple-project-1.0.jar

# Use spark-submit to run your application
$ YOUR_SPARK_HOME/bin/spark-submit \
  --class "SimpleApp" \
  --master "local[4]" \
  target/simple-project-1.0.jar
...
Lines with a: 46, Lines with b: 23
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

Other dependency management tools such as Conda and pip can be also used for custom classes or third-party libraries. See also [Python Package Management](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/api/python/tutorial/python_packaging.html).

## Where to Go from Here

Congratulations on running your first Spark application!

- For an in-depth overview of the API, start with the [RDD programming guide](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/rdd-programming-guide.html) and the [SQL programming guide](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/sql-programming-guide.html), or see "Programming Guides" menu for other components.
- For running applications on a cluster, head to the [deployment overview](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/cluster-overview.html).
- Finally, Spark includes several samples in the `examples` directory ([Python](https://github.com/apache/spark/tree/master/examples/src/main/python), [Scala](https://github.com/apache/spark/tree/master/examples/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/examples), [Java](https://github.com/apache/spark/tree/master/examples/src/main/java/org/apache/spark/examples), [R](https://github.com/apache/spark/tree/master/examples/src/main/r)). You can run them as follows:

```bash
# For Python examples, use spark-submit directly:
./bin/spark-submit examples/src/main/python/pi.py

# For Scala and Java, use run-example:
./bin/run-example SparkPi
```

# Open Source Data Engineering

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/open-source-data-engineering

Open source data engineering is the practice of building data pipelines, transformation jobs, and analytical tables on software that is freely licensed, community-governed, and portable across clouds. Instead of depending on a single vendor's proprietary engine or storage format, an open source data engineering stack stores data in open file and table formats on object storage, reads it with interchangeable compute engines, and governs access through an open catalog. The reference stack is Apache Spark and Apache Flink for compute; Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, and Apache Hudi for table storage; Unity Catalog and Apache Polaris for governance; Apache Airflow for orchestration; and MLflow for the machine learning lifecycle. Because every layer is open, the same data can be read by Spark, Trino, DuckDB, Flink, and future engines without copying or migration.

## The open source data engineering stack

| Layer | What it does | Common projects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Table formats | ACID tables on object storage | Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi |
| Compute engines | Batch, SQL, and streaming transforms | Apache Spark, Apache Flink, Trino, DuckDB, Apache DataFusion |
| Catalogs & governance | Namespaces, access control, lineage | Unity Catalog, Apache Polaris, Lakekeeper, OpenLineage |
| Orchestration | Scheduling and dependency management | Apache Airflow, Temporal |
| ML & AI lifecycle | Tracking, registry, evaluation, agents | MLflow |

## Projects in the stack

- **Apache Spark** - The most widely deployed open-source engine for large-scale batch and streaming data engineering. (https://spark.apache.org)
- **Delta Lake** - An open table format bringing ACID transactions, time travel, and schema enforcement to Parquet on object storage. (https://delta.io)
- **Apache Iceberg** - An open table format with wide multi-engine support and a strict separation of storage and catalog. (https://iceberg.apache.org)
- **Apache Hudi** - An open table format designed around upserts and incremental streaming ingestion. (https://hudi.apache.org)
- **Unity Catalog** - The open catalog for data and AI, with a three-level namespace, fine-grained access control, and lineage. (https://unitycatalog.io)
- **Apache Polaris** - An open, Iceberg-native catalog implementing the Iceberg REST specification. (https://polaris.apache.org)
- **Apache Flink** - A stream-processing engine for stateful, exactly-once event pipelines. (https://flink.apache.org)
- **Apache Airflow** - The reference orchestrator for scheduling and dependency management across data pipelines. (https://airflow.apache.org)
- **MLflow** - The open platform for the machine learning and GenAI lifecycle: tracking, registry, evaluation, and agents. (https://mlflow.org)

## Why teams choose open source data engineering

- **No lock-in on storage.** Tables live in open formats on object storage you control, so any compliant engine can read them.
- **Decoupled compute and storage.** You pay object-store prices for data at rest and run compute only when a job runs.
- **Interchangeable engines.** The same table is readable by Apache Spark, Trino, DuckDB, Flink, and engines that do not exist yet.
- **Neutral governance.** Core projects are hosted by the Linux Foundation or the Apache Software Foundation under permissive licenses.
- **One substrate for BI and AI.** The same tables feed SQL dashboards and model training without a copy into a separate warehouse.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is open source data engineering?

Open source data engineering is the practice of building data pipelines, transformation jobs, and analytical tables on software that is freely licensed, community-governed, and portable across clouds. It stores data in open table formats such as Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, and Apache Hudi on object storage, reads it with interchangeable engines such as Apache Spark, Trino, and DuckDB, and governs access through an open catalog like Unity Catalog or Apache Polaris.

### What is the best open source data engineering stack?

The most common open source data engineering stack combines four layers. For storage, Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, or Apache Hudi give ACID tables on S3, ADLS, or GCS. For compute, Apache Spark handles batch and ETL while Apache Flink handles streaming; Trino and DuckDB serve SQL. For governance, Unity Catalog or Apache Polaris provide namespaces, access control, and lineage. For orchestration, Apache Airflow schedules and coordinates the pipeline. MLflow covers the ML and GenAI lifecycle. Every layer is governed by the Linux Foundation or the Apache Software Foundation.

### What are the most popular open source data engineering tools?

The most widely used open source data engineering tools are Apache Spark and Apache Flink for compute; Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, and Apache Hudi for table storage; Unity Catalog and Apache Polaris for catalogs and governance; Apache Airflow for orchestration; dbt for SQL transformation; and MLflow for the ML lifecycle. This site documents each layer and how they interoperate.

### Is Apache Spark open source?

Yes. Apache Spark is open source under the Apache 2.0 license and is governed by the Apache Software Foundation. It was created by Matei Zaharia at UC Berkeley in 2009, open-sourced in 2010, and donated to the ASF in 2013. Spark is the most widely used engine for open source data engineering and the primary write engine for Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg tables.

### Delta Lake vs Apache Iceberg: which should I pick?

Both are mature open table formats. Choose Delta Lake if your stack is Spark-centric, you need first-class streaming writes, or you want Unity Catalog catalog-managed tables. Choose Apache Iceberg for the widest engine support and a strict separation of storage and catalog. Delta UniForm and Apache X-Table now publish cross-format metadata, so the choice is increasingly reversible.

### How do I build an open source data platform from scratch?

Start with object storage on S3, ADLS, or GCS. Add an open table format such as Delta Lake or Apache Iceberg for ACID tables. Choose a compute engine: Apache Spark for batch, Apache Flink for streaming. Put an open catalog such as Unity Catalog or Apache Polaris in front for governance and lineage. Schedule work with Apache Airflow. Track models and agents with MLflow. Each layer is independently replaceable because the formats and protocols are open.

### Is open source data engineering more expensive than a proprietary warehouse?

Usually it is cheaper in licensing and comparable in total cost. Storage and compute are decoupled, so you pay object-store prices for data at rest and only run compute when a job runs. There is no per-seat or per-terabyte license for the table format, catalog, or engine, and no egress penalty for reading your own Parquet files with a different engine. The trade-off is operating the stack yourself unless you use a managed distribution.

### What is the Open Lakehouse and how does it relate to open source data engineering?

The Open Lakehouse is the reference architecture for open source data engineering. It combines open table formats, open catalogs, open compute engines, and open ML tooling so that data written by one engine can be read by any other, on storage the organization controls. The term was popularized by the 2020 paper "Lakehouse: A New Generation of Open Platforms" and has become a default design for data and AI platforms.

---

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/agentic-lakehouse

# The Agentic Lakehouse

> An open lakehouse that AI agents can find, query and change, safely

An agentic lakehouse is an open data lakehouse built so that AI agents can find, query and change data safely. It combines open tables such as Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake on object storage; a catalog that tells agents what data exists and what they may touch; tools that expose lakehouse actions to agents through the Model Context Protocol (MCP); declarative pipelines that agents write and the platform validates before anything runs; policies that allow a tool call, deny it, or ask a person first; and tracing and lineage that record what every agent did. Because the data, the governance and the agent harness are open source, agents built on any model or framework work against the same governed tables.

## How the pieces fit, from agent to table

1. **A control plane decides what agents may do.** Omnigent runs each agent and checks every tool call, model request and file operation against policies set per session, per agent and server-wide; any DENY blocks the action and any ASK waits for a person. MLflow traces and evaluates each step and can front model providers through its AI Gateway.
2. **Each session runs in a sandbox.** The agent's code runs in a container or microVM, on a laptop or a Kubernetes cluster. Provider credentials stay outside the sandbox; the agent holds only its own identity.
3. **The agent gets a Spark client, not a database password.** Inside the sandbox it connects over Spark Connect. For fast iteration that can be a local Spark with Project Feather's shuffle-free single-task execution, working on a subset of the data; for production runs it is a remote endpoint pinned to the agent's or tenant's identity.
4. **Spark runs the work in the mode it needs.** Batch and SQL, Structured Streaming, Real-Time Mode for millisecond paths, and Spark Declarative Pipelines, which the platform dry-runs before anything executes.
5. **The catalog and the tables hold the line.** Unity Catalog OSS (or another Iceberg REST catalog) authorizes every request and vends storage credentials scoped to what the agent may touch; Apache Iceberg snapshots make every write inspectable and reversible.

## Why a lakehouse is a good home for agents

An agent can only act on what it can discover and only be trusted with what the platform can check. An open lakehouse provides both through interfaces that already exist for engines.

- **The catalog is a machine-readable map.** Namespaces, tables, schemas and permissions are available over an API (the Iceberg REST catalog or the Unity Catalog API), so an agent asks the catalog what exists instead of guessing from file paths.
- **Open formats work with any engine.** An agent can read the same Iceberg table with Spark, DuckDB or PyIceberg, so its tools do not depend on one vendor's engine.
- **Snapshots make changes reversible.** Every commit to an Iceberg or Delta table is a snapshot. A bad write by an agent can be inspected with time travel and rolled back.
- **Declarative pipelines are checkable output.** When an agent writes a Spark Declarative Pipelines spec instead of an imperative script, the platform can resolve every dataset and dependency with a dry run before any data is written.
- **Lineage and traces record what happened.** OpenLineage events show which tables an agent's job read and wrote; MLflow traces show which tools the agent called, with their inputs and outputs.

## The layers of an agentic lakehouse

Each layer is open source and replaceable, because the interface between layers is an open standard.

| Layer | What it does for agents | Open source projects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tables and storage | Durable, versioned data any engine can read | Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, Apache Parquet on S3-compatible storage |
| Catalog and permissions | Tells agents what exists and what they may read or write; vends scoped storage credentials | Unity Catalog OSS, Apache Polaris, Lakekeeper |
| Engines | Run the queries and pipelines agents request | Apache Spark (over Spark Connect), DuckDB, Trino |
| Pipelines | Give agents a declarative output the platform can validate | Spark Declarative Pipelines |
| Agent tools | Named actions with named arguments: read a table, dry-run a pipeline, run one SQL statement | Model Context Protocol servers, lakehouse-agent-kit skills |
| Agent harness and policy | Runs the agent and decides, per tool call, whether to allow, deny or ask a person | Omnigent |
| Models | The language model behind the agent, local or hosted | Open-weight models served by Ollama or vLLM; MLflow AI Gateway in front of providers |
| Observability and evaluation | Traces of every agent step, evaluation against trusted results, lineage of every write | MLflow tracing and evaluation, OpenLineage |
| Orchestration | Schedules approved pipelines so agents do not race scheduled runs | Apache Airflow |

## Guardrails that make it safe

Instructions are text a model weighs against everything else in its context. A guardrail is a fact the platform enforces. An agentic lakehouse relies on the second kind.

- **A sandbox namespace.** The agent reads production tables but writes only to its own namespace in the catalog, for example iceberg.sandbox_sdp in the lakehouse masterclass.
- **Dry run before run.** A pipeline that does not pass spark-pipelines dry-run does not run.
- **Policies on every tool call.** The harness evaluates each tool call and each tool result against policies that return ALLOW, DENY or ASK. A policy that raises an error counts as DENY, so the system fails closed.
- **No shell tool.** Agents get specific tools such as write_pipeline_file(path, content), which a policy can inspect exactly, instead of a shell whose effect a policy can only guess.
- **Identity-pinned access.** In production, each agent or tenant reaches Spark through its own authenticated Spark Connect endpoint, and the catalog vends storage credentials scoped to that tenant's tables.
- **A person approves irreversible steps.** Dropping tables, deleting objects or wiping volumes require explicit human confirmation.

## Agentic lakehouse vs. a lakehouse with a chatbot

A chatbot over a lakehouse answers questions by generating SQL. An agentic lakehouse lets agents act: create and change pipelines, run them, check the results and operate the platform. Acting needs more than read access to tables. It needs a sandbox to write into, a checkable output format, policies that stop unsafe calls, and a record of what was done. Those are the parts that make a lakehouse agentic.

Agents that only answer questions still benefit from the same design: a semantic layer such as Spark metric views gives them governed metric definitions, so their answers match the dashboards.

## Build one

1. **Start on a laptop.** The lakehouse masterclass builds Iceberg tables in Unity Catalog OSS on SeaweedFS with Spark 4.3, then adds an SDP agent on Omnigent with a local Ollama model, MCP tools and policies.
2. **Give agents a sandbox.** Create a namespace the agent owns and grant it write access only there.
3. **Make the output declarative.** Have the agent write Spark Declarative Pipelines and gate every run on a passing dry run.
4. **Add policies and tracing.** Write policies for the checks you care about (API use, performance, scope) and trace every session.
5. **Move to a governed deployment.** Put each agent behind an identity-pinned Spark Connect endpoint and a catalog that authorizes every request, as in the governed AI agents reference architecture.

## Reference architectures

- https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/agentic-lakehouse: The whole picture on one board: Omnigent and MLflow over sandboxed Spark Connect sessions, on Iceberg and Unity Catalog.
- https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/governed-ai-agents: The production shape: PR-only agent output, dry runs in CI, identity-pinned Spark Connect and a governed Iceberg REST catalog.
- https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/multi-engine-catalog: One catalog that every engine and every agent tool reads, with credential vending.
- https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/policy-and-lineage: Access rules enforced inside each engine's plan, and lineage for every job.
- https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/semantic-layer: Governed metric definitions that agents query instead of inventing SQL.
- https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/ml-lifecycle: Tracing, evaluation and a model gateway for the models behind your agents.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is an agentic lakehouse?

An open data lakehouse built so AI agents can find, query and change data safely: open tables, a catalog that agents read for metadata and permissions, MCP tools, declarative pipelines the platform validates, policies on every tool call, and tracing and lineage of what agents did.

### Is an agentic lakehouse a product?

No. It is an architecture you assemble from open source projects: Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake for tables, Unity Catalog OSS, Apache Polaris or Lakekeeper for the catalog, Apache Spark and DuckDB for engines, MCP for tools, an agent harness such as Omnigent for policies, and MLflow and OpenLineage for tracing and lineage.

### How do AI agents access lakehouse data?

Through tools the agent can call, usually served over the Model Context Protocol, which in turn use the catalog to find tables and an engine to read or write them. The catalog decides what the agent's identity may access and can vend short-lived storage credentials scoped to specific tables.

### How do you stop an AI agent from damaging production data?

Let it write only to its own sandbox namespace, require declarative pipelines that pass a dry run, evaluate every tool call against policies that fail closed, give it specific tools instead of a shell, and require a person to approve irreversible operations. Table snapshots let you roll back a bad write.

### Which table format is best for an agentic lakehouse?

Any open table format with a catalog API works. Apache Iceberg is a strong default because the Iceberg REST catalog specification is implemented by many catalogs and read by many engines, so agent tools can use one interface everywhere. Delta Lake works the same way through Unity Catalog.

### Can I build an agentic lakehouse on a laptop?

Yes. The open source lakehouse masterclass runs Iceberg, Unity Catalog OSS, Spark 4.3, Kafka, Airflow and MLflow in Docker and adds an agent on Omnigent with a local Ollama model, MCP tools and policies.

## Sources
- [Lakehouse masterclass](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/lakehouse-masterclass)
- [Safe, governed AI data engineering on Apache Spark (paper)](https://open-lakehouse.github.io/safe-spark-agents-paper/)
- [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io)
- [Iceberg REST catalog specification](https://iceberg.apache.org/rest-catalog-spec/)
- [Spark Declarative Pipelines guide](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/declarative-pipelines-programming-guide.html)

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/agentic-data-engineering

# Agentic Data Engineering

> AI agents write, test and run pipelines; the platform decides what they may do

Agentic data engineering is the practice of having AI agents write, test, run and maintain data pipelines, with the platform rather than the agent's instructions deciding what each agent is allowed to do. The agent produces declarative pipeline code; the platform validates it with a dry run against the real catalog, limits the agent to its own namespace, checks every tool call against policies, and records traces and lineage. People set the goals, own the policies and review the changes that matter. Built on open source (Apache Spark Declarative Pipelines, Apache Iceberg, Unity Catalog OSS, the Model Context Protocol, an agent harness such as Omnigent, and MLflow), it works with any model, local or hosted.

## What changes when an agent writes the pipeline

When a person writes a pipeline, much of the checking happens in their head: which tables are production, which calls are expensive, when to try a sample first. An agent knows none of that unless something tells it, and something has to stop it when it ignores what it was told. The lakehouse masterclass organizes that something into a harness of three parts.

- **Declare.** The agent writes declarative pipelines (Spark Declarative Pipelines). spark-pipelines dry-run resolves every dataset and its inputs without writing data, and a pipeline that fails the dry run does not run.
- **Scope.** The agent works in its own place: one folder of pipeline files and one namespace in the catalog. It can read production tables but writes only its own.
- **Context.** The agent is given what it needs to know, pinned to the versions you run: the pipeline API of your Spark release, the layout of a spec file, the rules a pipeline file must follow.

## The four checks on an agent's pipeline

| Check | The question | How the platform answers it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| API | Does the pipeline use the framework correctly? | A dry run, required by a policy before any run |
| Performance | Does the work stay on the cluster? | A policy that asks a person before code pulls results onto one machine |
| Scope | Did it touch only its own tables? | Policies plus a sandbox namespace in the catalog |
| Correctness | Are the numbers right? | Comparison against trusted gold tables |

## How an agentic data engineering workflow runs

1. **A person sets the goal.** For example: build a daily revenue table from the orders stream.
2. **The agent proposes a declarative pipeline.** It writes pipeline files through named tools, not a shell, so every write is visible to policies.
3. **The platform dry-runs it.** Spark Declarative Pipelines resolves every dataset against the real catalog and reports structural errors before data is touched.
4. **Policies gate each call.** The harness allows, denies or asks a person about each tool call and result. Errors in a policy count as deny.
5. **Changes go through review.** In production, agent output arrives as a pull request; CI dry-runs it and a controller applies it after approval.
6. **Runs happen under the agent's identity.** The agent's Spark Connect session and the catalog's credential vending limit what the run can read and write.
7. **Results are evaluated and traced.** Outputs are compared with trusted tables, sessions are traced in MLflow, and OpenLineage records which tables were read and written.

## Evidence: declarative pipelines catch agent mistakes early

The safe-spark-agents study ran AI agents on the same data engineering tasks with declarative and imperative pipelines: 528 runs across 22 tasks, 12 seeds and 2 arms. The Spark Declarative Pipelines dry run caught 79 structural defects before any data was processed; the imperative arm caught none at that stage. Declarative output was 49% fewer lines, at about 2.3 times the tokens. After a swap of the agent's skill file, timezone defects went from 7 to 0.

## Tools, not a shell

Agents get their tools from an MCP server. Each tool does one thing with named arguments: list, read or write a file in the agent's pipeline folder, dry-run or run its pipeline, run one SQL statement. A policy can read write_pipeline_file(path="spark-pipeline.yml", content=...) exactly; it can only guess what an arbitrary shell command will do. Skills packaged for the lakehouse, such as lakehouse-agent-kit, give agents connection profiles instead of hardcoded endpoints.

## The open source agentic data engineering stack

| Need | Open source choice |
| --- | --- |
| Pipeline framework the platform can validate | Spark Declarative Pipelines (Apache Spark 4.1 and later) |
| Tables with snapshots and rollback | Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake |
| Catalog with permissions and credential vending | Unity Catalog OSS, Apache Polaris, Lakekeeper |
| Remote, identity-pinned engine access | Spark Connect |
| Agent tools | Model Context Protocol servers |
| Agent harness, policies and sandboxing | Omnigent |
| Local or self-hosted models | Ollama, vLLM |
| Tracing and evaluation | MLflow |
| Lineage | OpenLineage |
| Scheduling approved pipelines | Apache Airflow |

## Reference architectures

- https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/agentic-lakehouse: Where the agent runs, how it reaches Spark and what the catalog lets it touch.
- https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/governed-ai-agents: The reference architecture for agents building Spark pipelines in governed, multi-tenant sandboxes.
- https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/batch-medallion: The declarative medallion pipelines agents write, scheduled by Airflow.
- https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/change-data-capture: AUTO CDC flows: a declarative target an agent can produce and the platform can check.
- https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/laptop-open-lakehouse: A full stack on a laptop to give an agent something real to work against.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is agentic data engineering?

The practice of having AI agents write, test, run and maintain data pipelines while the platform enforces what they may do: declarative output validated by a dry run, a sandbox namespace, policies on every tool call, and traces and lineage of every action.

### Will AI agents replace data engineers?

In agentic data engineering, agents do the writing and running, and people set goals, design the platform, own the policies and review the changes that matter. The work moves from typing pipelines to defining what correct and safe mean and checking that agents meet it.

### Why should agents write declarative pipelines instead of scripts?

Because the platform can check declarative output before it runs. In the safe-spark-agents study, the Spark Declarative Pipelines dry run caught 79 structural defects before any data was processed, against none for imperative pipelines at that stage.

### What is an agent harness?

The software that runs an agent: it connects the model to tools, keeps session state, and enforces policies and sandboxing around every tool call. Omnigent is an open source harness that evaluates policies returning ALLOW, DENY or ASK before and after each tool runs.

### Do I need a frontier model for agentic data engineering?

No. The lakehouse masterclass runs its pipeline agent on a local open-weight model (qwen3:14b in Ollama with a 16K context window). Stronger models make fewer mistakes, which is why the harness checks their work rather than trusting it.

### How do I get started with agentic data engineering?

Build the open lakehouse on a laptop with the lakehouse masterclass, then follow its agentic data engineering chapter to add an agent with MCP tools and policies. Move to the governed AI agents reference architecture for multi-tenant production.

# Spark Masterclass

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/spark-masterclass
Book: https://open-lakehouse.github.io/spark-masterclass/
Repository: https://github.com/open-lakehouse/spark-masterclass

Spark Masterclass is a free, Apache-2.0-licensed online book that teaches Apache Spark 4.3 by running it. It has 92 chapters in 14 parts, from how Spark runs your code through Spark SQL, Spark Connect, file formats, performance, Structured Streaming, lakehouse tables, Spark Declarative Pipelines, machine learning, production operations, extension APIs and engine internals. Each chapter has the exact code that ran, pinned to pyspark 4.3.0, and the real output saved next to it, including the query plans Spark printed and the metrics the Spark UI reported. The examples use one month of public New York City taxi trip data and run on a laptop.

### What is Spark Masterclass?

Spark Masterclass is a free, open-source online book about Apache Spark 4.3. It explains how Spark plans and runs work, from DataFrames and SQL to Spark Connect, Structured Streaming, Spark Declarative Pipelines and engine internals, and it backs every technical result with runnable code and saved output.

### Which version of Apache Spark does Spark Masterclass cover?

Apache Spark 4.3. The example environment pins pyspark==4.3.0, so the plans and output in the book come from that release.

### What does Spark Masterclass cover?

92 chapters in 14 parts: Background, Getting started, DataFrames and the other APIs, Spark SQL, Spark Connect, Files, formats and data sources, Performance, Streaming, Lakehouse tables, Declarative Pipelines, Machine learning and applied algorithms, Running Spark in production, Extending Spark, and Internals.

### How are the examples in Spark Masterclass verified?

Each technical claim is tied to a script in the repository's code/ directory and to the output that script saved, including printed query plans and Spark UI metrics. A reader can run the same script and compare the result.

### Do I need a cluster or a managed platform to follow Spark Masterclass?

No. The examples are designed to run on a laptop with Python 3.11 or later, Java 17, 21 or 25, and uv. Some chapters need more, such as Docker for catalogs, Kafka or Kubernetes with kind, extra Maven packages, or an NVIDIA GPU; each chapter states its requirements at the start.

### Is Spark Masterclass free?

Yes. The book is free to read online and its text and code are licensed under the Apache License 2.0, the same license as Apache Spark. Corrections are accepted as GitHub issues or pull requests.

# Spark Matrix

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/spark-matrix/table

Spark Matrix is an open-source comparison of Apache Spark features across managed Spark platforms. For each managed runtime it records the Apache Spark release the vendor states the runtime is based on, then reports which Spark features that runtime has and what support level the vendor documents. Every cell is traced either to the Apache Spark source tree at a release tag or to a primary vendor statement with a quotation and URL. Where vendor documentation is silent or contradictory, the matrix records an open question instead of guessing.

## Support levels

- **Documented.** The vendor's documentation says the feature is supported on this runtime, with a quotation.
- **Ahead of Apache.** The vendor documents the feature on a runtime whose Apache Spark base does not have it yet (a backport or vendor build).
- **In the Apache base.** The runtime's Apache Spark version contains the feature, verified in Spark's source at that release. The vendor's documentation says nothing either way.
- **Partial.** The vendor documents limits, such as only some APIs, languages or sources.
- **Preview.** Documented as preview, beta or experimental on this runtime.
- **Off by default.** Available, but the vendor turns it off by default (for example ANSI mode).
- **Unsupported.** The vendor documents that the feature is not supported or not available.
- **Not in this Spark.** The runtime's Apache Spark version predates the feature, and the vendor documents no backport. The cell names the Apache release that added it.
- **Not documented.** A platform capability (table format, engine) that the vendor's documentation does not mention for this runtime.
- **Unknown.** The vendor does not state which Spark version the runtime is based on, and documents nothing about the feature.

## Platforms covered (data build 2026-11-23)

- **AWS:** Amazon EMR on EC2; Amazon EMR on EKS; Amazon EMR Serverless; AWS Glue (Spark jobs); Amazon Athena for Apache Spark
- **Microsoft:** Microsoft Fabric (Spark runtime); Azure Synapse Analytics Apache Spark pools; Azure HDInsight (Spark clusters); Azure HDInsight on AKS (Spark)
- **Databricks:** Databricks Runtime (classic compute); Databricks serverless compute for notebooks and jobs; Databricks SQL warehouses; Databricks Connect
- **Google Cloud:** Managed Service for Apache Spark clusters (formerly Dataproc on Compute Engine); Managed Service for Apache Spark serverless (formerly Google Cloud Serverless for Apache Spark / Dataproc Serverless); Managed Service for Apache Spark on GKE (formerly Dataproc on GKE); Spark in BigQuery Studio notebooks; BigQuery stored procedures for Apache Spark
- **Oracle:** OCI Data Flow
- **Cloudera:** Cloudera Data Engineering (Cloudera on cloud); Cloudera Data Engineering (Cloudera Data Services on premises); Cloudera Runtime (Cloudera Base on premises / Data Hub on cloud)
- **Snowflake:** Snowpark Connect for Spark
- **IBM:** IBM watsonx.data Spark engine (Premium Edition 2.4.x); IBM watsonx.data Gluten-accelerated Spark engine (Premium Edition 2.4.x); IBM Analytics Engine (serverless)
- **Alibaba Cloud:** Alibaba Cloud EMR Serverless Spark

## What each Apache Spark release line added

Spark 4.0, 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3 are not interchangeable. These tracked features first shipped in each release line:

- **Apache Spark 3.5:** Reattachable execution; Streaming over Connect; RocksDB changelog checkpointing; dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark; IDENTIFIER clause; Named function arguments; Sketch aggregates (HLL, Theta, KLL); Arrow-optimized Python UDFs; Python UDTFs; Python UDTFs over Connect; Spark Connect UI tab
- **Apache Spark 4.0:** Pure-Python client package (pyspark-client); Session release and cloning; Rich error details; Spark ML over Connect; MERGE INTO from the DataFrame API over Connect; checkpoint() and localCheckpoint() over Connect; Execute external commands; transformWithState (Scala/Java); transformWithState in Python; State data source (read state as a table); Python streaming data sources; ANSI SQL mode on by default; SQL scripting; SQL pipe syntax; Session variables; EXECUTE IMMEDIATE; Stored procedures (CALL); MERGE WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION; CLUSTER BY on tables; DESCRIBE ... AS JSON; VARIANT type; Variant shredding in Parquet; Collations; Python data source API; DataFrame.toArrow; Native DataFrame plotting; DataFrame.mergeInto; DataFrame.lateralJoin; SQL user-defined functions; Polymorphic Python UDTFs (analyze); TABLE arguments with PARTITION BY; applyInArrow / mapInArrow; Unified Python profiler; Built-in XML source; Structured (JSON) logging; Java 21 support; Java 17 minimum (Scala 2.13 only)
- **Apache Spark 4.1:** JDBC driver for Spark Connect; Compressed plans; Chunked Arrow results; transformWithState over Connect; Real-time mode; Spark Declarative Pipelines (SDP); spark-pipelines CLI; Pipelines Python API; Pipelines SQL (materialized views, streaming tables, flows); Append flows; Sinks; Temporary views; Dry run; Project scaffolding (spark-pipelines init); Full and selective refresh; Pipeline progress events; Recursive CTEs; Table constraints (PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK, UNIQUE); SQL scripting on by default; Colon path syntax for VARIANT; Default collation for schemas; approx_top_k; Theta and KLL sketches; TIME type; GEOMETRY and GEOGRAPHY types; Filter pushdown for Python data sources; Arrow UDFs (pyarrow-native); Arrow UDTFs; Arrow aggregate UDFs; Iterator-based applyInArrow / applyInPandas; @udf picks the vectorized path from type hints; Python worker logging; Unix domain sockets for Python workers; Traceback dumps for slow Python UDFs; Join pushdown to DSv2 sources; Checksum-based shuffle retry; Python 3.14 support
- **Apache Spark 4.2:** Operation status RPC; Full Catalog API over Connect; Connect tab in the History Server; Real-time mode in PySpark; Named streaming sources; Rate limits for Python streaming sources; Automatic state store snapshot repair; State store row checksums; Auto CDC flows (SCD Type 1); Cursors in SQL scripts; QUALIFY clause; Change data feed reads (CHANGES clause); SQL PATH name resolution; NEAREST BY top-K join; INSERT INTO ... - **Apache Spark 4.3:** REST API for sessions and operations; Reusable local Connect server; Stateful real-time mode; Auto CDC in SQL; Auto CDC with SCD Type 2 history; ASOF JOIN; JSON_TABLE; ANSI UNNEST; COMMENT ON COLUMN; @ time travel syntax; BIN BY relation operator; counter_diff window function; jaro_winkler_similarity; collect_union; VARIANT transformation functions; Nanosecond timestamps; Nanosecond TIME precision; DataFrame.zip; Python UDF transpilation (experimental); Pipelined Python UDF data transfer; Local variables in UDF tracebacks; Language-agnostic UDF worker protocol (experimental); DSv2 connector developer guide; Read files inside archives; Arrow-native Dataset caching; Shuffle-free single-task execution for small queries; Pipelined shuffle and concurrent stages; AQE converts sort-merge to shuffled hash joins; Content Security Policy on by default in the UI

- Apache Spark 4.3: 175 of 175 features
- Apache Spark 4.2: 146 of 175 features

- Apache Spark 3.5: 37 of 175 features
